If you ask what kind of special qualities it has: it is the heart of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all the Tathagatas; the deity who has become the essence. Therefore, this is not an issue, because at the very time of the fourth initiation, sentient beings who enter with sharp faculties will achieve the accomplishment of the Great Seal. For others, the instructions of the Great Seal should be shown.

Now, to actualize the meaning of the initiation, the divisions of the three channels will be taught via "Wisdom is the nature of Lalanā" and so forth. Lalanā is the left channel, the nature of the *Āli* <gloss>vowels</gloss> and the essence of Wisdom. Rasanā is the right channel, the nature of the *Kāli* <gloss>consonants</gloss> and the essence of Method. That which resides in the central region as the essence of their union is Avadhūtī. Lalanā is the Truth Body <term>dharmakaya</term>, Rasanā is the Enjoyment Body <term>sambhogakaya</term>, and Avadhūtī is the Emanation Body <term>nirmanakaya</term>. They correspond appropriately to Body, Speech, and Mind. From the non-dual union of the three circles and the three channels, Great Bliss will arise. When Great Bliss is realized, the distinctions of the four initiations, the moments, and the joys will also become known. Just as the order of the number of circles was established for the generation stage, it should be understood for the side of the initiations as well.

The "four noble truths" and so forth correspond to the four initiations in order: suffering is to be fully known, origin is to be abandoned, cessation is to be realized, and the path is to be meditated upon; this is the purification. B.text:
Through the complete ascertainment of the three <term>vajras</term> <gloss>indestructible realities of body, speech, and mind</gloss>, one realizes selflessness and thoroughly cuts through the delusions of worldly existence. When that very reality becomes one's own <term>mantra</term>, the means of excellence are easily found. For such a <term>vajra</term> holder, <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>spiritual accomplishment</gloss> resides in the very palm of their hand. This is what is taught in the passage beginning with those words.

Therefore, this is not just anything; because at the very time of the fourth empowerment, sentient beings with the sharpest faculties will achieve the accomplishment of <term>mahamudra</term> <gloss>the Great Seal</gloss>. For others, it is established that the pith instructions of the Great Seal should be shown.

Now, to further establish the meaning of empowerment through the passage beginning with "The nature of wisdom is <term>Lalana</term>," the divisions of the three <term>nadis</term> <gloss>subtle energy channels</gloss> will be shown:

<term>Lalana</term> is the left channel. It is the nature of the <term>ali</term> <gloss>the vowel series</gloss> and the essence of wisdom. 

<term>Rasana</term> is the right channel. It is the nature of the <term>kali</term> <gloss>the consonant series</gloss> and the essence of skillful means. 

That which exists in the central region as the essence of their union is the <term>Avadhuti</term>. 

<term>Lalana</term> is the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss>. <term>Rasana</term> is the <term>sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>enjoyment body</gloss>. <term>Avadhuti</term> is the <term>nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>. In the same way, they appropriately correspond to body, speech, and mind. 

From the non-dual union of the three <term>chakras</term> <gloss>energy centers</gloss> and the three channels, <term>mahasukha</term> <gloss>great bliss</gloss> arises. If great bliss is realized, then the four empowerments, the moments, and the divisions of joy will also be understood. Just as the numerical order of the centers was established for the generation stage, it should be understood similarly for the empowerment stage. 

Regarding the Four Noble Truths and so forth, they also correspond respectively to the four empowerments: 
1. Thoroughly knowing suffering. 
2. Abandoning the origin. 
3. Manifesting cessation. 
4. Meditating on the path. 
These are the purifications. 

Likewise, there are four realities. Regarding the reality of the self: "In short, the five aggregates are well known as the five Buddhas. The <term>vajra</term> sense sources themselves are the <term>mandala</term> of the <term>Vajradakinis</term>," as it was said. Regarding the reality of the deity and so forth, in the Hevajra... <note>The text cuts off mid-title or mid-sentence referring to the Hevajra Tantra</note>

A.text:
In the phrase "Blazing in the navel," the word "navel" refers to the middle, meaning the Avadhūtī between those two. "Burning" refers to the fire of great passion [burning] the five aggregates. "Locana and so forth" refers to earth and so forth. "Having burned" means burning the "I" and "mine." "The Hare-marked One drips Haṃ" means the wisdom of Great Bliss will arise. This will be explained:
"Co-emergent is not described by others,
It is not found anywhere else.
From the instruction on the Guru's timing,
One knows it oneself through merit."
This is also the explanation of the perfect gift.

*Caṇḍā* is Wisdom, the practice of the samadhis of the generation and completion stages. *Āli* is the mind which has the nature of great compassion. Therefore, emptiness and compassion are expressed by the term *Caṇḍālī*. The "navel" is the center of those two, characterized by the luminosity of the Great Seal. The "blazing of Inner Heat" there is the unsurpassed wisdom. If one asks what that does: "**The five Tathagatas**" and so forth is said—Akshobhya and the others, the lord of the mandala and the members of the mandala, and Locana and the others. "Burning" means without even a trace of ash remaining. Afterward, having burned them, "the Hare-marked One, Haṃ"—because there is nothing else other than the elaborations of "I" and "mine," one says "I am mind-only." 

If one asks what the burning does: "**The Hare-marked One drips**" is said. Therefore, having arisen from the samadhi of luminosity, the "Hare-marked One" who remains is Vajradhara. As it is said:
"The past and the future,
And the present are the three worlds themselves.
In that moment purified by luminosity,
One sees them all without exception."

Regarding the title "The Chapter on the Vajra Family": "Vajra" here is Hevajra. "Family" <term>kula</term> is the body. Alternatively, that which arises from it is the family. The chapter that makes that clear is "The Chapter on the Vajra Family."

B.text:
The phrase **blazing in the navel** refers to the word **navel** as the center, specifically the <term>avadhuti</term> <gloss>central channel</gloss> between the other channels. The phrase **being burned** refers to the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates of being</gloss> being consumed by the fire of great passion. The phrase **Locana and the others** refers to the elements such as earth and so forth. Regarding the phrase **having burned**, it means the burning away of the ego and the sense of "mine" <note>the fixation on a self and its possessions</note>.

The phrase **the moon-holder <term>Ham</term> drips** refers to the arising of the <term>jnana</term> <gloss>primordial wisdom</gloss> of great bliss. This is explained as follows:

->The innate is not described by others, and is found nowhere at all;<-
->Through the timing shown by the Guru, and through one's own merit, it is known.<-

This is an explanation of the perfect realization. <term>Canda</term> <gloss>the fierce one</gloss> is <term>prajna</term> <gloss>transcendent wisdom</gloss>, which practices the <term>samadhi</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> of the generation and completion stages. <term>Ali</term> is the mind characterized by great compassion. Therefore, emptiness and compassion are expressed by the term <term>Candali</term> <gloss>the fierce inner heat</gloss>.

The **navel** is their center, characterized by the <term>mahamudra</term> <gloss>Great Seal</gloss> of clear light. If one asks what is done there by the blazing of the <term>tummo</term> <gloss>inner heat</gloss> and the unsurpassed wisdom, the text says **the five Tathagatas** <gloss>Buddhas</gloss> and so forth. This includes Akshobhya and the others who are the lords of the mandala and the deities within the mandala, as well as Locana and the other consorts. **Burning** means they are consumed without even ash remaining.

Furthermore, the phrase **having burned, the moon-holder <term>Ham</term>** indicates that because there is nothing other than the mental proliferation of "self" and "mine," the "self" is realized as mind-only. If one asks what occurs through that burning, the text says **the moon-holder drips**. Therefore, the **moon-holder** is Vajradhara, who remains after arising from the meditative absorption of clear light. As it is said:

->The past, the future, and the present are the three worlds themselves;<-
->In that moment purified by clear light, they are all seen without exception.<-

Regarding the **Chapter on the Vajra Family**, **Vajra** here refers to Hevajra. **Family** <note>original: <term>kula</term></note> refers to the body. Alternatively, that which arises from it is the family. The chapter that makes this manifest is the Chapter on the Vajra Family. This is the commentary on the difficult points of the <term>Hevajra Tantra</term>.

<summary>This page explains the esoteric symbolism of the inner heat yoga within the Hevajra tradition, defining terms like Candali as the union of wisdom and compassion. It describes the transformation of the aggregates and the realization of the mind as clear light through the dripping of the syllable Ham.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra, Candali, inner heat, clear light, Vajradhara, five Tathagatas, avadhuti, mahamudra, prajna, compassion</keywords>

One should first recite **"Oṃ Hūṃ Svāhā"** one hundred thousand times for the preliminary retreat. Afterward, on an unbaked clay bowl, one should write the syllable *Paṃ* with soapstone. In its center, write: "Oṃ Hūṃ, paralyze <note>original: stambhaya</note> [name of person], Hūṃ Svāhā." Fill it with ashes from a cemetery and cover it with another unbaked clay bowl joined face-to-face. Upon it, draw a four-cornered Great Power Mandala <note>the mandala of the element Earth</note> adorned with vajras. Bury it underground and press it with the left foot. Remaining in the previously described meditative absorption, recite the mantra: "Oṃ Hūṃ Vajra, paralyze [name of person], Hūṃ Svāhā." If recited one hundred and eight times or one thousand times, they will be paralyzed.

Likewise, one should perform the yoga of Gaurī, saffron-colored, emerging perfectly from the syllable *I*. She holds a noose and a hook. One should meditate on the syllable *Aṃ*, like the color of a Bandhuka flower, in one's own heart. Recite the mantra **"Oṃ Aṃ Svāhā"** one hundred thousand times for the preliminary retreat. Then, meditate on the target <gloss>the person to be influenced</gloss> in front of oneself, red in color, without clothes, and with hair loosened. In her vulva, imagine the syllable *Oṃ* the color of fire. If the target is a man, imagine it in his heart. Imagine them melting and becoming intoxicated by the light of the syllable *Aṃ*. Recite: "Oṃ Aṃ Gaurī, bring [name of person] under my power <note>original: vashamanaya</note>, Haṃ Svāhā." Imagine binding them by the neck with the noose, piercing their heart with the hook, and drawing them perfectly until they arrive at your feet. If so meditated, they will certainly be brought under power.

Likewise, imagine the yogini Cauri, perfectly emerged from the syllable *Ī*, blue in color, making a mudra with the thumb and index finger. In the heart, upon a sun disc, imagine a blue syllable *Khaṃ*. For the preliminary retreat, recite "Oṃ Khaṃ Svāhā" one hundred thousand times. Imagine the target without clothes, hair disheveled, riding a blue camel. Imagine them facing south, fleeing while being chased by a person swinging a club in a state of agitation. Recite the mantra: "Oṃ A Khaṃ Vira Yogini, expel <note>original: uccataya</note> [name of person], Khaṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ." Within seven days, they will certainly be expelled.

Likewise, meditate on the yoga of Vajra-Dakini from the syllable *U*...

Afterward, on an unbaked clay vessel, write the syllable <term>Pam</term> using <term>steatite</term> <gloss>soapstone or magnesium silicate</gloss>. In the center of that, write <term>Om Hum Devadatta Stambhaya Hum Svaha</term> <note>Devadatta is a placeholder for the name of the target person to be paralyzed</note>. Fill the vessel with ashes from a cemetery and cover it with another unbaked clay vessel to form a joined pair. Upon this, draw a four-cornered mandala of the Great Powerful One <note>likely referring to Mahabala or a form of Hayagriva</note> beautifully adorned with <term>vajras</term> <gloss>ritual scepters or diamond-bolts</gloss>. Place this underground and press down upon it with your left foot. While remaining in the meditative absorption described previously, recite the mantra. If you recite <term>Om Hum Vajra Devadatta Stambhaya Hum Svaha</term> one hundred and eight or one thousand times, the person will be paralyzed.

Likewise, through the complete transformation of the syllable <term>I</term>, perform the yoga of the White Goddess <note>Gauri</note> who is the color of saffron and holds a noose and a hook. Meditate on the syllable <term>Am</term>, which is the color of a <term>bandhuka</term> flower <gloss>a bright red flower, Pentapetes phoenicea</gloss>, in your own heart. Recite the mantra <term>Om Am Svaha</term> one hundred thousand times for the preliminary service. Then, visualize the target person in front of you, red in color, naked, and with loose hair. Visualize a fire-colored syllable <term>Om</term> in her <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>vulva</gloss>. Alternatively, if it is a man, visualize it in his heart. Think that the person melts and becomes intoxicated by the light of the syllable <term>Am</term>. Recite <term>Om Am Gauri [Name] Me Vashamanaya Ham Svaha</term>. Visualize that the person is bound by the throat with a noose, pierced through the heart with a hook, and pulled completely until they arrive at your feet. If you do this, they will certainly be brought under your power.

Likewise, through the complete transformation of the syllable <term>I</term>, visualize the Water Goddess Yogini. She is blue in color and makes a hand gesture with the thumb and forefinger. In your heart, visualize a blue syllable <term>Kham</term> upon a sun disk. For the preliminary service, recite <term>Om Kham Svaha</term> one hundred thousand times. Visualize the target person naked, with disheveled hair, riding a blue camel. Visualize them facing south, agitated, and fleeing as they are struck with a stick. Recite the mantra: <term>Om A Kham Vira Yogini [Name] Ucchataya Kham Hum Hum Hum Phat</term>. Within seven days, they will certainly be expelled. Likewise, from the syllable <term>U</term> comes the Vajra Dakini <unclear>...</unclear>

Therefore, next the Chapter on Signs is taught, and in this chapter which clarifies signs, it is said: Brother refers to the male yogi. Sister refers to the female yogini. Showing a silk scarf refers to showing the manner of tying a silk scarf with those two fingers. Three points means the little finger is pressed by the thumb while the remaining three are extended like three points. The boundary refers to the boundary of the crown of the head. The wheel refers to showing the manner of the wheel. Frowning is the movement of the eyebrows. Loosening the topknot and so forth is the explanation of the literal meaning. Regarding: One finger points, and so forth; whatever it is, one finger refers to the index finger, or the index and middle fingers together pointing to the lotus of wisdom—this should be the prompting. Regarding: In the gesture of illness, and so forth; the gesture of illness is the accomplishment of the sphere of phenomena <term>dharmadhatu</term> which is the ultimate bliss; one knows those. If one asks what that is like: By grasping the left thumb, and so forth is said. Left refers to wisdom, which is the interior of her lotus. The practicing <term>yogi</term> <gloss>practitioner of yoga</gloss> must not become intoxicated. Because delusion becomes primary, it creates a great obstacle to yoga. This is how one should train. This concludes the commentary on the sixth chapter, the Chapter on Conduct, from the <term>Hevajra Panjika Ratnamala</term> <gloss>The Precious Garland: A Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Hevajra Tantra</gloss>.

The <term>samaya</term> <gloss>symbolic signs</gloss> are the language of the <term>mleccha</term> <gloss>barbarians</gloss> through which the <term>yoginis</term> <gloss>female practitioners</gloss> indicate their realization. One should understand this as the supreme method itself. Therefore, the Chapter on Signs and so forth is taught. Regarding the chapter that clarifies the signs, it says the following. A brother is a <term>yogi</term>. A sister is a <term>yogini</term>. The phrase "one finger" refers to the forefinger; it means "Has he come?" The phrase "which one" means "Which one should be looked at?" The phrase "with two" refers to the forefinger and the middle finger together. "Showing the silk scarf" refers to the manner of binding a silk scarf with those two fingers. "Three points" refers to pressing the little finger with the thumb and extending the remaining three in the manner of three points. "The boundary" refers to the boundary of the crown of the head. "The wheel" shows the manner of a wheel. "Frowning" is the movement of the eyebrows. The explanation of "loosening the topknot" and so forth belongs to the interpretable meaning.

Regarding the phrase "showing one finger" and so forth: any mention of one finger refers to using the forefinger, or the middle and forefingers, to point to the <term>padma</term> <gloss>lotus/consort</gloss> of <term>prajna</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss> to stir it. Regarding "that itself is the 'well-come' <note>original: "svagata"</note>," the term "well" refers to the fluid <note>seminal essence</note>, meaning it was brought down through the union of the fingers. Regarding the "mudra of illness" and so forth: the <term>mudra</term> <gloss>hand gesture</gloss> of illness is the accomplishment of the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss>, which is the ultimate limit of bliss; these are to be known. If one asks what that is like, it is said: "From grasping the left thumb" and so forth. "Left" refers to <term>prajna</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss>, specifically the interior of her lotus. The "thumb" is the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>diamond/phallus</gloss>; when it reaches the state of emission, it is to be pressed. Regarding the "ring finger" and so forth: the ring finger is the primordial wisdom of <term>prajna</term>.

<summary>This page concludes the sixth chapter on conduct and begins the commentary on symbolic hand gestures and secret signs used between yogis and yoginis. It provides specific tantric decodings for physical gestures, interpreting them as metaphors for the union of wisdom and method.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, Ratnamala, yogi, yogini, symbolic signs, mudra, prajna, lotus, vajra, tantric conduct</keywords>

A.text: Regarding: Wisdom; this is the <term>vajra</term>. Regarding: Meditate; this is the entry. These three are the beginning, and the two "co-emergents" are the end; meditation should be performed between these two. The act of resting in equanimity is called "meditative attainment" <term>samapatti</term>. The bliss arising from meditating on and generating that is "by its bliss." What is called the "wheel" is to be called the "wheel of <term>yoginis</term>"; because that very great bliss gathers them together. If one asks what that bliss is like, the text says: As is appropriate. "Self-awareness" <term>svasamvedana</term> means the essence of knowing for oneself without depending on other conditions. That very self-awareness is enlightenment <term>bodhi</term>; the mind that is the nature of enlightenment is called the "mind of enlightenment" <term>bodhicitta</term>. The word "activity" is for the sake of inclusion. Because it makes the body persist, it is called "deity." Regarding: How it arises; it arises just as the object is; without depending on the perceived or the perceiver, just as it occurs. The "fluid" <term>shukra</term> <gloss>semen/nectar</gloss> is the form of the fluid like a jasmine flower <term>kunda</term> or the moon. Why is it so? Because: The co-emergent is of two kinds. There are two kinds of co-emergent joy. If that is the co-emergent, then what are "man" and "woman"? The text says: First, the consort, and so forth. Regarding: In these; there are seven, and two kinds of joy. If one asks what they are like: Relative and ultimate; the essence of great bliss is the ultimate. That which arises just as it is is the relative, because it possesses a mere portion of relativity. Regarding: For that very reason; this means "because of the two kinds." Regarding: Of the four; this means "of the four kinds." Regarding: Classification; this is by the general classification of the co-emergent. If it were otherwise, would one not assert four joys? If one asks how asserting it differently here is not contradictory, the text says: Thus the co-emergent, and so forth. It will arise through the sequence of the four—joy, supreme joy, and so forth; this is the side of the generation stage.

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
The lotus <note>referring to the female generative organ in tantric symbolism</note>. Wisdom <note>original: "prajñā"</note> refers to the vajra <note>referring to the male organ or the indestructible nature of reality</note>. Meditation <note>original: "bhāvanā"</note> refers to the application or entry into practice. These three are present at the beginning, while the two forms of the co-emergent <note>original: "sahaja"</note> are at the end. That which is to be meditated upon exists between these two. The act of meditative absorption is called equipoise <note>original: "samāpatti"</note>. The bliss arising from the cultivation and generation of that state is called "by its bliss."

The term "circle" <note>original: "cakra"</note> refers to what is called the circle of the Yogini, because all these elements are gathered within that very Great Bliss <note>original: "mahāsukha"</note>. If one asks what that bliss is like, it is described as "just as it is appropriate." This means self-awareness <note>original: "svasaṃvedana"</note>, which is the essence of knowing by oneself without depending on external conditions. That very self-awareness is awakening <note>original: "bodhi"</note>. The mind that has the nature of awakening is called the Mind of Awakening <note>original: "bodhicitta"</note>. The word "action" <note>original: "kriyā"</note> has the sense of gathering or collecting. Because it causes the body to remain, that itself is called the "deity" <note>original: "deva"</note>.

The phrase "how it arises" refers to arising according to the actual nature of reality; it arises without depending on a subject to grasp or an object to be grasped. Semen <note>original: "kunda"</note> refers to the form of the fluid which is like the jasmine flower or the moon. Why is it so? It is said, "The co-emergent is of two types," meaning there are two types of co-emergent joy.

If the co-emergent is like that, one might ask what are the "man" and "woman"? The text says, "The consort," and so forth. Regarding "among these," there are seven, which are the two types of joy. If one asks what they are, they are the relative and the ultimate. The essence of Great Bliss is the ultimate <note>original: "paramārtha"</note>. That which arises according to appearances is the relative <note>original: "saṃvṛti"</note>, because it possesses a mere portion of the relative itself. For that very reason, it is said "of the two types." The word "of the four" refers to the four types. "The distinction" refers to the general distinction of the co-emergent. 

If one objects, "Is it not elsewhere asserted that there are four joys? How is this different assertion not contradictory?" The text explains, "Thus, the co-emergent," and so forth. It means they arise through the sequence of the four, such as joy <note>original: "ānanda"</note> and supreme joy <note>original: "paramānanda"</note>, from the perspective of the generation stage <note>original: "utpattikrama"</note>.

<summary>This page provides a technical commentary on tantric terminology, defining the symbolic meanings of the lotus, vajra, and the two types of co-emergent joy within the context of the generation stage. It clarifies the relationship between relative and ultimate bliss and the role of self-awareness in achieving awakening.</summary>
<keywords>co-emergent, sahaja, Great Bliss, mahāsukha, Bodhicitta, self-awareness, svasaṃvedana, generation stage, four joys, yogini cakra</keywords>

The "six faculties" are the eyes and so forth that reside in the body. "Stable and moving" refers to external things that possess mind and those that are without mind. "I am indeed" means not only am I <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>Vajra-Holder</gloss>, whose nature is great bliss, but also <note>all things</note>. "Equally in equality" means in an indivisible essence.

If you ask "What is that like?", "By meditating on thatness" was spoken. The explanation for this is "equal taste." Again, the explanation for this is "equal" and so forth. "Equal" means the meaning of becoming the same. "That" refers to the low, the middling, and so forth. "Taste" means essence, which is a synonym for "thing." If you ask "What is the taste?", it means the co-emergent characterized by great bliss upon the wheel. To show the condensed meaning, it says: "Meditation is the equality of single taste."

Again, if you ask "How should the equality of single taste be meditated upon?", "From me" and so forth was spoken. "The yogi, knowing thus" means having held it with certainty in that way. "Highly composed" means in all states. To clarify that very point, "eating and drinking" and so forth was spoken. "By nature" means engaging by its own nature. Regarding "<term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>Great Seal</gloss>" and so forth, it means "In order to accomplish the Great Seal." This teaches the yoga of great devotion.

Now, to show the mind in this very context, "All beings will become meditation" and so forth was spoken. "All beings" refers to sentient beings and the vessel-like world; it means they arise from meditating on all of them. If you ask "Why?", it says "By the mind," meaning by the consciousness that possesses conceptual thought. If it is asked: "If one does not analyze, will it not also not become meditation?", "All phenomena" and so forth was spoken. This means that fully knowing the essence of the co-emergent

B.text:
The six faculties are the eyes and so forth that reside in the body. The terms <term>stable</term> <gloss>stationary or inanimate</gloss> and <term>moving</term> <gloss>mobile or animate</gloss> refer to external things that either possess or lack a mind. Regarding the phrase "I myself am," this means that not only am I the Vajradhara <gloss>Holder of the Scepter</gloss> whose nature is uniquely Great Bliss, but that I encompass all.

The phrase "equal in sameness" refers to the essence of indivisibility. If one asks how that is so, the text says, "by meditating on that reality." The explanation for this is called <term>equal taste</term> <gloss>sameness of experience</gloss>. Furthermore, the explanation for this is "equality" and so forth, where "equality" means the state of becoming identical. The word "that" refers to things that are inferior, middling, and so on. The word "taste" refers to the essence, which is a synonym for "entity" or "thing." If one asks what that "taste" is, it refers to the innate nature characterized by Great Bliss atop the <term>cakras</term> <gloss>energy centers</gloss>. In order to show the summarized meaning, it is said: "The meditation is the equality of a single taste."

Furthermore, if one asks how to meditate on the equality of a single taste, the text says "from me" and so forth. The phrase "the practitioner knowing thus" means having understood this with certainty. "Extremely composed" <gloss>meditative equipoise</gloss> means remaining in that state at all times. To clarify that very point, the text mentions "eating and drinking" and so forth. The phrase "by nature" means engaging according to one's own natural disposition. Regarding "Mahamudra" <gloss>The Great Seal</gloss> and so forth, it means "for the sake of accomplishing the Great Seal." This demonstrates the yoga of superior devotion.

Now, in order to show the mind within this very context, the text says "all beings will be meditated upon" and so forth. "All beings" refers to sentient beings and the vessel-like world <gloss>the external environment</gloss>; all of these arise precisely from meditation. If one asks why, it is said "by the mind," meaning by the consciousness that possesses conceptual thought. If one objects that if things are not investigated, they cannot be meditated upon, the text says "all phenomena" and so forth. This means thoroughly knowing the innate essence.

<summary>This page provides a commentary on the nature of Great Bliss and the yoga of Mahamudra, explaining that all animate and inanimate phenomena share a single essence or taste. It emphasizes that the practitioner should maintain meditative equipoise during all activities, including eating and drinking, to realize the indivisibility of the mind and the world.</summary>
<keywords>Great Bliss, Vajradhara, equal taste, Mahamudra, meditative equipoise, innate essence, six faculties, conceptual thought</keywords>

Regarding "Passion" and so forth, it refers to passion and so on. "The ground of all those" is this state of self-awareness that is to be meditated upon. "Even the sixteenth part" means being unable to be impaired. 

Now, to show the nature of self-awareness, "Born from the source of phenomena" <note>original: "dharmodaya"</note> and so forth was spoken. "Phenomena" <gloss>dharma</gloss> refers to the noble qualities. Because they arise from this, it is called the "source of phenomena," which is the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss>. Here, as it is shown as its seal, the lotus of the consort is called the "source of phenomena." It is through the power of devotion to that. Because the arising from that exists in this, it is called "born from the source of phenomena," which is primordial wisdom.

If you ask "What is it like?", it is "Equal to space," meaning it has the nature of space. "Method" is the path. That is also explained and shown in many ways. Even for the meditation on just the co-emergent itself in the context of the completion stage, it is through many methods.

If it is asked: "How will one obtain the level of Great <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>Vajra-Holder</gloss> by this?", "The three worlds" and so forth was spoken. Because the secrets of the body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times are each immeasurable, they are called the "three worlds." The gathering of those is called the "three worlds," which is Great <term>Vajradhara</term>; he is born from that. Therefore, that primordial wisdom should be meditated upon. 

If you ask "What is its essence?", "From the nature of method and wisdom" was spoken. The distinguished primordial wisdom is wisdom, which is the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss>. Method is the method of acting for the benefit of beings. The cause-conforming results of those are the two—the <term>sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>enjoyment body</gloss> and <term>nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>. Their very nature means they are "born from their nature." 

If you ask "How are they born from their nature?", "Of the fluid" and so forth was spoken. By "the Blessed One," the method comprised of the two bodies is spoken. "Its bliss" refers to that primordial wisdom equal to space, which

B.text:
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it refers to desire and the other afflictions. "That which is the abode of all" refers to the cultivation of the level of self-knowing awareness. The phrase "even all sixteen parts" means that they are incapable of being diminished. Now, in order to demonstrate the nature of self-knowing awareness, it is said "born from the source of phenomena" <term>dharmodaya</term> <gloss>source of phenomena</gloss> and so forth.

"Phenomena" <term>dharma</term> refers to the qualities of the noble ones. Because these arise from this, it is called the "source of phenomena," which is the sphere of reality <term>dharmadhātu</term>. In this context, shown as its seal <term>mudrā</term>, the lotus of the consort is called the "source of phenomena." This is by the power of devotion to that. Since that which arises from it exists here, it is called "born from the source of phenomena," which is primordial wisdom <term>jñāna</term>.

If one asks what that is like, it is "equal to space," meaning it has the nature of space. "Method" <term>upāya</term> is the path. Furthermore, it is explained and shown in many ways. Regarding the side of the completion stage <term>sampannakrama</term>, even the cultivation of only the innate <term>sahaja</term> itself is accomplished through many methods.

If one asks how the level of the Great Vajra Holder <term>Mahāvajradhara</term> is obtained through this, it is said, "the three worlds" and so forth. Because the secrets of the body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times are each immeasurable, they are called the "three worlds." The synthesis of these is the "three worlds," the Great Vajra Holder, who is born from that. Therefore, one should cultivate that primordial wisdom.

What is its essence? It is said, "From the nature of method and wisdom." Distinguished primordial wisdom is wisdom <term>prajñā</term>, which is the truth body <term>dharmakāya</term>. Method is the means of acting for the benefit of beings. The results that correspond to the causes of these are the two: the enjoyment body <term>sambhogakāya</term> and the emanation body <term>nirmāṇakāya</term>. To be "born from their nature" means the very nature of those bodies.

If one asks how it is born from their nature, it is said, "from the vital essence" <term>śukra</term> and so forth. By the term "Blessed One" <term>Bhagavān</term>, the method comprised of the two <note>form</note> bodies is taught. "His bliss" refers to that very primordial wisdom which is equal to space.

<summary>This page explains the tantric concept of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) as both a metaphysical reality and a physical seal, identifying it as the origin of primordial wisdom. It defines the relationship between method and wisdom in achieving the state of Vajradhara and the three bodies of a Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>dharmodaya, jñāna, Vajradhara, dharmakāya, sambhogakāya, nirmāṇakāya, prajñā, upāya, completion stage, innate bliss</keywords>

A.text:
knowing the past, future, and present minds of oneself and others. Regarding "The higher realms and the human world" and so forth, "single form" means having a single nature. The meaning of "the parts of self and others" and so forth has already been shown.

To show the distinguished <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>Joyous Vajra</gloss> from other scriptures, "Knowing all the Vedas" and so forth was spoken. The "Vedas" are the Rig Veda, Atharva Veda, Sama Veda, and Yajur Veda <note>original: "nges brjod, srid srung, snyan dngags, mchod sbyin"</note>. "Philosophical tenets" refers to the views of the non-Buddhists such as the Jainas <note>original: "rnying ba"</note> and so forth, and the sutras of the Shravaka <gloss>Hearer</gloss> pitakas and so forth, because one acts as the end of rebirth through these. "Extensive rituals" refers to the Action Tantras and so forth. The accomplishment characterized as explained in these does not exist. 

If it is asked "Does it exist in the Paramitayana <gloss>Perfection Vehicle</gloss> or not?", "Existence will be purified" and so forth was spoken. "Purified" means it exhausts the obscurations of mental afflictions and the knowable; it is the path characterized by the six perfections. Through that purification, enlightenment will be obtained; however, "at the end of existence" means after three immeasurable eons, passing from one birth to another.

If it is asked "If obtaining enlightenment in this life is also spoken of in the Yoga Tantras, what makes this superior?", "Even without that" and so forth was spoken. If "that"—the co-emergent characterized by self-awareness—is absent, it is not spoken that there is accomplishment in this life or in other lives. 

"Then what is the difference between that and this?", "He who does not know Hevajra" and so forth was spoken. This is because other tantras merely teach the co-emergent, while this Hevajra speaks of the fully clear aspect. Therefore, it is very clearly shown that for whoever does not know Hevajra, the hardship of hearing, reflecting, and meditating becomes meaningless.

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page: this text continues a discussion on the cognitive powers of a practitioner and the superiority of the Hevajra Tantra.</meta>

One knows the minds of oneself and others in the past, future, and present. Regarding the phrase "the realms of higher beings and the human world" <note>original: mtho ris mi yul</note> and so forth: "single form" refers to being of a single nature. The meaning of "the parts of oneself and others" has already been explained.

In order to demonstrate how the <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>The Joyful Vajra</gloss> is more distinguished than other scriptures, the text says, "the knower of all <term>Vedas</term> <gloss>Knowledge/Ancient Indian scriptures</gloss>," and so forth. The Vedas are the <term>Rig Veda</term> <gloss>hymns of praise</gloss>, the <term>Atharva Veda</term> <gloss>protection from existence</gloss>, the <term>Sama Veda</term> <gloss>chants</gloss>, and the <term>Yajur Veda</term> <gloss>sacrificial formulas</gloss>. <note>The Tibetan text uses descriptive names for the four Vedas: nges brjod, srid srung, snyan dngags, and mchod sbyin.</note>

"Tenets" <note>original: grub mtha'</note> refers to the views of the <term>Tirthikas</term> <gloss>non-Buddhist extremists</gloss> such as the <term>Vaisheshika</term> <gloss>Ancient school of atomism</gloss>, and the discourses <note>original: mdo sde</note> of the <term>Shravaka</term> <gloss>Hearer/Foundational vehicle</gloss> collections. These are called tenets because they serve to bring one to the "end of rebirth" <note>original: yang srid kྱི་ mtha'</note>. "Extensive rituals" refers to the <term>Kriya Tantra</term> <gloss>Action Tantra</gloss> and similar classes. Accomplishments <note>original: dngos grub; Sanskrit: siddhi</note> characterized by what is explained in these systems do not exist <note>meaning they do not lead to ultimate realization</note>.

One might ask: does such accomplishment exist in the <term>Paramitayana</term> <gloss>Vehicle of Perfection</gloss> or not? The text says, "existence will be purified," and so forth. It is "purified" because it exhausts the afflictions and the obscurations to knowledge. This refers to the path characterized by the six perfections. Through that purity, enlightenment will be attained; however, the phrase "at the end of existence" means it is attained by passing from one birth to another throughout three immeasurable eons.

If one then asks: "Since the <term>Yoga Tantras</term> also state that enlightenment is attained in this very life, how is this <note>the Hevajra system</note> superior?" The text says, "without that," and so forth. "That" refers to the <term>Sahaja</term> <gloss>Co-emergent/Innate</gloss> nature, characterized by self-knowing awareness. Without this, it is not taught that accomplishment exists in either this life or other lives.

If one then asks: "What is the difference between that system and this one?" The text says, "one who does not know the <term>Hevajra</term>," and so forth. Other tantras merely point toward the Innate, but this Hevajra Tantra explains it in a completely clear and vivid manner. Therefore, it is shown very clearly that for one who does not know the Hevajra, the hardships of hearing, contemplating, and meditating will be meaningless. <summary>The text explains the superiority of the Hevajra Tantra over the Vedas, foundational Buddhist vehicles, and other Tantra classes by emphasizing its unique, vivid presentation of the Innate nature.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, Vedas, Sahaja, Innate, Paramitayana, Yoga Tantra, Enlightenment, Tenets</keywords>

A.text:
The purification of the arms was spoken. The thatness of the sixteen arms is the sixteen types of emptiness. These are: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, ultimate emptiness, 
conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, emptiness beyond extremes, emptiness without beginning or end, emptiness without rejection, natural emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, 
emptiness of non-existence, and the emptiness of the essence of non-existence. These themselves are represented as the arms. The legs are the purification of having conquered the demons, namely: the demon of the aggregates, the demon of afflictions, the demon of the Lord of Death, and the demon of the son of the gods <note>The four maras or obstacles to enlightenment</note>. "Faces" 
refers to the actual faces of the deity. Regarding "The three vajras," these are the Vajra Body, Vajra Speech, and Vajra Mind. By "The earth is..." and so forth, the purification of the earth and the other elements is shown, meaning the goddesses Pukkasi and so forth. Regarding "By this..." and so forth, "Aggregates" 
refers to the aggregates and so on. Thus, having shown the purification from the perspective of the generation stage, in order to show the purification of the single taste of thatness from the perspective of the completion stage, "By whichever..." and so forth was spoken. By whatever things like form and so forth the 
world becomes bound, by those very things the self should be liberated. One should not even perform the meditation on the form of the deity. If it is asked, "If one is liberated by those very things, how is it that people in the world are bound?", because the people of the world are deluded, they have 
clinging toward this very thing as being real and thus do not know thatness; they have not realized the unborn thatness of those things. Regarding "Discarding that," it means being devoid of the meditation on the unborn. "Siddhi" <gloss>attainment</gloss> is the state of Vajradhara; the intent is that it will not be obtained.

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
The purification of the hands is described. The reality of the sixteen hands is the sixteen types of emptiness. These are: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness, the emptiness of greatness, the emptiness of emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the emptiness of that which transcends limits, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of that which is not to be discarded, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-entities, and the emptiness of the essence of non-entities. These very things are represented as the hands.

The feet represent the purification that overcomes the <term>maras</term> <gloss>demonic obstructions or influencers</gloss>. These are the <term>mara</term> of the aggregates, the <term>mara</term> of afflictive emotions, the <term>mara</term> of the Lord of Death, and the <term>mara</term> of the son of a god.

The term "faces" refers to the literal faces of the deity. The term "three vajras" refers to the <term>vajra</term> body, <term>vajra</term> speech, and <term>vajra</term> mind. By the phrase "the earth is," and so forth, the purification of elements such as earth is shown; this refers to <term>Pukkasi</term> <gloss>a female deity representing the earth element</gloss> and the others. Regarding the phrase "by this," and so forth, "aggregates" refers to the five aggregates and the rest.

In that way, having briefly shown the purification from the perspective of the generation stage <note>Tibetan: bskyed rim; the yoga of visualizing oneself as a deity</note>, the text then presents the purification of the single taste of reality from the perspective of the completion stage <note>Tibetan: rdzogs rim; the yoga of internal energy and subtle channels</note>. It says, "by whichever and whichever," and so forth. Those very things such as form, by which the world is bound, are the very means by which one should liberate oneself. One should not even perform the meditation on the appearance of the deity <note>at this advanced stage of completion</note>.

If one asks: if liberation comes through those very things, then how is it that people in the world are bound by them? It is because worldly beings are deluded; they are ignorant of reality because they cling to these things as being true in themselves. They have not realized the unborn reality of these things. The phrase "abandoning that very thing" means being devoid of the meditation on the unborn. It is intended that "attainment," which is the state of the <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>the Holder of the Thunderbolt, representing supreme enlightenment</gloss>, will not be found <note>by those who cling to dualistic appearances</note>.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic purification of a deity's sixteen hands as the sixteen types of emptiness and the feet as the conquest of the four maras. It transitions from the symbolic generation stage to the completion stage, emphasizing that the same sensory objects that bind the ignorant can liberate the wise.</summary>
<keywords>sixteen types of emptiness, four maras, generation stage, completion stage, Vajradhara, purification, tantric symbolism</keywords>

A.text:
<meta>continues from the previous page: ...as indicated by the syllables</meta> *om ah hum phat svaha*. The phrase "offering and making requests" refers to the Guru. "In the same way as it was explained" refers to sources such as the *Compendium of Reality* <note>original: *Tattvasamgraha*</note> and others. "Vajrasattva" <note>Adamantine Being</note> here refers to Hevajra. The word "afterwards" means immediately following the empowerment. "Completely pure" means the stains of cyclic existence <term>samsara</term> have been purified. "One who possesses the form of wisdom" <note>original: *jnanamurti*</note> refers to an equality with the wisdom of the omniscient one.

Regarding the phrase "cyclic existence and complete purification": this refers to that wisdom in which there is not even the slightest difference between existence and nirvana. This is the "surpassing" state, with the intended meaning being that it is utterly beyond all conceptual elaboration. This very point will be clearly demonstrated by the two verses beginning with "in supreme joy."

"Supreme joy" <term>paramananda</term> is the supreme transcendent wisdom; it is the wisdom characterized by clear light. "There is no meditation there" means there is not even a single thing to be meditated upon. The "meditator" is the mind, and that too does not exist. "Body" is the physical body. "Objects" are the things that appear. "Subjective perceivers" are the eyes and the other senses. Likewise, flesh, blood, and so forth also do not exist. Having thus established that the obscuration of disturbing emotions does not exist, the text says "there is no seeing" and so forth to show that the obscuration to knowledge also does not exist. This means that external objects such as things to be seen also do not exist.

In the phrase "without waves," "waves" refers to conceptual thoughts. When these are exhausted, it is "without waves." "Manifold" refers to appearing in various different forms. When those are absent, it is "without the manifold." The phrase "this was said" refers to these words spoken by the Bhagavan <gloss>Blessed Lord</gloss>. "Requested" refers to the questions asked by Vajragarbha. As for what meaning was requested, the text says "for what reason" and so forth. The intended meaning is this: by its very nature, the co-emergent essence is completely pure.

<summary>This page provides a technical commentary on the nature of Vajrasattva and the state of non-dual wisdom, explaining that in the ultimate state of supreme joy, both the objects of meditation and the meditator's mind are non-existent. It defines key terms related to the purification of cyclic existence and the cessation of conceptual thought.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrasattva, Hevajra, supreme joy, paramananda, clear light, non-duality, emptiness of subject and object, Vajragarbha, co-emergent, Sahaja</keywords>

B.text:
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Hevajra Tantra, specifically focusing on the meaning of the mantra and the nature of ultimate reality in the context of empowerment.</meta>

The mantra is **Om Ah Hum Phat Svaha**. The phrase "offering and making requests" refers to the teacher. The phrase "in the same way as explained" refers to the *Compendium of Reality* <note>original: Tattvasamgraha</note> and other similar texts. "Vajrasattva" <gloss>the Adamantine Being</gloss> here refers to **Hevajra**. The phrase "afterward" means immediately following the empowerment. "Completely pure" means being purified of the stains of cyclic existence <term>samsara</term>. "Having the form of wisdom" means being equal to the wisdom of the All-Knowing One.

Regarding the phrase "cyclic existence and complete purification": This refers to that wisdom in which there is not even the slightest distinction between existence <term>samsara</term> and liberation <term>nirvana</term>. It is said to be "surpassing" because it is completely beyond all conceptual elaboration <term>prapancha</term>. 

This very point will be clearly demonstrated by the two verses beginning with "in supreme joy." "Supreme joy" is the highest transcendent wisdom <term>prajna</term>, which is the wisdom characterized by clear light. 

The phrase "there is no meditation" means there is not even the slightest thing to be meditated upon. The "meditator" is the mind, and that too does not exist. "Body" refers to the physical body. "The apprehended" refers to the objects that appear. "The apprehender" refers to the eyes and the other sense faculties. Similarly, flesh, blood, and so forth also do not exist. 

Having established that the obscuration of disturbing emotions <term>klesha-avarana</term> does not exist in this way, in order to show that the obscuration to knowledge <term>jneyavarana</term> also does not exist, the text says "there is no seeing" and so on. This means that external objects such as things to be seen do not exist. 

In the phrase "without waves," "waves" refers to conceptual thoughts. When those are exhausted, it is "without waves." "Manifold" refers to appearing in various different forms. When that is absent, it is "without the manifold." 

The expression "these words" refers to the words spoken by the Blessed One. "Asked" refers to the request made by **Vajragarbha**. What was the meaning of the request? He said, "For what reason?" and so forth. The intended meaning is this: the nature of the Co-emergent <term>sahaja</term> is inherently pure.

<summary>This page provides a philosophical commentary on the non-dual nature of Vajrasattva and the lack of inherent existence in meditation, the body, and sensory perception. It explains that ultimate wisdom is free from conceptual "waves" and the distinction between samsara and nirvana.</summary>

<keywords>Vajrasattva, Hevajra, wisdom, non-duality, emptiness, meditation, Vajragarbha, clear light, sahaja</keywords>

A.text:
Just as those who speak of the <term>Alaya-vijnana</term> <gloss>All-ground consciousness</gloss> assert that the all-ground consciousness is what holds the seeds of all wandering beings, so too is <term>mahasukha</term> <gloss>great bliss</gloss> realized through the empowerment of the wisdom of primordial awareness. The nature of the emptiness of all phenomena is also praised in the Great Vehicle Secret Mantra <note>Mahayana Vajrayana</note> as being the very foundation of all phenomena.

To achieve that very realization, the text says "dark bliss" and so forth. "Union" refers to the meditative equipoise of <term>upaya</term> <gloss>skillful means</gloss> and <term>prajna</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss>. "Entity" refers to the nature of the five Buddhas. "Non-entity" refers to the state of being free from conceptual elaboration regarding those very Buddhas.

If one asks how the nature of bliss arises within the mandala of the glorious Hevajra, which is the nature of skillful means and wisdom, the text says "Vajrasattva" and so forth. From the union of the sun and moon, which are the nature of skillful means and wisdom, a seed syllable arises. From that seed arises the hand-symbol, the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>scepter or diamond</gloss>. The seed syllable residing in the center of that is the <term>sattva</term> <gloss>being</gloss>. The being together with the vajra is Vajrasattva. That very state is described as bliss.

Regarding the phrase "Vajragarbha requested," what was the purpose of his request? Because the Blessed One praised the reality of the generation stage as being the essence of bliss, the text says "perfection" and so forth. "Meditation" refers to the meditation on the deity itself. "What is the need for a non-existent generation?" means there is no need. The intention is as follows: what is the need for this effort in meditating on the mandala cycle if one is devoted to great bliss? If one asks whether the desired goal can be accomplished by great bliss alone, the text says "degenerated through the force of faith" to show respect. This means that one who possesses respect for the generation stage and yet "degenerates" is one who actually abandons the generation stage. "The non-entity of the body" refers to that very generation stage <unclear>one or two words illegible</unclear>.

<summary>This page explains the philosophical foundation of Great Bliss by comparing it to the All-ground consciousness and details the symbolic emergence of Vajrasattva from the union of wisdom and means. It addresses the relationship between the generation stage of meditation and the ultimate realization of Bliss within the Hevajra tradition.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrasattva, Mahasukha, Alaya-vijnana, Hevajra, generation stage, skillful means, wisdom, mandala, Vajragarbha</keywords>

B.text:
Just as those who speak of the <term>Alayavijnana</term> <gloss>all-basis consciousness</gloss> assert that it is the holder of the seeds of all wandering beings, so too is the Great Bliss <note>original: "mahasukha"</note> realized through the empowerment of primordial wisdom and insight. That which is characterized as the emptiness of all phenomena is praised in the <term>Mantrayana</term> <gloss>Secret Mantra vehicle</gloss> of the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss> as being the very foundation of all phenomena. To accomplish that very state, the text says "Great Bliss" and so forth. "Union" refers to the meditative equipoise of method and insight. "Entity" refers to the nature of the five Buddhas. "Non-entity" refers to the very state of being free from conceptual elaboration.

How does one come to have the essence of bliss within the mandala of Shri Hevajra, which is the nature of method and insight? The text says "Vajrasattva" and so forth. This refers to the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>scepter symbol</gloss> as the hand symbol arising from the seed produced by the perfect union of the sun and moon, which are the nature of method and insight. The seed residing in the center of that is the <term>sattva</term> <gloss>being</gloss>. The being who possesses the vajra is Vajrasattva. This very state is called Bliss.

Regarding the phrase "Vajragarbha asked," for what purpose did he ask? Because the Blessed One praised the reality of the generation stage as being the very essence of bliss. The text says "perfection" and so forth. "Meditation" refers to the meditation on the deity itself. "What is the need for a non-existent generation?" means that there is no such need. This is the intended meaning: what is the use of this effort in meditating on the mandala circle if one aspires to Great Bliss? If one thinks that the desired goal will be achieved through Great Bliss alone, then to show respect, the text says "degenerated by the force of faith." In this context, being "degenerated" despite having respect for the generation stage means actually abandoning the generation stage. The phrase "the non-entity of the body" refers to that very generation stage.

<summary>This page explains the relationship between the all-basis consciousness and Great Bliss within the Hevajra Tantra tradition. It defines Vajrasattva as the union of method and insight and discusses the necessity of the generation stage in spiritual practice.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrasattva, Great Bliss, Alayavijnana, Hevajra Tantra, generation stage, method and insight, emptiness, Mahayana</keywords>

place of Great Bliss is called Sukhavati <gloss>The Blissful</gloss> in the Buddha-field of the Tathagata Amitabha <gloss>Buddha of Infinite Light</gloss>. Here, the <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>source of phenomena/womb</gloss> of Nairatmya <gloss>She Who Has No Self</gloss> and the others is called Sukhavati. This is because it protects the unsurpassed bliss of the nature of the condensed essence. It is there that "I" reside.

In order to symbolize all phenomena as being one within the form of Great Bliss, it says: "The form of the shape of the letter E." The Buddhahood itself is the jewel. Its casket <gloss>precious container</gloss> is the place where it is set. Now, to show the greatness of such a self, it says "I am the teacher" and so forth. This means one who explains such teachings as the *Hevajra Tantra*. "The listener" refers to the student who possesses good qualities. "The object to be accomplished is I" refers to what was previously shown. Its accomplisher is also the self.

"The teacher of the wanderers" refers to the two <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Enjoyment Bodies</gloss>, which are the self. Regarding the phrase "the world and the transcendent world," that which arises from the elaboration of both is the "world." This means that the very moment which is the end of the "supreme joy" and the beginning of the "joy of cessation" is that very thing.

It was said previously that you are the very Great Bliss which is the self of all that is to be accomplished. If so, even if the co-emergent bliss of a worldly person is not the object to be accomplished, how could it be you? To this it says: "even by the son" and so forth. The word "even" <note>original: "kyang"</note> indicates the reasoning. Because that itself is primarily to be shown through an example,

<summary>This page defines the "Blissful" realm as the source of phenomena and identifies the Buddha-nature with the teacher, the student, and the seminal essence of enlightenment. It introduces the technical distinction between the different stages of joy in tantric practice.</summary>
<keywords>Sukhavati, Nairatmya, Hevajra Tantra, Sambhogakaya, Bodhicitta, Sahaja, Co-emergent Joy, Bhaga</keywords>

B.text:
The buddha-field of the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>One Gone Thus</gloss> Amitabha is called Sukhavati <gloss>The Blissful</gloss>. Here, however, the <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>source of phenomena/womb</gloss> of Nairatmya <gloss>She Who Realizes Selflessness</gloss> and the other goddesses is called "the Blissful." This is because it protects the unsurpassed bliss of the essential nature in its condensed form; I abide there. In order to symbolize all phenomena as being one with the form of Great Bliss, it says: "The appearance of the form is in the shape of the letter E."

The state of Buddhahood itself is the Jewel. Its casket is the place where it is deposited. Now, in order to show the greatness of such a nature, the text says: "I am the teacher," and so forth. This means I am the one who explains such teachings as the Hevajra Tantra. "The listener" refers to the disciple possessed of good qualities. "The goal to be accomplished is myself" refers to what was explained previously. The one who accomplishes that is also the self. "The teacher of the world" refers to the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Complete Enjoyment Body</gloss> forms, which are my own self.

Regarding the phrase "the worldly and the transcendent," that which arises from the conceptual elaboration of both is the worldly. The transcendent is the <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>enlightened mind/seminal essence</gloss> in the form of fluid, which acts as the cause for those very states. Because this is necessary for the world and because its essence is the <term>Sambhogakaya</term>, it is my own self.

If one asks: "If you are primarily the essence of Great Bliss, what is that like?" the text says: "Co-emergent Joy," and so forth. If one asks: "What is the specific character of that co-emergent joy?" the text says: "The end of the supreme," and so forth. The meaning is that it is the very point where Supreme Joy ends and the Joy of Cessation begins.

Previously it was stated: "You are the very nature of all Great Bliss that is to be accomplished." If that is so, then since the co-emergent bliss of worldly beings is not the goal to be accomplished, how could that be you? In response, the text says: "Even so, by a child," and so forth. The word "even" <note>original: "kyang"</note> functions as a logical reason. This is because that very bliss is primarily shown through examples.

<summary>This page provides a tantric commentary on the nature of Great Bliss and the symbolism of the letter E. It identifies the teacher, the listener, and the goal of practice as expressions of the internal enlightened nature.</summary>
<keywords>Amitabha, Sukhavati, Nairatmya, bhaga, Great Bliss, Hevajra, Sambhogakaya, bodhicitta, Co-emergent Joy</keywords>

A.text:
it will become similar. Since it is to be established by the example itself, that is what is primarily shown, while this is a metaphorical designation. To show that, it says: "Like a lamp in the darkness" and so forth. Just as some establish how a lamp illuminates objects like pots or cloths staying in a dark place, so too should one view the worldly co-emergent bliss as an example that establishes the Great Bliss which has the characteristics of the object to be accomplished.

Regarding the phrase "in the dwelling of bliss," to clearly show what was previously said, it says: "the thirty-two" and so forth. This is the body blazing with the major and minor marks. "The Lord" is the Master of the Buddha-Dharma. "The Consort" is the example, the Vajra Consort. The phrase "the fluid in her <term>bhaga</term>" refers to where the self resides. "Fluid" is the bliss, the external seminal fluid. The phrase "without that" means if that fluid is absent. Because bliss arises in dependence upon the fluid, if the fluid is absent, such bliss cannot be produced by any other cause.

Therefore, it is said that bliss also arises from the deity yoga. Desiring a Great Bliss similar to that, one must certainly practice the deity yoga. Its path is neither a thing nor a non-thing, because it is the essence of both the fluid and the bliss. The Buddha who is its result is also neither a thing nor a non-thing. If you ask how, it says: "the form of face and hands" and so forth. The essence of the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> has form. Through the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss> of supreme bliss, it is formless. Therefore, because it is a non-abiding form, it says: "Neither having form, nor being formless." It does not abide in either.

Why is it so? Because "all wanderers are co-emergent," meaning all sentient beings.

<summary>The text explains that worldly bliss serves as a metaphorical example for ultimate Great Bliss and emphasizes the necessity of deity yoga. It describes the Buddha's nature as being beyond the duality of existence and non-existence, possessing both form and formlessness.</summary>
<keywords>Deity Yoga, Sambhogakaya, Dharmakaya, Vajra Consort, Bhaga, Co-emergent, Major and Minor marks</keywords>

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page: establishing the relationship between the example and the actual realization</meta>

By using the example of that which is similar, the actual nature is established. Therefore, that very nature is the primary teaching, while this <note>referring to the example used</note> is a conventional designation. To demonstrate this very point, it is said: *Like a lamp in the darkness*, and so forth. Just as some objects like a vase or a cloth located in a dark area are made visible and established by a lamp, so too should one view this. The great bliss, which is the quality to be established, is established by means of the exemplary worldly <term>sahaja</term> <gloss>co-emergent</gloss> bliss.

Regarding the phrase *in the abode of bliss* and so forth, in order to clarify what was previously stated, it says: *thirty-two*, and so forth. This refers to the body blazing with the major and minor marks of a Buddha. The *Lord* refers to the Master of the Buddha-Dharma. The *Consort* is the example, namely the <term>Vajra</term> <gloss>Diamond</gloss> Consort. The phrase *fluid in her womb* <note>original: "bhaga"</note> means residing in oneself. *Fluid* is bliss, specifically the external fluid. The phrase *without that* means if that fluid is absent. Because bliss arises in dependence upon the fluid, if the fluid is absent, such bliss cannot be produced by any other cause. 

Therefore, it is said that bliss will also arise from the <term>deity yoga</term> <gloss>meditative union with a divine form</gloss>. One who desires that same great bliss must certainly practice the deity yoga. Its path is neither a thing nor a non-thing, because it is the essential nature of both the fluid and the bliss. The Buddha, who is the fruit of that path, is also neither a thing nor a non-thing. How is this so? The text says: *possessing the aspect of faces and hands*, and so forth. The essence of the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Complete Enjoyment Body</gloss> is formed. Due to the very <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss> of supreme bliss, it is formless. Therefore, because it is a non-abiding formed nature, it is said: *It is not formed, yet not formless*; it does not remain in either state. Why is it so? For that reason, *all beings are co-emergent*, which refers to all sentient beings. Co-emergent...

<summary>This page explains the relationship between worldly bliss and the Great Bliss of enlightenment using the metaphor of a lamp in darkness. It clarifies that the Buddha's nature transcends the duality of existence and non-existence through the union of form and emptiness.</summary>
<keywords>Sahaja, Great Bliss, Deity Yoga, Sambhogakaya, Dharmakaya, Vajra Consort, Co-emergent</keywords>

A.text:
If you ask what the meaning of "co-emergent" is, it says: "Nature is called co-emergent." This is a synonym for saying it is born together with the nature of all phenomena. That itself is Nirvana. If you ask how it is made so, it says: "By the mind in the form of total purity" and so forth. "Total purity" means being stainless, the nature of Luminosity. The meaning is that when the mind takes that form, it becomes Nirvana.

If the world is the nature of Buddha because it is the essence of things and non-things, then why meditate on the form of a deity? It says: "That is true, but of the deity's form" and so forth. "The face, hands, and color" and so forth refers to the "ordinary body." If you then think that meditation is therefore useless, it says: "However," and so forth. The "habitual tendencies" of the distinct ordinary body refers to the "remnants." The intention is that one should meditate on the deity's body in order to abandon those and to expand the habitual tendencies of the uncontaminated aggregates.

Now, because it is to be established that the meditation on the body is itself the cause for non-abiding Nirvana, it establishes this through many examples. It says: "By that very one who knows the poison" and so forth. "To extract" means to overcome. Why was it called "wind" in the previous part? Because it is the cause of breath. How is it reversed? Because it is of the same class. Its examination is that very benefit. "Existence" is <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>cyclic existence</gloss>. "Purity" is total exhaustion.

The phrase "by existence itself" means that through the total transformation of the sun, moon, hand-symbols, and seed-syllables, there is "existence." The meaning is that through the very form of the deity, those <note>samsaric states</note> are exhausted. "Conceptual thought" is <term>Samsara</term>. The meaning is that through the conceptual thought of the deity's form, it will be exhausted. The phrase "Just as water enters the ear" is the example

<summary>This page argues that while all beings are naturally 'co-emergent' with Buddha-nature, deity meditation is necessary to clear away ordinary habitual tendencies. It uses the analogy of using poison to cure poison to show how conceptual meditation can exhaust samsaric concepts.</summary>
<keywords>Nirvana, Luminosity, Deity Meditation, Habitual tendencies, Samsara, Purity, Non-abiding Nirvana</keywords>

B.text:
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the nature of the innate and the practice of deity yoga from the previous section of the Tengyur.</meta>

What is the meaning of the word "born"? It refers to the <term>Sahaja</term> <gloss>innate or co-emergent</gloss> nature. It is said, "It is called the co-emergent nature of all phenomena," which is a synonymous expression. That very nature is <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>transcendence of suffering</gloss>. 

If one asks how this is so, the text says: "By the mind that is of a completely pure aspect," and so forth. "Completely pure" means stainless, the very essence of <term>Prabhasvara</term> <gloss>clear light</gloss>. The meaning is that when the mind takes on that aspect, it becomes Nirvana.

One might ask: "If the world is the very nature of the Buddha because its essence is both existence and non-existence, why then should one meditate on the forms of deities?" To answer this, the text says, "While that is true, the form of the deity," and so forth. The mention of "face, limbs, and color" refers to the ordinary body. 

If one then argues that meditation is therefore useless, the text says, "Nonetheless," and so forth. This refers to the <term>Vasana</term> <gloss>habitual tendencies</gloss> of the ordinary body which remain as residues. The intention is that one should meditate on the divine body of the deity in order to discard those tendencies and to increase the tendencies of the <term>Anasrava</term> <gloss>uncontaminated</gloss> aggregates.

Now, it must be established that the meditation on the body is itself the cause of <term>Apratishthita Nirvana</term> <gloss>non-abiding nirvana</gloss>. Therefore, to prove this through various examples, the text says, "By that very knowledge of the poison," and so forth. To "extract" means to neutralize or overcome. 

How was it called "wind" previously? Because it is the movement of the breath. How is it reversed? Because it belongs to the same class. Testing that is what is beneficial. <term>Bhava</term> <gloss>existence</gloss> refers to <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of rebirth</gloss>. "Purity" refers to its total exhaustion. By saying "through existence itself," the meaning is that through the transformation of the sun, moon, hand-symbols, and seed-syllables, which constitute existence, those very things are exhausted by the aspect of the deity. 

"Conceptual thought" is Samsara. The meaning is that conceptual thought is exhausted by the "conceptualization" of the deity's form. It is like the example: "Just as when water has entered the ear," and so forth.

<summary>This page explains the Innate (Sahaja) as the pure, clear-light nature of mind and justifies deity meditation as a method to purify ordinary habitual tendencies. It uses the principle of using the cause of a problem as its cure, such as using conceptualization of a deity to exhaust ordinary conceptual thought.</summary>
<keywords>Sahaja, Innate, Nirvana, Clear Light, Deity Yoga, Vasana, Habitual Tendencies, Non-abiding Nirvana, Samsara, Purification</keywords>

A.text:
because they are the nature of the support. "From that joy, it will be born. Set apart by the division of moments." This refers to being set apart by the divisions of "various" and so forth. If the joy itself exists, what is the use of the division of moments? To this it says: "Having known the moments" and so forth. The intention is that if one knows the nature of the moments, one will fully know the action of bliss through the joys, but not otherwise.

To show those very divisions of the moments, it says: "The various and..." and so forth. "Various" means being skilled in diversity, which is the work of the Master. Regarding "The ripening" and so forth: "reversed from that" means becoming unlike it. "Primordial wisdom" <term>jnana</term> is the primordial wisdom of Great Bliss. "Eating that" means experiencing it. Regarding "The dissolving" and so forth: "Eaten" means remembering what has just passed and disintegrated.

Alternatively, the discerning knowledge is called "eaten," which is the prior certain grasping that "I have enjoyed bliss." "Devoid of characteristics" refers to the three previously shown. "Passion and freedom from passion" means being free from both <term>Samsara</term> and Nirvana. The phrase "The various and..." and so forth establishes the four joys and the four empowerments. The intention is that through the individual joys, one obtains the "Master," the "Secret," the "Wisdom," and the "Fourth" empowerments.

For that very reason, it says "by the joys and so forth" regarding the actions. "Called the sequence" means: Joy is the Master's empowerment. Supreme Joy is the Secret empowerment. Cessation of Joy is the Wisdom empowerment. Co-emergent Joy is the fourth empowerment. Thus, the four empowerments, the four moments, and the four joys should be known as applied from the Guru's oral instructions. In this way, one should know the categories of the four empowerments.

<summary>This page details the technical correlation between the four joys (Joy, Supreme Joy, Cessation, and Co-emergent) and the four tantric empowerments. it explains how 'moments' are used to understand the progression of bliss during practice.</summary>
<keywords>Four Empowerments, Four Joys, Four Moments, Primordial Wisdom, Samsara, Nirvana, Guru's instructions</keywords>

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
should be performed, because it is the very essence of the support for those <note>referring to the foundational nature of the yogic practices or deities mentioned previously</note>.

"Joy arises from that, distinguished by the division of moments," means that it is categorized by divisions such as "various" and so forth. If joy itself exists, one might ask, what is the purpose of distinguishing these moments?

The text says, "By knowing the moments..." and so forth. The intent is that if one knows the essence of the moments themselves, one will fully understand the functioning of bliss through the various joys. Otherwise, one will not.

To demonstrate those very divisions of the moments, the text says, "The various..." and so forth. "Various" <term>nana</term> <gloss>diverse or multifaceted</gloss> refers to being skilled in diversity, which is the activity of the Master <term>Acarya</term>. Regarding the section beginning with "Ripening" <term>vipaka</term> <gloss>the fruition of karma</gloss>, the phrase "reversing from that" means becoming unlike that <note>shifting from ordinary causal results to yogic experience</note>.

"Wisdom" <term>jnana</term> <gloss>primal awareness</gloss> refers to the wisdom of great bliss. "Eating that" means experiencing it. Regarding the section beginning with "Dissolution" <term>vimalabdha</term> <gloss>thoroughly agitated or refined</gloss>, the term "eaten" refers to the memory of what has just passed and ceased. Alternatively, the knowledge of individual realization is called "eaten," meaning the definite apprehension that "I have experienced bliss."

"Devoid of characteristics" refers to the three <note>moments or joys</note> previously explained. "Attachment and freedom from attachment" refers to being free from both existence <term>samsara</term> and passing beyond sorrow <term>nirvana</term>.

By the passage starting with "The various..." and so forth, the four joys are established as the four empowerments <term>abhiseka</term>. The intent is that through each respective joy, one attains what are called the Master, the Secret, the Wisdom, and the Fourth empowerments.

For that very reason, the text discusses the activities of joy and so forth. "In stages" refers to the following:
1. Joy is the Master Empowerment.
2. Supreme Joy is the Secret Empowerment.
3. Joyless Joy <note>also translated as 'freedom from joy' or 'extraordinary joy' depending on the tantric context</note> is the Wisdom Empowerment.
4. Co-emergent Joy is the Fourth Empowerment.

In this way, one should understand the application of the four empowerments, the four moments, and the four joys based on the oral instructions of the Guru. Thus, the enumeration of the four empowerments should be understood.
