By that, it is accomplished; one should directly realize the <term>Sahaja</term> <gloss>Co-emergent or Innate joy</gloss>. If one abides in that, the <term>yogi</term> will accomplish the <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>spiritual attainment</gloss> of <term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>the Great Seal</gloss>. How is this so? It is the <term>yogi</term> of the <term>mudra</term> <gloss>symbolic hand gesture or consort</gloss>; because they have become a suitable vessel, they accomplish the <term>siddhi</term> of the <term>Mahamudra</term> endowed with <term>vidya</term> <gloss>transformative knowledge or awareness-mantra</gloss>.

The accomplishment of the characteristics is the primary cause itself, while the application of the <term>mudra</term> is its concurrent condition; furthermore, this is because it constitutes the <term>samaya</term> <gloss>sacred bond or commitment</gloss> in this context. The <term>siddhi</term> of <term>vidya</term> and the person, and the <term>siddhi</term> of <term>Mahamudra</term>, are the <term>siddhi</term> of the person of the family; this is because, in this context, realization is impossible without the <term>vidya</term> of the specific <term>kula</term> <gloss>buddha family</gloss>. During the time of the three initial <term>samadhi</term> <gloss>states of meditative concentration</gloss>, one does not contemplate that, as at that time it would only cause distraction.

The phrase "in this way" refers to the giving of <term>abhisheka</term> <gloss>empowerment/consecration</gloss> and the purpose of accomplishing the <term>yogi</term> through the <term>mudra</term>. The statement "the <term>mandala</term> was taught for the sake of empowering the student and achieving <term>siddhi</term>" refers to the <term>mandala</term> of the <term>samaya</term> and the <term>mandala</term> of practice; this is the meaning of "showing it."

Everything such as "the four pairs of distinctions of the <term>mandala</term>" is easy to understand. "Place in the east" means to arrange it there. The section beginning with "of the Lord of the <term>mandala</term>" explains the preliminary <term>seva</term> <gloss>liturgical retreat or service</gloss>. "Of the <term>mandala</term> deities" refers to each individual deity of the <term>mandala</term>. The phrase "where it is spoken" refers to this: <term>Om Vajra Raksha Raksha Hum Phat Svaha</term> <note>original: ཨོཾ་བཛྲ་རཀྵ་རཀྵ་ཧཱུཾ་ཕཊ་སྭཱ་ཧཱ།; translates to "Om, Vajra protection, protect, protect, Hum Phat Svaha"</note>. "Prior to" means prior to the purification of the ground.

The phrase "the <term>mantra</term> starting with A" refers to this <term>mantra</term>: <term>Om Akaro Mukham Sarva Dharmanam Adyanutpannatvat Om Ah Hum Phat Svaha</term> <note>original: ཨོཾ་ཨ་ཀཱ་རོ་མུ་ཁཾ་སརྦ་དྷརྨཱ་ཎཱཾ། ཨཱདྱ་ནུཏྤན་ན་ཏྭཱཏ་ཨོཾ་ཨཱཿཧཱུཾ་ཕཊ་སྭཱ་ཧཱ།; translates to "Om, the letter A is the door to all phenomena, because they are originally unproduced, Om Ah Hum Phat Svaha"</note>. "Protection" refers to the fence, the lattice, and so forth. "By this" means that even while drawing, one should make offerings and supplications to the <term>Guru</term> <gloss>spiritual teacher</gloss>. "In this" refers to the drawn <term>mandala</term> of the support. <term>Vajrasattva</term> <gloss>Vajra Being</gloss> refers to the stable mind, which is his pride. "Right leg extended" <note>original: གཡས་བརྐྱང་; Alidha posture</note> means extending the right. "Leg" refers to the lower leg. "In the <term>mandala</term>" means inside the <term>mandala</term>. "Then, the reality" <note>original: དེ་ཁོ་ན་; tathata</note> refers to the generation...

<summary>This page explains the technical requirements for achieving Mahamudra siddhi, focusing on the relationship between the practitioner, the mandala, and specific protective mantras. It provides commentary on ritual procedures including the purification of the ground and the symbolic meaning of Vajrasattva's posture.</summary>
<keywords>Mahamudra, siddhi, mandala, Vajrasattva, mantra, abhisheka, samaya, yoga</keywords>

A.text:
abandoning non-virtue is itself the "changing of the three robes." In that state, because it clears away the stains of the afflictions, conceptual thoughts, and signs, it is the "bathing three times." Burning the conceptual thoughts of the afflictions with the nature of the fire of primordial wisdom which is free from elaboration is itself the "fire offering." 

That very <term>bodhicitta</term> is <term>Hevajra</term>, and by its very nature of wisdom, it is the cycle of <term>Yoginis</term>; therefore, it is the "mandala deity." The support for these is the very cause for the abiding of meditative concentration; since that too is a quality of the mind, it is therefore the "mandala." In the section beginning "In brief...", the meaning of the previously spoken verses is summarized in a single phrase. "In brief" means that by the stated reasoning, those practices such as mantra recitation are summarized and maintained, so the mind becomes of a "collected nature"—this is the remaining word. 

"Mind" is the <term>bodhicitta</term> as previously described. "Collected" means that all phenomena are collected into a single taste. The one who has that nature is the "yogi," for apart from that nature, no self is perceived. This is the "supreme empowerment," because it visibly washes away the stains of afflictions and conceptual thoughts. The chapter that clarifies this empowerment is the Chapter on Empowerment. This concludes the explanation of the tenth chapter from the *Pearl Garland* <term>Muktāvalī</term>, a difficult-point commentary on the <term>Hevajra Tantra</term>.

To lead sentient beings into the teaching, one should perform the four "gazes": the gaze that causes to fall, the gaze of subduing, the gaze of summoning, and the gaze of stiffening. The characteristics of these are shown in order by four half-verses. There, whatever is looked at with a face directed straight ahead and a wrathful expression, with the two pupils shown at the forehead, is the "gaze that causes to fall." That which relies on the left and looks to the left is the "gaze of subduing." That which relies on the upper direction and looks to the right is the "gaze of summoning." That which relies on the tip of the nose and looks straight ahead is the "gaze of stiffening."

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>The abandonment of misdeeds is itself the changing of the three garments. In that regard, the act of bathing three times is the removal of the stains of the mental afflictions, discursive thoughts, and conceptual signs. The fire offering <term>homa</term> <gloss>burnt offering ritual</gloss> is itself the burning of discursive mental afflictions through the nature of the fire of non-elaborated primordial wisdom.

The <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>awakening mind</gloss> is itself <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>Joyful Vajra</gloss>, and it is the wheel of the <term>yogini</term> <gloss>female tantric practitioner</gloss> through its nature of transcendent wisdom. Therefore, it is the mandala. The support for these is the very cause of abiding in meditative concentration; since that is a quality of the mind, it is therefore the mandala.

In brief, with a single phrase, the meaning of the previously spoken verses is summarized. Regarding "in brief," through the reasoning explained, the practices such as mantra recitation are summarized and maintained, so that the mind becomes concentrated in nature; this is the remaining meaning of the text. The "mind" refers to the awakening mind as previously described. That itself is the "assembly," meaning the collection of all phenomena into a single taste. The one who possesses that nature is the <term>yogin</term> <gloss>tantric practitioner</gloss>, for apart from that nature, no self is observed. This is the supreme initiation, as it directly washes away the stains of mental afflictions and discursive thoughts. The chapter that clarifies the initiation is the Chapter on Initiation. This concludes the explanation of the tenth chapter from the *Pearl Garland* <note>original: "Mukhavali"</note>, a commentary on the difficult points of the *Hevajra Tantra*.

In order to lead sentient beings into the teaching, one should perform the four gazes: the gaze that causes to fall, the gaze of subjugation, the gaze of summoning, and the gaze of stiffening. The characteristics of these are shown in sequence by four half-verses. Regarding these, looking with a straight face and a wrathful expression while directing both pupils toward the forehead is the gaze that causes to fall. Looking toward the left while leaning to the left is the gaze of subjugation. Looking toward the right while leaning upward is the gaze of summoning. Looking straight ahead while focusing on the tip of the nose is the gaze of stiffening.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic meaning of tantric rituals as internal mental processes and concludes the tenth chapter of the Hevajra commentary. It then introduces the specific physical techniques for the four ritual gazes used to influence sentient beings.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra, bodhicitta, mandala, initiation, ritual gazes, mental afflictions, yoga, Pearl Garland commentary</keywords>

A.text:
and thus subject to birth and death, and therefore there is no path of liberation in the stage of generation; to clear that away, it is said: "Birth and..." and so forth. "Means and wisdom" refer to the body of self-cognition and one's own body. "Not binding" means untainted. If one asks why, it is said: "Means..." and so forth. "Continuous arising" is the arising. Through the power of the two accumulations, for the sake of wandering beings, the mind that appears as the body and so forth through compassion arises continuously and uninterruptedly, equal to the realm of space; this is "means." 

Therefore, why would the perfect fruit of meditation through means ever perish? "Perishing" is non-perception; because individual appearances are false, it shows an appearance as a body like the moon in water or a star. That itself is perishing, which is "wisdom." Therefore, this is the "end of existence," making an end to the existence rooted in conceptual attachment to objects; it brings it to an end. For that reason, there is no perishing in this, and there is also no birth, because there is no perishing. Furthermore, in reality there is no perishing, so there is no birth; because one knows that this body of <term>Mahāmudrā</term> appears falsely as false to itself, those too appear in reality, so there is no birth itself. 

If one thinks that even mundane people are in <term>saṃsāra</term> <gloss>cyclic existence</gloss>, it is said: "Perished..." and so forth. The meaning of this is: among those who have achieved the accomplishment of <term>Mahāmudrā</term>, if there is no one who conceptually clings to their own body as something that will perish, who is there to be exhausted? For there is no perishing. There is no corruption; it should be known thus. Again, for Brahma and so forth, although there is no true thing in the body, there is conceptual attachment to it as a thing; therefore there is arising, and from arising there is perishing. The accomplishment of <term>Mahāmudrā</term> is not like that, for there is no conceptual attachment to it as a thing. Thus, having crossed over <term>saṃsāra</term> and <term>nirvāṇa</term>, through the nature of the non-abiding <term>nirvāṇa</term>,

B.text:
If you think that the <term>generation stage</term> <gloss>utpattikrama; the visualization phase of deity yoga</gloss> provides no path to liberation because it involves birth and death, this passage is spoken to clear that doubt. Regarding the words "birth and so forth": <term>method</term> <gloss>upaya</gloss> and <term>wisdom</term> <gloss>prajña</gloss> refer to the body of self-cognition and one’s own body. The phrase "not bound" means not being stained.

As for why this is, it is explained by the term "method." "Arising continuously" refers to manifestation. Through the power of the two accumulations <note>merit and wisdom</note>, the mind appears as the <term>kayas</term> <gloss>buddha bodies</gloss> for the benefit of beings. Because this continuity is never interrupted, it arises equal to the realm of space; this is "method." Therefore, why should the perfected fruit of meditation through method ever perish? 

"Perished" means non-observation <note>unfindability through analysis</note>. Since diverse appearances are {false, deceptive}, the manifestation of the body is shown to be like a moon in water or a star. That very perishing is "wisdom." Therefore, this is the "end of existence" <note>bhutakoti</note>; it brings to an end the cycle of existence rooted in grasping at objects as real. It brings that existence to its finality.

Because of that reason, since there is no perishing in this, there is also no birth, for there is no perishing. Furthermore, in the state of reality <note>tattva</note>, because there is no perishing, there is no birth. Because one knows that this body of <term>mahamudra</term> <gloss>the Great Seal; the ultimate nature of mind and reality</gloss> appears to itself as a {false, deceptive} appearance of what is {false, deceptive}, these appearances themselves arise as reality, and thus there is no birth.

If you then think that worldly beings themselves are just <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of suffering</gloss>, it is explained by the words "perished" and so forth. Among those who have attained the <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>spiritual accomplishment</gloss> of <term>mahamudra</term>, if there is no one who clings to their own body as real, who is it that could be exhausted? There is no perishing. There are no <term>contaminations</term> <gloss>asravas; mental defilements</gloss>; it should be understood in this way. 

Furthermore, although beings like <term>Brahma</term> and others have no inherent existence in their bodies, because they possess clinging to them as real things, they have origins and they have destruction arising from those origins. The accomplishment of <term>mahamudra</term> is not like that, because there is no clinging to things as real. In that way, having transcended both cyclic existence and <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>suffering and the peace of cessation</gloss>, by the nature of non-abiding <term>nirvana</term>—

<summary>This page explains how the generation stage and Mahamudra practices transcend birth and death by viewing appearances as illusory like a moon in water. It distinguishes the enlightened state from worldly existence and worldly deities by the absence of clinging to the reality of the body.</summary>
<keywords>generation stage, method and wisdom, Mahamudra, non-abiding nirvana, two accumulations, siddhi, illusion</keywords>

A.text:
because the path is neither entity nor non-entity, the result, Buddha, is also not an entity; that is the characteristic of the exhaustion of all afflictions without exception. "That itself" refers to the Buddha. "Nor is it the manner of a non-entity" refers to the Truth Body itself, which is the nature of the perfectly pure primordial wisdom of one taste. "The aspect of faces and hands" refers to the Enjoyment and Emanation bodies. From what does the formless arise? It is the "holy bliss," meaning it is even through enjoying the "bliss of the Dharma" of the Truth Body. Because of that, the result is neither entity nor non-entity. Therefore, all beings are co-emergent joy; that co-emergent joy is connected to the co-emergence of Buddhahood itself. "All beings" refers to all sentient beings. If one wonders why it is called the "co-emergence of Buddhahood itself," it is said: **Co-emergent**, and so forth. "Nature" <note>original: "prakṛti"</note> and "essence" <note>original: "svabhāva"</note> are synonyms for the word "co-emergent" <term>sahaja</term>. This refers to the principal Truth Body of Buddhahood. Regarding that, it is said: **perfectly pure**, and so forth. "Perfectly pure" is the very nature of stainless luminosity. The mind is that which possesses its aspect. Because its nature is its essence, it is spoken of in that way. That very nature is Nirvana; it is the perfectly pure nature and it is also the mind. Since it is ultimately pure and in Nirvana, it is not an entity. Since the mind itself is the perfectly pure nature, it is also not a non-entity; this is the intended meaning. By this, it is taught that through the mind being luminous by nature, the seed of Buddhahood is established from beginningless time. "Well then, at that time the Complete Enjoyment Body would be without a seed, because an ordinary body belongs to that very body and is of a discordant type," if one thinks this, it is said: **The deity's**, and so forth. Here too, the word "deity's form" refers to its very seed.

<summary>The author argues that the result of the path, Buddhahood, transcends the duality of entity and non-entity. He identifies the mind's luminous nature as the beginningless seed of Buddha-nature (Tathāgatagarbha) present in all beings.</summary>
<keywords>entity, non-entity, Truth Body, co-emergent, luminosity, Nirvana, seed of Buddhahood</keywords>

B.text:
Furthermore, because the path is neither a functional entity nor a non-entity, the result, which is Buddhahood, is also not a functional entity. This is the definition of the exhaustion of all afflictions without exception. That itself is the Buddha. The phrase "nor is it the manner of non-existence" refers to the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss> itself, which is the nature of the utterly pure, single-taste wisdom. The phrase "the aspects of faces and hands" refers to the <term>sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>enjoyment body</gloss> and the <term>nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>. From what does "formless" arise? It is called "supreme bliss." This means that the <term>dharmakaya</term> also enjoys the bliss of the <term>dharma</term> <gloss>reality</gloss>. Because of that, the result is neither a functional entity nor a non-entity. Therefore, all beings are the <term>sahaja</term> <gloss>co-emergent</gloss> joy. This co-emergence is connected to the co-emergence of Buddhahood itself. "All wandering beings" refers to all sentient beings.

In response to the thought "Why is it called the co-emergence of Buddhahood itself?", it is said, "Co-emergent," and so forth. "Nature" <note>original: "rang bzhin"</note> and "essence" <note>original: "ngo bo"</note> are synonyms for the word co-emergent. Buddhahood is primarily the <term>dharmakaya</term>. With respect to that, it is described as "utterly pure" and so forth. "Utterly pure" refers to the stainless nature, luminosity itself. The mind possesses that aspect. Because its nature is that essence, it is described in that way. Its very nature is <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>the state beyond suffering</gloss>. The utterly pure nature is that, and the mind is also that. Because it is pure in the ultimate sense and is <term>nirvana</term>, it has no functional existence. Because the mind itself is the utterly pure nature, it is also not a non-entity; this is the intended meaning. By this, it is said that because the mind is luminous by nature, the seed of Buddhahood is established from beginningless time.

One might ask: "In that case, the <term>sambhogakaya</term> would be without a seed, for the ordinary body belongs to that very [ordinary] body and is of a different type than that [Buddha body]." Therefore, it is said, "Of the deity," and so forth. Here too, the word "deity's form" refers to its very seed.

<summary>This text explains that Buddhahood and the nature of the mind are neither existing entities nor non-existent voids. It identifies the luminous nature of the mind as the beginningless seed of the three bodies of a Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>Buddha nature, dharmakaya, co-emergent joy, luminosity, nirvana, mind nature, three bodies, seed of awakening</keywords>

A.text:
There too, it resides as soon as embodied beings are born. If one asks why, it is the phrase **faces and hands**, and so forth, meaning they are generally concordant as a body. Just as the mind is naturally pure and is the seed free from adventitious stains, so too the ordinary body itself is intended to be the "seed of the deity's body." "If that is so, then meditating on the deity's body and so forth is useless," if one thinks this, it is said: **However**, and so forth; "the cause of the ordinary nature of the body" is the remaining phrase. Therefore, for the sake of abandoning that and for the sake of nourishing one's own seed, the meditation on the deity's body is intended not to be useless. "It is hard to endure that the ordinary body is abandoned just by meditating on the body," if one thinks this, then for the sake of establishing this through many examples, it is said: **That itself**, and so forth. How? **Just as the wind**, and so forth. Just as, without knowing it, urine, feces, and wind are cleared away. "Recognized as medicine in reverse" refers to being of a concordant type; "recognition" of that is the ritual. "Existence" <term>bhava</term> is cyclic existence. "To be purified" means it has become exhausted. **By existence itself** means by the worldly path. For example, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four feet of miracle, the five faculties, and the five powers—these twenty-two factors are the worldly path. Without realizing them, the transcendent path cannot arise. Furthermore, if those fifteen factors—the seven branches of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path—do not exist, there is no exhaustion of existence. Therefore, by following from one to another, existence is exhausted by existence itself. "Conceptualization" refers to ordinary concepts; "becoming pure" happens from one to another. Likewise, even correct individual conceptualization itself, by the power of meditating on reality, through succession generates non-conceptual primordial wisdom, and thereby conceptualization is exhausted. "Entered" means entered there. "Extracting" means definitely extracting.

<summary>This page justifies the practice of Deity Yoga by explaining that although beings possess the 'seed' of a deity's body, they must cultivate it to overcome ordinary perceptions. It uses the metaphor of 'existence curing existence' to explain how worldly paths lead to transcendence.</summary>
<keywords>Deity Yoga, ordinary body, seed, worldly path, transcendent path, conceptualization, existence</keywords>

B.text:
<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on the relationship between the ordinary physical body and the divine body of a deity in the context of Vajrayana practice.</meta>

In that regard, embodied beings exist simply by being born. If one asks why, it is because of what is called "faces and hands" and so forth; this means that in general, they are similar in body. Just as the mind is naturally pure and is the seed that is free from adventitious stains, similarly, the ordinary body itself is considered the seed of the deity's body.

If that is the case, one might ask if meditating on the deity’s body and so forth is useless. It is said: "However," and so forth; the phrase "cause of the natural ordinary body" is an additional explanation. Therefore, it is intended that meditating on the deity’s body is not useless, because it is for the purpose of abandoning that <note>the ordinary body</note> and for the purpose of nourishing one's own seed <note>the potential for divinity</note>.

If one says it is difficult to endure this abandonment of the ordinary body simply by meditating on the <term>Kaya</term> <gloss>enlightened body</gloss>, then, in order to establish this through many examples, it is said: "That very thing," and so forth. If one asks how, it is like the phrase "Just as wind," and so forth. Just as wind unknowingly clears away urine, feces, and gas. 

"Examining the reverse as medicine" refers to being of a similar type; the "examination" of that is the <term>Vidhi</term> <gloss>ritual procedure</gloss>. "Existence" <note>Sanskrit: bhava</note> refers to <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss>. "To purify them" means they become exhausted. The phrase "by existence itself" refers to the mundane path.

How so? The four applications of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four feet of miraculous power, the five faculties, and the five strengths—these twenty-two qualities constitute the mundane path. Without realizing these, the supramundane path cannot arise. Furthermore, without the fifteen qualities consisting of the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path, there is no exhaustion of existence. Therefore, by proceeding from one to the next, existence is exhausted by existence itself.

"Conceptualization" refers to ordinary conceptual thoughts. "Becoming pure" happens progressively from one stage to the next. In that way, even correct individual investigation, through the power of meditating on suchness, progressively generates non-conceptual primordial wisdom <note>Sanskrit: jnana</note>, and thereby exhausts conceptualization. "Entered" means having entered into that. "Extracting" means definitely extracting.

<summary>This text explains that the ordinary human body serves as the seed for the divine body of a deity. It argues that mundane spiritual paths and even conceptual thoughts are necessary stages used to eventually transcend existence and reach non-conceptual wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>deity yoga, seed of enlightenment, mundane path, supramundane path, conceptualization, primordial wisdom, Samsara exhaustion</keywords>

A.text:
"Concepts of entities" refers to the conceptualization of the five aggregates and so forth. "By the aspect" refers to the aspects of the deities such as Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and so forth. "Purifying" means making them exhausted. Attachment is the fire of the affliction of attachment. "Burned by that" means being tormented; it produces the suffering of the lower realms and so forth. "Passion" <term>rāga</term> refers to the passion for reality itself. That itself is the fire; it burns the fuel of the afflictions. By that, it is "accomplished," meaning it makes it ripen. "Unbearable actions" are things like killing arising from hatred. The "means" <term>upāya</term> is the protection of the Buddha's teaching through compassion and so forth. **By attachment** means by the attachment of the afflictions. **By attachment itself** means by the attachment to reality. "Reversing" means through the discordant side. The discordant side is what appears to be similar; that ultimate reality itself becomes the antidote. A "Buddhist heretic" <term>tīrthika</term> is a "Buddha-heretic." If one asks how they are "Buddhist," it is because they have entered the teaching of the Buddha. If one asks how they are "heretics," it is because they hate the Vajrayāna, the heart of the Buddha's teaching. By all of this, the meditation on the enjoyment of the Vajra Goddess is definitely established. For the sake of establishing it also through the cause of the infinite families of this and that, it is said: **Kunturu**, and so forth. "Kunturu" is great joy; those which arise from the lotus of the Vajra Goddess. "Elements" are the primary elements. "Five" refers to the five contacts; "nature of the five elements" means by the nature of the earth, water, fire, wind, and space elements. If one asks what those elements are, it is said: **Only one**, and so forth. Great joy is the Vajra-holder of great joy. "Five itself" means the nature of the five families. "By division" means by the division of the elements. The elements are reality <term>tattva</term>.

<summary>The text employs the logic of using afflictions (like attachment) as a path to purification and describes the 'Buddhist heretic' as one who follows the Buddha but rejects the Vajrayāna. It introduces the five elements as being of the nature of the five Buddha families.</summary>
<keywords>attachment, passion, Buddhist heretic, Vajra Goddess, five elements, five families, Kunturu</keywords>

B.text:
The conceptualization of entities refers to the conceptualization of the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates of experience</gloss> and so forth. The phrase by way of form refers to the forms of the eternal ones, the deities such as the Jewel Lords <note>referring to the Ratnasambhava buddha family</note> and others. Purification means to bring to exhaustion. Desire, namely the desire of the mental afflictions, is fire.

Burning by that means being tormented, which produces the suffering of the lower realms and so forth. The word passion refers to the passion for reality <note>original: "tattva"</note> itself. That very thing is the fire that burns the firewood of the mental afflictions. Through that, accomplishment will occur, which means to bring to complete ripening. Terrible deeds are those such as killing that arise from hatred. Method refers to the protection of the Buddha’s teaching through compassion and so forth. By desire means by the desire of the mental afflictions. By desire itself means by the passion for reality itself. Reversal refers to the use of opposing factors. These opposing factors appear similar <note>to the afflictions themselves</note>, yet that ultimate reality acts as the very antidote.

A Buddhist heretic <note>original: "mu stegs pa," typically meaning a non-Buddhist extremist, used here paradoxically</note> is a Buddhist outsider. In what way are they Buddhist? Because they have entered the teaching of the Buddha. In what way are they heretics? Because they harbor hatred toward the Vajrayana, which is the heart of the Buddha's teaching. By all these means, the meditation on the enjoyment of the Vajra Goddess is established. To establish this through the cause of the infinite families of this and that, it is said: "Everywhere" and so forth.

Everywhere <note>original: "kuntu ru"</note> means supreme joy, which arises from the lotus <note>the female reproductive organ in tantric metaphor</note> of the Vajra Goddess. Elements refers to the elements. Five refers to the five touches, which have the nature of the five elements. This means having the nature of the earth, water, fire, wind, and space realms. If one asks what these elements are, it is said: "The single one" and so forth. Great Joy is the supreme joy of the Vajra Holder <note>Vajradhara</note>. The fivefold nature refers to the nature of the five Buddha families. By division means by the division of the elements. The elements are reality itself.

<summary>This page provides a tantric commentary on transforming mundane desires and elements into spiritual realization. It defines "passion" as a tool for purifying mental afflictions and clarifies the distinction between worldly desire and the "passion for reality" used in the Vajrayana path.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrayana, five aggregates, mental afflictions, fire of desire, Vajra Goddess, five elements, Buddha families, Vajradhara, purification</keywords>

A.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
"Delighted" means having become joyful. "That which, if practiced, blesses one as Vajrasattva" is the blessing. To "show" that is to make it clear. "Offering itself is the Vajra" means for the sake of showing it, by its power. "With desire" means with respect. "Bodhisattva" means appearing as an illusion and so forth, or by a mind without individual appearances. That itself is spoken: "By the mind of non-dual wisdom," where non-dual wisdom is the absence of appearance. "Mind" is by way of conceptualization. "Impure" means not having been purified by the form of the deity. Whatever number is fixed as six, they are called by these names. Therefore, the intention is "Please speak of their purity!" If one thinks, "From what should the senses themselves be seen as pure?", it is said, "The purity of all objects..." and so forth; "all objects" means all objects of knowledge are pure as deities, as was said above. Therefore, the meaning of the intent is "This is not to be explained here." The nature of the purity of the eyes and so forth is the essence of their support, Delusion-Vajra and so forth. Therefore, the transformations of these are divided into three: the first, the sixth, and the seventh. "Intention" is the hidden intent. "Speaking with just a hint" means it is spoken; the meaning is that the intent is the primary thing spoken, not the literal words. "Great Commitment" <note>original: <term>mahasamaya</term></note> is the secret sign. "Unwavering" means it cannot be shown <note>note: to the uninitiated</note>. By this, the secret is spoken. Spoken as extremely secret: "Laughter and..." and so forth. "By the four" refers to the Action, Performance, Yoga, and Highest Yoga Tantras, which also symbolize laughing, looking, embracing, and union; thus, in the Action Tantras and so forth, where the deities of method and wisdom show attachment through a smile, in some by looking thereafter, in some by embracing, and in some by union...

B.text:
The one who is pleased. Regarding that which, if practiced, results in the blessing of <term>Vajrasattva</term> <gloss>the Adamantine Being</gloss>, it is called receiving the blessing. To teach that is to make it clear. The offering itself is the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>indestructible reality</gloss>, for the sake of the teaching itself, through its power. The phrase with desire means with devotion. The phrase <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>Awakening Being</gloss> refers to one who appears as an illusion and so forth, or one who acts with a mind that does not perceive individual distinctions. That very point is stated: through the mind of non-dual primordial wisdom. Here, non-dual primordial wisdom is that which is without appearances. Mind refers to conceptual thought. The term impure refers to that which has not been purified through the form of the deity. Regarding those whose number is fixed at six, this is what is said. Thus, the intention is to say, please explain the purity of these. 

If one wonders from what the sensory faculties themselves are seen as pure, it is stated: the complete purity of all objects, and so forth. All objects refers to the purity of all objects of knowledge as deities, as was stated above. Therefore, the intended meaning is that this does not need to be explained here. The nature of the purity of the eyes and so forth is the essence of the support, such as <term>Moha-vajra</term> <gloss>Delusion-Vajra</gloss> and the others. Thus, the transformation of these is divided into three: the first, the sixth, and the seventh. 

The intention is the hidden meaning. To speak only of a portion is what is said; the meaning is that the hidden intention is spoken of as primary, whereas the literal words are not primary. The phrase great <term>samaya</term> <gloss>sacred commitment</gloss> refers to the secret symbolic language. The term unshakeable means that which cannot be illustrated. By this, the secret is spoken. Regarding that which is spoken of as the most secret, it says laughing and so forth. By the four refers to the <term>Kriya</term> <gloss>Action</gloss>, <term>Charya</term> <gloss>Conduct</gloss>, <term>Yoga</term>, and <term>Anuttarayoga</term> <gloss>Unsurpassed Yoga</gloss> tantras. It also symbolizes laughing, looking, embracing, and the union of the two. Thus, in the Action Tantras and so forth, where the deities of method and wisdom demonstrate their passion, it is shown through smiling, in some cases through looking at one another, in some through embracing, and in some through the union of the two.

<summary>This text explains the symbolic language and classifications of the four classes of Tantra. It emphasizes that the secret meaning or intention of the teachings takes precedence over literal interpretations.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrasattva, Bodhisattva, non-dual wisdom, sensory purity, four tantras, samaya, symbolic language</keywords>

A.text:
Why are these called <term>Bodhi</term> <gloss>Awakening</gloss>? He says, "fainting" and so forth. Fainting refers to being intoxicated by having eaten poison. In this context, "not knowing" refers to the absence of the mental engagement that acts as the antidote to poison. Abandoning ignorance refers to knowing the essential nature of the poison. Because one possesses the mind of the essential nature that removes poison, it is linked to the phrase "whatever mind that is." The phrase "it completely cuts off their suffering" refers to cutting off the miseries of those tormented by the pain of having eaten poison. This is the example.

To apply this to the actual meaning, he says: "In that same way," and so forth. Liberation refers to <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the state beyond suffering</gloss>. "Exerted" means having performed great toil. Because it is not associated with the <term>kleshas</term> <gloss>mental afflictions</gloss>, "not knowing" refers to <term>avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss>. The word "and so forth" includes stinginess, anger, laziness, and others. Ignorance here is the ignorance of the mental afflictions. The word "and so forth" refers to the afflictions of attachment and so on, which are the actual bonds.

To explain the logic of why sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, he says: "Not a Buddha," and so forth. "A single sentient being" means even one individual sentient being. "Complete Awakening" refers to perfect realization. "One's own" refers to the mind's, using the sixth <note>the genitive or possessive</note> grammatical case for the agent. In terms of their family or nature, he speaks in the singular, meaning all sentient beings.

If one asks what the perfect realization of these beings is, it is "the perceived object itself." The word "itself" is used for emphasis, meaning the "very nature." That nature is the emptiness of all phenomena from duality. Seeing that is the very act of seeing emptiness. That itself is Awakening; thus all sentient beings are Buddhas. Simply seeing emptiness is not Awakening. If one wonders what it is like at that time, it is "whatever is Great Bliss." If one thinks there is no bliss in the hells and such places, he says: "The hells," and so forth. "Nature" refers to the equality of nature; it is the inseparable state of merely seeing emptiness.

<summary>This page provides a commentary on the nature of Awakening, using the metaphor of poison and its antidote to explain how ignorance is overcome. It argues that all sentient beings are inherently Buddhas because their fundamental nature is Great Bliss and the emptiness of duality.</summary>
<keywords>Awakening, Bodhi, emptiness, Great Bliss, sentient beings, Buddha nature, ignorance, mental afflictions, kleshas</keywords>

B.text:
Why are these called awakening? It is said, "not knowing," and so forth. Fainting is the intoxication caused by eating poison. Not knowing refers to the lack of mental application <note>Sanskrit: manasikāra</note> intended to remove the poison, which here refers to the mind. Abandoning delusions means knowing the true nature <note>Sanskrit: tattva</note> of the poison. Because one possesses the mind that understands the reality that removes poison, that mind is connected to the phrase "whoever." "Completely cutting through that misery" means cutting through the miseries of those tormented by the suffering of having eaten poison; this is an analogy. To apply this to the actual meaning, it says, "likewise," and so forth.

Liberation is <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the state beyond sorrow</gloss>. "Exerted" means having become very weary. Because it is not afflicted, "not knowing" refers to <term>Avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss>. The word "and so forth" includes stinginess, anger, laziness, and others. Delusion refers to the delusion of the mental afflictions <note>Sanskrit: kleśa</note>. The word "and so forth" refers to afflictions such as attachment and the like, which are themselves the bonds.

Another reasoning for the statement "sentient beings are the state of Buddhahood" is spoken: "not a Buddha," and so forth. "A single sentient being" means even one single being. "Perfect awakening" <note>Sanskrit: samyak-bodhi</note> means to correctly realize. "One's own" refers to the mind; it is the sixth <note>genitive</note> case of the agent. Mentioning the singular term "species" <note>Sanskrit: gotra</note> refers to the meaning of "all sentient beings." 

If one asks, "What is the correct realization of those beings?" it is "the perceived object itself." "Itself" is an emphatic term meaning "the very nature." Furthermore, that nature is the emptiness <note>Sanskrit: śūnyatā</note> of all phenomena from duality. To see that is to see emptiness itself. That itself is awakening, and thus all sentient beings are the state of Buddhahood. 

Merely seeing emptiness is not awakening. If one wonders what it is like at that time, it is "whatever is Great Bliss" <note>Sanskrit: mahāsukha</note>. If one thinks there is no bliss in the hells and so forth, it is said, "hell," and so forth. "Nature" means by the nature of equality; it means the mere seeing of emptiness without differentiation.

<summary>This page explains the nature of awakening and Buddhahood through analogies of poison and recovery. it argues that all sentient beings possess the potential for Buddhahood because their underlying nature is emptiness and great bliss.</summary>
<keywords>awakening, emptiness, Buddha-nature, Great Bliss, mental afflictions, ignorance, liberation</keywords>

Because it aims at what is produced <note>the arising of sensory or mental objects</note>, it is desire. Because it aims at the <term>Sahaja-ananda</term> <gloss>co-emergent joy</gloss> that arises immediately after the cessation of that desire, it is freedom from desire. Because the first joy is even lower than those, it is called the "middle" <note>here meaning mediocre or intermediate</note>. Clarity is called the "medium" just as one might speak of a medium-sized body or a medium-sized <term>chillon</term> <gloss>a type of garment or measurement</gloss>. That which is none of those three is the ultimate.

The phrase "the end of the first supreme joy" refers to making the immediately preceding state perfectly clear. The phrase "this is supreme great bliss" means this is the very highest form of great bliss, which is the meaning of co-emergent joy. To explain the certainty of that very moment, it is said: "There is no self and no other." In that very state, the appearance of "another" as the perceived object and the appearance of "self" as the perceiver do not exist. This is the meaning of "natural joy" <note>original: "prakriti-ananda"</note>, which is perfectly clear because it is infinite, non-dual, and beyond conceptual observation, being nothing but the most excellent bliss.

As it is said in the *Chapter on Union*:
Joy is a slight bliss;
Supreme joy increases from that.
Special joy becomes free from desire;
The remaining one is co-emergent joy.
The first is the desire for touch;
The second is the desire for bliss.
The third is the exhaustion of bliss;
Therefore, the fourth is what should be meditated upon.
Supreme joy is described as craving;
Nirvana is the absence of joy.
The middle is merely joy;
Co-emergent joy abandons all of these.

And from the *Chapter on Student Empowerment*:
Neither without desire nor possessing desire,
Not even observed in the middle;
Because the three are separated,
It is called the perfectly awakened nature.

And also:
Either it is the nature of everything,
Or it is completely abandoned.
The first distinction to be made
Is the abandoning of the three joys.

That which is to be meditated upon in this way is the fourth joy. Also, from the *Chapter on Student Empowerment*:
The first is merely joy;
Supreme joy is the second in number.
The third is explained as special joy;
The fourth is called the co-emergent.

While this identifies special joy as the third, how is the fourth described as the "nature"? After counting the three joys that are to be abandoned, then the co-emergent joy which is to be adopted <insert>is established</insert>.

<summary>This page analyzes the four joys of the tantric path, distinguishing between ordinary joys based on desire and the fourth joy, co-emergent bliss, which transcends the subject-object duality. It cites scriptural authority to define the progression from sensory joy to the realization of natural, non-dual awakening.</summary>
<keywords>four joys, co-emergent joy, Sahaja, bliss, non-duality, tantric empowerment, meditation, Tengyur</keywords>

A.text:
The non-duality of mere consciousness that has abandoned <note>dualistic appearances</note> is emptiness. Furthermore, emptiness is the non-appearance of that very mere consciousness itself; that is emptiness, and that itself is Heruka, because he has consumed dualistic grasping and dualistic appearances. The word "indeed" <note>Tibetan: ni</note> is used for the purpose of distinction. This explains its own essence; however, it means that even by being shown, it is not something that becomes manifest <note>through intellectual effort alone</note>.

Thus, if even the "metaphorical simultaneous wisdom" <note>the joy experienced in meditation with a consort</note> is extremely difficult to realize, what need is there to mention the "actual simultaneous wisdom" <note>the ultimate realization</note>? As stated in the *Chapter on the Assembly of Yoginis*:
"The innate nature cannot be shown by another,
It will not be found anywhere else.
From the showing of the Guru’s lineage and methods,
And from one's own merit, it is realized by oneself."

This is the summary of the meaning of this chapter. For an extensive treatment, one should look at *The Emergence of Hevajra: A Sadhana of the Mandala* which I have composed. This concludes the explanation of the fifth chapter of the second part from the *Difficult Points Commentary on the Hevajra Tantra* called the *Pearl Garland* <note>original: Muktāvalī</note>.

Regarding the phrase beginning with "Goddess," "in the armpits" means in the two armpits. "Five mudras" means for the sake of holding the five symbolic seals. "Ritual" <note>original: vidhi</note> means the method. "Activity" means the conduct. "One possessing the pledge" <note>original: samayin</note> means by abiding in the same commitments. "With a brush" means with the brush itself. "The application of the blessing of the pledge" means for the sake of meditating on the form of the goddess. "Should be eaten" means after having eaten; "should be drawn" is connected to the previous statement. Whoever possesses good fortune through their form and age is addressed in that way. This concludes the explanation of the sixth chapter of the second part from the *Difficult Points Commentary on the Hevajra Tantra* called the *Pearl Garland*.

Regarding the phrase beginning with "Then," "How" means "How should it be done?" "Ink" refers to ink made from the smoke of great fat <note>human fat</note> in a place of black oil. "Will not be accomplished" refers to the practitioner. "Nor in another world" means another world, namely in future births. "Endowed with perfect giving" means one who has entered into the practice of perfect generosity. "Occasionally" means once in a hundred paths. "The sphere of the path" means while traveling on the road. "Should be shown" refers to the teacher. "Where" means in the mandala of the assembly. "Village" means a house. "Nine" refers to the number nine. "Pledge" <note>original: samaya</note> means that which is born from fine grain <note>original: śāli</note>...

B.text:
Non-dual consciousness alone, having abandoned <note>apprehension of subject and object</note>, is emptiness. Furthermore, that very non-dual consciousness, devoid of appearances, is emptiness itself, and that is <term>Heruka</term> <gloss>the Unmitigated Blood-drinker deity representing enlightened awareness</gloss>. This is because it has consumed both the grasping for duality and the appearance of duality. The particle "indeed" <note>original: "ni"</note> is used for the purpose of distinction. This explains the essential nature <note>original: "svabhava"</note> of it; it does not mean that it is something made manifest by further teaching.

Thus, if even the "metaphorical innate" <note>the state of bliss realized through practice that serves as a pointer</note> is so very difficult to realize, what need is there to mention the "actual innate" <note>the ultimate realization of the true nature of reality</note>? As stated in the chapter on the assembly of the <term>yoginis</term> <gloss>female tantric practitioners</gloss>:

The fundamental nature cannot be shown by another,
Nor can it be found anywhere else.
Through the instructions on the methods of the lineage gurus,
And through one's own merit, it is realized by oneself.

This is the summary of the meaning of this chapter. For a more extensive explanation, one should look at the *Mandalasadhana of Hevajra* <note>original: "Hevajra-abhyudaya"</note> composed by myself. This concludes the explanation of the fifth chapter of the second section from the *Difficult Point Commentary on Hevajra* known as the *Pearl Rosary* <note>original: "Mukhavali"</note>.

Regarding the phrase "Goddess" <note>original: "lhamo"</note> and so forth: "in the armpits" means in both armpits. "Five seals" <note>original: "mudra"</note> refers to maintaining the five ritual ornaments. "Ritual" <note>original: "cho ga"</note> means the method. "Activity" <note>original: "bya ba"</note> refers to the conduct. "Possessing the commitment" <note>original: "samaya"</note> means abiding in the same shared commitments. "With a brush" means by using an actual brush. "Joining with the blessing of the commitment" refers to meditating on the form of the Goddess. "Should eat" means after having eaten; "should draw" is connected to the previous statement. "One who is fortunate in terms of form and age" is described by those words. This concludes the explanation of the sixth chapter of the second section from the *Difficult Point Commentary on Hevajra* known as the *Pearl Rosary*.

Regarding "Then" and so forth: "How" means "how shall it be done?" The ink is made from the smoke produced by using "great fat" <note>human fat in a tantric context</note> in place of black oil. "Will not be accomplished" refers to the practitioner. "Not even in another world" refers to another world, meaning in future lives. "Possessing perfect giving" means being thoroughly engaged in perfect generosity. "Sometimes" means occasionally or once in a hundred times. "The scope of the path" refers to traveling on the road. "Is to be shown" refers to the teacher. "Where" means in the <term>ganachakra</term> <gloss>tantric feast assembly</gloss>. "Village" refers to a house. "Nine" refers to the number nine. "Commitment" refers to that which is born from <term>shalu</term> <gloss>rice</gloss> <unclear>...</unclear>

<summary>This page contains the concluding commentary on the fifth chapter and the beginning of the sixth chapter of a technical commentary on the Hevajra Tantra, focusing on the nature of non-dual consciousness and specific ritual requirements.</summary>
<keywords>Heruka, Hevajra Tantra, non-dual consciousness, innate bliss, yoginis, ritual conduct, samaya, Mukhavali</keywords>

A.text:
and so forth. "Great fortune" refers to a great being <note>original: mahātman</note>. This concludes the explanation of the seventh chapter of the second part from the *Difficult Points Commentary on the Hevajra Tantra* called the *Pearl Garland*.

Regarding the phrase beginning with "Then," "vow" <note>original: saṃvara</note> refers to the union and so forth. "Conduct" <note>original: caryā</note> refers to speaking pleasantly and so forth. "Form" refers to color, shape, scent, and so forth. "Musk deer <note>Tibetan: ri dgas/ri dwags</note> navel" refers to musk. "A vessel equal to that" means appearing similarly. "Utpala" is the blue lotus itself; the word "like that" is also applied here. "Cause" means the source, which is connected to the "scent." "Sweet smelling" means a scent that is pleasing to the mind. "Crow’s beak" refers to black aguru <note>aloeswood</note>. "In birth after birth" means in all successive births. "May it become" means "May it be obtained." "Discipline" <note>original: vinaya</note> refers to that which is to be tamed. "Fasting" <note>original: upavāsa</note> means abiding in the eight bases of training from dawn to dawn on days such as the full moon.

"The ten bases of training" means, for as long as one lives, the vow to refrain from the seven wrong actions of body and speech, and not performing the three types of wrong actions of the mind. "One who speaks of being free from attachment" refers to the *Vaibhashika* <note>the "Great Exposition" school of early Buddhism</note>; such a person is a Vaibhashika. That itself is the *Shravakayana* <note>the vehicle of the disciples</note>, which includes the scriptures such as the *Hundred Instructions* and the *Garland of Three Interwoven Sets*.

"Sutra" refers to the Mahayana sutras that are not extremely profound, such as those called the *Single Verse*, the *Four Verses*, the *Dharani of Two Verses*, the *Six Gates*, the *Aspiration to Good Conduct* <note>original: Bhadracaryā</note>, the *Four Dharmas*, the *Lalitavistara*, the *Ten Bhumis Sutra*, and so forth. "Yogachara" <note>the "Yoga Practice" or Mind-Only school</note> means that all these various appearances are mere mind; objects that appear are not true, and they arise as such from the power of mental latencies <note>original: vāsanā</note>, just like a dream. Regarding "Madhyamaka" <note>the "Middle Way" school</note>, Madhyamaka is the path; its meaning is that the mind does not exist by way of a dualistic nature, nor is it non-existent by way of a nature empty of both.

"Shown" means it should be shown gradually in that way. Regarding the phrase "By all Tantras," the following should be joined to it. "All" refers to the five classes: Kriya, Charya, Yoga, Yoga-Uttara <note>Higher Yoga</note>,...

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>and so forth. The term <term>Mahatman</term> <gloss>Great Soul</gloss> refers to the Great Self. This concludes the explanation of the seventh chapter, which is the second section of the commentary on the <term>Hevajra Tantra</term> <gloss>The Diamond of Joy</gloss> titled the <term>Muktikavali</term> <gloss>The Pearl Necklace</gloss>.

Regarding the phrase "from then on" and so forth: <term>Samvara</term> <gloss>vow/commitment</gloss> refers to the union <note>the stabilization of energy and mind</note> and so on. <term>Carya</term> <gloss>conduct</gloss> refers to joyful speech and so forth. "Form" refers to color, shape, scent, and so on. The "navel of the deer" refers to musk. A "vessel similar to that" means appearing in the same likeness. <term>Utpala</term> <gloss>blue lotus</gloss> refers to the blue lotus itself, and the word "such" is also applied here. The word "cause" refers to the elements and is connected to the word "scent." "Fragrant scent" means an agreeable or pleasant odor. "Crow's beak" refers to black <term>agaru</term> <gloss>aloe wood</gloss>. The phrase "in birth after birth" means in all successive lifetimes. "May it become" means may it be obtained.

"Discipline" <note>Sanskrit: Vinaya</note> refers to that which is to be tamed. <term>Upavasa</term> <gloss>fasting/restoration</gloss> refers to abiding by the eight basic precepts from dawn to dawn during the full moon and other specific dates. The "ten basic precepts" refers to the commitment to refrain from the seven wrong actions of body and speech for as long as one lives, and the refraining from the three wrong actions of the mind.

The phrase "speaking of being free from passion" refers to the <term>Vaibhashika</term> <gloss>Great Exposition School</gloss>; that very person is a follower of the <term>Vaibhashika</term>. This belongs to the <term>Sravakayana</term> <gloss>Vehicle of Hearers</gloss>, following the traditions of the "One Hundred Instructions" and the "Series of Three Mixed Works" and so forth.

"Sutras" refers to the Mahayana sutras that are not extremely profound, such as the "One Verse Sutra," the "Four Verse Sutra," the "Incantation of Two Verses," the "Sutra of the Six Doors," the "Conduct of Excellence" <note>Sanskrit: Bhadracarya</note>, the "Four Dharmas," the "Detailed Play" <note>Sanskrit: Lalitavistara</note>, and the "Ten Bhumis Sutra" and others.

<term>Yogacara</term> <gloss>Yoga Practice School</gloss> refers to the view that these various appearances are "Mind Only." Objects that appear are not real; rather, mind itself arises in that way through the power of habitual tendencies, just like a dream.

Regarding the "Middle Way" <note>Sanskrit: Madhyamaka</note>: the Middle Way is the path. This means that mind does not exist by way of a dualistic nature, nor is it non-existent by way of an nature empty of those two.

"Taught" means it should be taught gradually in that manner. Regarding "by all tantras" and so forth, this should be connected to what follows. "All" refers to the five classes: <term>Kriya</term> <gloss>Action</gloss>, <term>Carya</term> <gloss>Performance</gloss>, <term>Yoga</term> <gloss>Union</gloss>, and <term>Anuttarayoga</term> <gloss>Highest Union</gloss>...

<summary>This page provides a philological commentary on the Hevajra Tantra, defining terms related to sensory objects, Buddhist vows, and the tenets of the four major Buddhist philosophical schools.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, Muktikavali, Vaibhashika, Sravakayana, Mahayana, Yogacara, Madhyamaka, Vinaya, Vows</keywords>

A.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
With a waistband made of an elephant hide, she binds her clothing. In her hands, she holds a spear and a sword, intoxicated by the wine of blood.
Her eyes have become blood-red. Traveling to charnel grounds at night, she is seen by the common spirits.
She wears a garment made of a large, fresh, stretched hide, and is half-covered and half-wrapped in a coarse hair-blanket.
Her moon-like face is adorned with the hollow tubes of fresh human intestines, and she rings a bell at her cheek.
Her body is freshly anointed with grease, and she is painted with circular marks made of blood, fat, and other substances.
O Skull-Bearer who makes a crunching sound while biting human flesh with your teeth: protect me!
Terrifying god and goddess, holding unbearable human flesh in your mouths; upon seeing you, who have never appeared like this before,
Even the <term>Mamo</term> <gloss>matrix goddesses or fierce female spirits</gloss> are terrified and agitated. Panting and with wide-staring eyes, they bow to you.
Good Black One, whose body color is deep black and difficult to endure, even <term>Indra</term> <gloss>Lord of the Gods</gloss> and the others
Offer praises to you every single day, and even <term>Yama</term> <gloss>the Lord of Death</gloss> himself always trembles and bows.
The end of the hair of all humans and beings without exception is tucked behind one ear.
A serpent <note>literally "chest-goer"</note> with a thousand hoods is placed as an ornament upon your back.
On the other ear, you wear a peerless lion, and you trample the entire earth surrounded by the ocean.
The sun that moves above with its thousand rays is placed at the level of your navel.
You are the fire burning from the depths of the ocean, capable of drying up the waters.
In order to pacify all women, you are placed as half of the Great God’s <note>Shiva’s</note> body.
O Fortress, O Great Black One who repels difficulties, worshipped by gods and non-gods,
You know whatever human diseases exist; please make us free from fear.
I praise the sister of <term>Yama</term>, the mother of demons, the Mistress of the Desire Realm.
The Eight-Fold Praise to the Glorious Goddess <term>Mahakali</term>, the Mistress of All Diseases, composed by the supreme Brahmin <term>Abhiruchi</term> <gloss>Highest Longing</gloss>, is complete.

{D1778} # In the language of India <note>Sanskrit</note>: <term>Shri Mahakala Ashtamantra Stotra Nama</term>.
In the language of Tibet: The Eight-Fold Praise to the Glorious <term>Mahakala</term> <gloss>The Great Black One</gloss>.

<summary>This page concludes a praise to the goddess Mahakali, detailing her terrifying iconography including ornaments of intestines and human flesh. It then transitions into a new eight-verse praise dedicated to the wrathful protector Mahakala.</summary>
<keywords>Mahakali, Mahakala, Yama, iconography, charnel grounds, protective deity, Abhiruchi, Shiva, goddess</keywords>

B.text:
Bound with a waistband made of a flayed skin, holding a spear and a sword in her hands, she is intoxicated by the wine of blood. Her eyes are bloodshot, and she wanders the charnel grounds at night, visible to the great assembly of <term>bhuta</term> <gloss>spirits or elementals</gloss>. Wearing a garment made of a large, freshly torn-open hide, she is half-clothed and half-wrapped in a coarse hair-blanket. The moon of her face is adorned with the tubes of fresh human entrails, and she rings a bell against her cheek. Her body is freshly anointed with grease and marked with spots of blood, fat, and other substances. May the skull-bearer, who crunches and tears at human flesh with her teeth, protect me.

You are the fierce god and goddess, the unbearable one with human flesh in your mouth. Seeing you, such as has never appeared before, even the <term>mamo</term> <gloss>wrathful maternal goddesses</gloss> are terrified and agitated; gasping for breath and with staring eyes, they bow to you. Noble Black Lady, your body color is pitch black and difficult to endure; even Indra and the other gods offer praises to you every single day. Even Yama, the Lord of Death, constantly trembles and bows before you.

For all humans and living beings without exception, you have subdued their pride. On one ear, a serpent with a thousand hoods serves as an ornament from behind. On the other ear, she holds a peerless lion and tramples the entire earth surrounded by the ocean. The sun that moves above, possessing a thousand rays, is positioned at the level of your navel.

You are the fire blazing from the depths of the ocean, capable of drying up the waters. For the sake of pacifying all women, you are placed as half of the body of the Great God <note>This refers to the Ardhanarishvara form, where the goddess makes up half of Shiva's body.</note>. Great Black One, the Fortress and the Dispeller of Difficulties, you are worshipped by gods and anti-gods alike. Whatever human diseases exist, you know them; pray, make us free from fear.

I praise the Sister of Yama, the Mother of Mara, the Powerful Goddess of the Desire Realm.

The Eightfold Praise to the Great Goddess Palden Lhamo <note>The Glorious Goddess</note>, the mistress of all diseases, composed by the supreme Brahmin Vararuci <note>original: "mchog sred"</note>, is hereby completed.

That very thing is what is called the secret mantra <term>dharani</term> <gloss>incantation/retention</gloss>. In this way, during the first countless eon, a Bodhisattva must completely perfect the collection of primordial wisdom. After that countless eon has passed, they obtain the first stage <note>the first bhumi</note>. On that stage, through having thoroughly purified primordial wisdom, they enter into a thoroughly purified meditative absorption and meditative equipoise and obtain mastery over it. 

Through generating the power of mastery over meditative absorption and generating the power of former aspirations, they bless these secret mantra bases, thinking: "May all these contagious diseases, harms, infectious illnesses, and disturbances of sentient beings be pacified!" By the power of mastery over meditative absorption, they bless the secret mantra bases that pacify the contagious diseases and harms of sentient beings. Through their having blessed them in that way, those secret mantra bases will become accomplished; they will become supremely accomplished and permanently accomplished. 

Likewise, for the Bodhisattva Mahasattvas who abide on the higher stages, however they bless those secret mantra words for the sake of sentient beings and for their benefit, they will be accomplished in every way. Therefore, because they hold the secret mantras through having attained such mastery of meditative absorption, it is called the "secret mantra <term>dharani</term>." Those secret mantra bases which have become the object of that power of <term>dharani</term> are also called "<term>dharani</term>" because they are the objects of <term>dharani</term>. 

In that context, what is the <term>dharani</term> of phenomena <note>Dharma-dharani</note>? Here, when Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages listen to the Dharma from Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the "Dharma <term>dharani</term>" refers to the mindfulness and wisdom that retains—without forgetting for a long time and in their proper order—the measureless, countless, and infinite phenomena belonging to the collections of names, collections of phrases, and collections of syllables which were previously unknown and previously unobtained.

B.text:
That which is such is called the <term>Mantra Dharani</term> <gloss>incantation for retaining secret spells</gloss>. In this way, a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment being</gloss> must first completely perfect the collection of wisdom throughout countless eons. After those countless eons have passed, the first <term>bhumi</term> <gloss>level of awakening</gloss> is attained. On that level, through the thorough purification of wisdom, the Bodhisattva enters into perfectly purified <term>samadhi</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> and meditative equipoise, thereby gaining mastery.

Through generating the power of mastery over <term>samadhi</term> and the power of previous aspirations, the Bodhisattva blesses these foundations of secret mantras, intending that all epidemics, harms, infectious diseases, and disturbances of sentient beings be pacified. By the power of mastery over <term>samadhi</term>, the foundations of the secret mantras that pacify the epidemics and harms of sentient beings are consecrated. Those foundations of the secret mantras consecrated in such a way will become accomplished, supremely accomplished, and permanently accomplished.

Similarly, for the <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattvas</term> <gloss>great enlightenment beings</gloss> dwelling on the higher levels, for the sake of sentient beings, however they bless those words of the secret mantras, those words will be accomplished in every possible way. Therefore, because they hold the secret mantras through such mastery of <term>samadhi</term>, it is called the <term>Mantra Dharani</term>. These foundations of the secret mantras, which are the objects of that power of <term>dharani</term>, are also called <term>dharani</term> because they are the objects of <term>dharani</term>.

In that context, what is the <term>Dharma Dharani</term> <gloss>incantation for retaining the teachings</gloss>? Here, when Bodhisattvas who have entered the levels listen to the teachings from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they possess mindfulness and wisdom that retain, in that very sequence and without forgetting for a long time, the immeasurable, innumerable, and infinite teachings. These teachings consist of collections of names, collections of words, and collections of letters that were previously unknown and previously unattained. This is called the <term>Dharma Dharani</term>.

To the question: why does the Tathāgata enter into meditative equipoise in the meditative concentration called the King of Meditative Concentrations? Do they not accomplish or act without entering meditative equipoise? It is not that they do not act, but rather, since the Tathāgatas do not delight in nor are they graced by acting with distraction, they are always in meditative equipoise. Thus, dwelling in meditative equipoise is the very nature of the Tathāgata. Why enter into that specific meditative concentration and not another? This meditative concentration is the accomplisher of all purposes. Therefore, it is said: the meditative concentration in which all meditative concentrations are included. This means that all the individual functions of all meditative concentrations can be accomplished by this single meditative concentration alone. Regarding the terms "gathered" and "fully immersed," it is "gathered" by way of its essence, and it is "fully immersed" by its activity. The qualities of that meditative concentration should be understood in detail from the sutra called the King of Meditative Concentrations. Therefore, it is also shown by the definitive term "King of Meditative Concentrations." What kind of state is this meditative concentration associated with, and what are its characteristics? It is free from conceptual thought, discernment, joy, and bliss. It is associated with equanimity. Its characteristic is immovability. Regarding the phrase **with the natural light**, if one asks what the difference is between **light** <term>prabhā</term> and **radiance** <term>raśmi</term>, it is as follows. That which arises from within is called **radiance**. That which arises from the outer skin is called **light**. Alternatively, that which arises from the radiation of primordial wisdom <term>jñāna</term> is called **radiance**, while that which arises from the radiation of color is called **light**. Even in the scriptures <term>śāstra</term>, it is said: The radiances of the Buddha emerged at the time of perfectly realizing the Dharma at the seat of enlightenment <term>bodhimaṇḍa</term>. Therefore, one should understand that since the illumination of primordial wisdom arises from within, radiance also emerges.

Due to causes, many sufferings appear among sentient beings in hell, animals, <term>pretas</term> <gloss>hungry ghosts</gloss>, the ranks of <term>asuras</term> <gloss>demigods</gloss>, and humans. In most Buddha-fields, this is not the case. The <term>kalpa</term> <gloss>aeon</gloss> is also of a degenerate nature. By the power of the intermediate aeon of famine, the unbearable suffering of hunger arises intermittently in the world. By the power of the intermediate aeon of illness, many diseases arise. By the power of the intermediate aeon of weapons, much mutual harm occurs.

Many defects of time arise: by the power of destruction by water, the afflictions of the realm of existence become dominant; by the power of destruction by fire, the side of hatred becomes dominant; and by the power of destruction by wind, the side of ignorance becomes dominant.

Regarding the dregs of lifespan, the life of sentient beings is uncertain. At some times the lifespan is immeasurable, while at other times the lifespan becomes ten years, and even that is not fixed. Some die in the very womb. Some die immediately after birth, or in childhood, or in youth, or in the prime of life, or in maturity, or when half of life is spent, or in old age. Because there is no certainty regarding death, there are many instances of grief, lamentation, suffering, and mental unhappiness in the world.

As for the dregs of views, there are sixty-two distinct types of very evil views that destroy all virtue. Regarding those who have definitely entered into such wrong views, even a thousand Buddhas cannot heal them. Furthermore, all <term>tirthikas</term> <gloss>non-Buddhist extremists</gloss> are by nature prone to disparaging others, lack faith, do not join the assembly, are highly contemptible, and are naturally unfit vessels. The continuum of their minds has mostly become like salty, barren soil; the continuum of their minds has mostly become like garlic, such that the sublime Dharma cannot enter their minds.

It was asked: "Blessed One, although Hearers who are without outflows and who have cut the stream of the fetters of existence possess the lineage, how can they manifest the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of Buddhahood?" 

The Blessed One replied: "Son of noble family, therefore, listen to this analogy. Son of noble family, it is like this. For example, a kshatriya king who has been consecrated on the crown of his head had a son. While learning all the various crafts, because his faculties were dull and not sharp, he first learned what should be learned later, and later learned what should be learned first. Son of noble family, what do you think? Because of that reason, should he be called 'not the king's son'?" 

It was answered: "Blessed One, no. Sugata, that is not so. Blessed One, he is indeed called the king's son." 

"Son of noble family, likewise, if a Bodhisattva possessed of the lineage but with dull faculties first exhausts the afflictions through the path of meditation and later manifests the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of Buddhahood, son of noble family, what do you think? Because of that reason, should it be said that he has not manifest Buddhahood?" 

It was answered: "Blessed One, no. Sugata, that is not so." 

And as was said: "Maitreya, there is such a specific type of lineage where one first seeks a lower distinction, attains that lower state, and having known it as lower, does not rest content with just that, but by seeking a superior distinction above it, attains the superior state itself." 

When this was spoken, the Bodhisattva Maitreya said to the Blessed One:

B.text:
Those are the prophecies made by observing their lineages.

The Buddha was then asked: Blessed One, since those <term>Sravakas</term> <gloss>Hearers</gloss> who are without <term>asravas</term> <gloss>mental impurities or taints</gloss> and who have severed the fetters of all existence do indeed possess a lineage, how is it that they will achieve the manifest and complete awakening of unsurpassable, true, and perfect <term>bodhi</term> <gloss>enlightenment</gloss>?

The Blessed One replied: Noble son, therefore, listen as I provide an analogy. Noble son, it is like this. For example, a king of the <term>Kshatriya</term> <gloss>warrior or ruling</gloss> caste, who has been consecrated upon his crown, has a son. That son studies all the fields of craftsmanship, yet because his faculties are dull and not sharp, he studies later what should have been studied earlier, and studies earlier what should have been studied later. Noble son, what do you think? Because of that reason, should it be said that he is not the king’s son?

The reply was given: Blessed One, that is not so. <term>Sugata</term> <gloss>One Gone to Bliss</gloss>, that is not the case. Blessed One, he is indeed to be called the king's son.

The Buddha continued: Noble son, in the same way, there are Bodhisattvas belonging to the lineage of dull faculties who first exhaust their afflictions through the path of meditation and only later achieve the manifest and complete awakening of unsurpassable, true, and perfect enlightenment. Noble son, what do you think? Because of that reason, should it be said that they have not achieved manifest and complete Buddhahood?

The reply was: Blessed One, that is not so. Sugata, that is not the case, and so forth. 

Furthermore, as it has been said: Maitreya, there is a certain type of lineage where one initially seeks the lower distinction, attains that lower state, and having recognized it as lower, does not remain satisfied with just that. Instead, by seeking the higher, excellent distinction above it, one comes to attain excellence itself.

When this was spoken, the Bodhisattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One...

<summary>The Buddha uses the analogy of a king's son with dull faculties to explain how those who initially follow a lower spiritual path can still reach full Buddhahood. The text emphasizes that the sequence of attainment does not disqualify one from their inherent noble lineage or ultimate enlightenment.</summary>
<keywords>Bodhisattva, Sravaka, enlightenment, lineage, Maitreya, analogy, spiritual faculties, Buddha nature</keywords>

By that "way of no-relinquishing," one does not observe the three: the thing to be given as an entity, the self as the giver, and the beggar as the receiver. This is the state of being free from the essence of observation. The word "for" implies that by relying upon and grasping this, one should perfectly fulfill the Perfection of Generosity. 

Initially, by the power of compassion, one abides in the manner of the relative truth and practices giving by the power of worldly conduct. Then, by the power of wisdom, one abides in the manner of the ultimate truth, and by the power of transcendent conduct, when everything is searched for by wisdom and becomes unobservable, at that time, it receives the name "perfect fulfillment of the Perfection of Generosity." Thus, the original objects of the generation of the mind—sentient beings and awakening—are not abandoned. Because of this, the name "Bodhisattva" <gloss>Awakening Hero</gloss> possesses its true meaning. 

If it is asked: "Since the non-observation of the gift, the giver, and the receiver is completely contradictory to giving, how can they be non-contradictory?" They become so through the power of the Perfection of Skillful Means. The Perfection of Skillful Means consists of compassion which grasps the relative and wisdom which grasps the ultimate. Just like the application of creatures that move on land and those that move in water, even though the specific applications are completely contradictory, they assist each other without contradiction through the mode of application and are accomplished and engaged in simultaneously. It is taught that accomplishing all the collections of merit and wisdom until awakening is the supreme way of benefiting awakening and sentient beings. These will also be explained below according to their occasions.
