Thus, because those five aggregates are of the essence of non-existence, they are like a dream, an echo, an optical illusion, a reflection, an emanation, and a mirage. Since the six sense-fields are also these very things, there is no "bodhisattva" at all, because the essence of non-existence is emptiness and so forth. Having thus shown the training as being like an illusion and so forth, in order to open the section on practice regarding skill in means, he said: "Blessed One, will a bodhisattva newly entered into the vehicle not be terrified, frightened, and awestruck upon hearing this teaching?"

He showed that one who is unskilled in means and has not come into the hands of a spiritual friend will be terrified and frightened, but one who is skilled in means will not be terrified or frightened. Then, through the question "Blessed One, what is the skill in means of a bodhisattva-mahasattva who, upon hearing this teaching, is not terrified, frightened, or awestruck?" he showed skill in means. The meanings of terror, fright, and so forth have been explained previously.

That skill in means is shown in four types: skill in means in investigating all phenomena, skill in means in perfecting the six perfections, skill in means in relying on a spiritual friend, and skill in means in avoiding sinful friends. B.text:
After explaining that one will attain that state, it is concluded that a student who practices in this way, through the manner of non-observation <note>original: "mi dmigs pa," the meditative state where one does not perceive phenomena as having inherent existence</note>, will certainly emerge and attain it. In that same way, because those five aggregates <note>original: "phung po lnga," the components of a person: form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness</note> are by nature without substantial entity, they are like dreams, echoes, optical illusions <note>original: "mig yor," specifically the appearance of floating spots or hair-like shapes in the vision</note>, reflections, emanations, and mirages. Since the six sense bases <note>original: "skye mched drug," eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind</note> are also like that, there is no such thing as a "Bodhisattva" <gloss>Hero of Awakening</gloss> because they are empty of substantial entity and so forth.

After teaching this training in seeing things as like illusions and so on, in order to categorize the practice of skillful means <term>upaya-kaushalya</term>, the text states: "O Blessed One, will a Bodhisattva who has newly entered the vehicle not be terrified, frightened, and awestruck upon hearing this teaching?" It is then explained that one who lacks skillful means and has not come under the guidance of a spiritual friend <term>kalyanamitra</term> <gloss>virtuous teacher</gloss> will indeed be terrified and frightened in that way. Conversely, one who possesses skillful means will not be terrified or frightened. This is followed by the question: "O Blessed One, by what skillful means does a Bodhisattva Mahasattva <gloss>Great Hero of Awakening</gloss> hear this teaching and not feel terrified, frightened, or awestruck?" through which skillful means is taught.

The meanings of terror, fright, and so on have already been explained previously. Those skillful means are taught in four aspects:

1. Skillful means in the analytical investigation of all phenomena.
2. Skillful means in the complete perfection of the six perfections <term>paramitas</term>.
3. Skillful means in relying upon a spiritual friend.
4. Skillful means in avoiding a spiritual friend who is a negative influence <note>original: "sdig pa'i grogs po," literally a sinful or non-virtuous friend</note>.

Regarding these, beginning from the passage: "One analytically investigates form as impermanent, yet even that is not observed," up until the passage: "This should be understood as the skillful means of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva practicing the Perfection of Wisdom <term>Prajnaparamita</term>."

<summary>This page discusses how Bodhisattvas avoid fear when facing the doctrine of emptiness by employing four types of skillful means. It compares the aggregates and sense bases to illusions and emphasizes the necessity of a spiritual teacher.</summary>
<keywords>skillful means, emptiness, five aggregates, six sense bases, spiritual friend, Perfection of Wisdom, fearlessness</keywords>

A.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
"is not form and so on" and "why is it that they are not counted among the number of those which are non-dual?" These twenty-eight questions, along with the detailed questions and answers that occur in parts by the two Elders below, should be understood as the definitive establishment up to the chapter where Kausika is questioned.

Regarding that, Subhuti, the meaning of the term <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment being</gloss> is the "meaning of having no basis." There are four types of meaning for Bodhisattvas: <note>1</note> Enlightenment, <note>2</note> the Being <note>original: "sattva"</note>, <note>3</note> the conventional Bodhisattva as the nature of the aggregates, and <note>4</note> the ultimate Bodhisattva. Because all four of these are of the nature of non-entities, the meaning of the term "Bodhisattva" is that there is no meaning of a basis. 

"No meaning of a basis" refers to having no standing. If the so-called "Bodhisattva" were to exist as some kind of entity, the meaning of that term would have a basis and a standing. However, in this way, both enlightenment and the being, as well as the Bodhisattva, do not exist. Therefore, the meaning of the term Bodhisattva has no basis, which is a synonym for saying it has no standing.

To distinguish that very point: because enlightenment is unarisen and the being is also unarisen; "Subhuti, regarding enlightenment and the being, arising and existence itself do not exist and are not perceived." This is because enlightenment, being unconditioned, has no arising. The being also, because it does not exist, has no arising. 

Therefore, "Subhuti, enlightenment has no arising" and "regarding the being, existence itself is not perceived" should be applied respectively. Following that, to explain the sound of the meaning of the word, it is said: "Subhuti, enlightenment also has no basis; the being also has no basis."

B.text:
<meta>This page continues the analytical commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom sutras within the Tengyur, specifically focusing on the ontological status of a Bodhisattva.</meta>

Regarding the statement that form and the other aggregates <note>the five skandhas: form, sensation, perception, formation, and consciousness</note> do not exist, and the question of why these elements are not counted among things that are non-dual: these twenty-eight questions, along with the subsequent detailed questions and answers provided by the two elders <note>likely referring to Subhuti and Sariputra</note> in sections, should be understood as the definitive establishment <note>original: གཏན་ལ་དབབ་པ་, Sanskrit: viniscaya</note> of the teaching up until the chapter where Kausika <note>an epithet for Indra</note> asks his questions.

In that context, Subhuti, the meaning of the term <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment-hero</gloss> is the "meaning of having no foundation." Regarding this, there are four aspects to the meaning of Bodhisattva:
1. Enlightenment <note>bodhi</note>
2. The Hero <note>sattva</note>
3. The conventional Bodhisattva consisting of the nature of the aggregates
4. The ultimate Bodhisattva

Because all four of these are of the nature of non-existence, the meaning of the word Bodhisattva is the meaning of lacking a foundation. Lacking a foundation means having no localized existence. If the so-called Bodhisattva possessed any kind of substantial nature, the meaning of that term would have a foundation and a localized existence. However, in this way, enlightenment does not exist, the hero does not exist, and even the union of the two as "Bodhisattva" does not exist. Therefore, the foundation for the meaning of the word Bodhisattva does not exist; this is the meaning of the phrase "without localized existence."

To categorize this very point: it is because enlightenment is unproduced and the hero is also unproduced. Subhuti, regarding enlightenment and the hero, birth and existence itself do not exist and are not observed. In this regard, enlightenment is unproduced because it is unconditioned <note>asamskrta</note>. The hero is unproduced because they do not truly exist. Therefore, Subhuti, the phrases "enlightenment is unproduced" and "existence is not observed in the hero" should be applied respectively. Following that, in order to explain the sound of the meaning of the words, it is said: "Subhuti, enlightenment has no foundation, and the hero also has no foundation."

<summary>This text provides a linguistic and philosophical analysis of the term Bodhisattva, arguing that neither enlightenment nor the individual being possesses a foundational reality or inherent existence.</summary>
<keywords>Bodhisattva, foundation, unproduced, non-existence, aggregates, Subhuti, ultimate truth, conventional truth</keywords>

A.text: ...by their own power alone; they arise by the power of causes and conditions. For example, when a seed produces a sprout, it does not produce it by its own power alone, but by the power of the collection of earth, water, and so forth. Similarly, all phenomena arise by the power of the assembly of causes and conditions. Because they do not arise by their own power alone, they are strictly dependently originated. Those phenomena that arise depending on other phenomena—even though they may possess the nature of being suitable as form, or being feeling, and so forth—are called "born from a collection" because they arise only from the assembly of causes and conditions. How can that which is "born from a collection" be called an "intrinsic nature"? Therefore, because all phenomena arise through the entities of others, they lack their own entity and thus lack intrinsic nature. Because they lack their own entity, it is called "the nature of non-entities." Therefore, it is said: "Subhuti, the nature of phenomena born from a collection does not exist, because they are dependently originated." This itself is the "nature of non-entities" of all phenomena, and it is called "the emptiness of the nature of non-entities." The other explanation is: "Entities are empty of entities; non-entities are empty of non-entities." Entities and intrinsic natures are "entities and intrinsic natures." The absence of entities and intrinsic natures is "non-entities and the absence of intrinsic nature." In this conceptualization, the term "non-entity" understands that entities do not exist, so both entities and non-entities are included. The term "no intrinsic nature" understands that it is not one's own entity, so both the entities of others and one's own entity are included. Those four emptinesses are called "the emptiness of the nature of non-entities." Because they arise from that, they are called "entities." The term "entity" refers to conditioned phenomena. Therefore, it is said "entities are empty of entities." By the term "non-entity"...

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Birth does not occur <note>independently</note>, but rather it arises through the power of causes and conditions. For example, when a seed produces a sprout, it is not produced by its own power alone. Just as it is produced through the combined power of earth, water, and other factors, likewise all phenomena arise through the power of the collection of causes and conditions.

Because they do not arise through their own power alone, they are exclusively <term>pratityasamutpada</term> <gloss>dependent origination</gloss>. Those phenomena which arise depending upon other phenomena may possess the nature of being suitable as form, or the nature of experiencing <note>referring to the five aggregates of form and feeling</note>, yet because they arise precisely from the collection of causes and conditions, they are called "arisen from aggregation" <note>original: "saṃskṛta" or conditioned</note>.

How can that which arises from aggregation be called its own intrinsic nature? Therefore, because all phenomena arise through the entity of another, they lack their own entity and thus are without intrinsic nature. Because they lack their own entity, they are called "the intrinsic nature of non-entities." Therefore, it is said: "Subhuti, conditioned phenomena have no intrinsic nature because they arise dependently." This itself is the "intrinsic nature of non-entities" of all phenomena, and this "emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-entities" is so named.

The other explanation is as follows: "Entities are empty of entities. Non-entities are empty of non-entities." In this context, entity and intrinsic nature are synonyms. Non-entity and the absence of intrinsic nature are also synonyms. In this conceptual analysis, the term "non-entity" is understood as the non-existence of an entity; thus both "entity" and "non-entity" are apprehended. By the term "lacking intrinsic nature," one understands that it is not one's own entity; thus both "the entity of another" and "one's own entity" are apprehended. These four types of emptiness are called the "emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-entities."

Because it arises from those <note>causes</note>, it is called an entity. The term "entity" refers to conditioned phenomena. For that reason, it is said that "entities are empty of entities." By the term "non-entity"...

<summary>This page explains the philosophical concept of dependent origination and the lack of intrinsic nature in conditioned phenomena. It argues that because things arise from causes and conditions rather than self-power, they are empty of a permanent, independent essence.</summary>
<keywords>dependent origination, intrinsic nature, emptiness, conditioned phenomena, causes and conditions, Subhuti, entities, non-entities</keywords>

A.text:
This is the fifth unshared quality.

The statement "he has no equanimity that is not investigative" means that just as Arhats might neglect the welfare of sentient beings without investigation, the Tathagata does not do so. He sets things aside only after investigating the time and the non-time, the fortunate and the unfortunate, the meaningful and the meaningless, and not otherwise; this is the sixth.

"He has no loss of aspiration." "He has no loss of diligence." "He has no loss of mindfulness." "He has no loss of meditative concentration." "He has no loss of wisdom." "He has no loss of liberation." "He has no loss of the wisdom-vision of liberation." These mean that Arhats, due to the nature of their sphere of activity, do not naturally generate aspiration for the level of a Buddha or the activities of a Buddha, but rather aspire only to the deeds of a Listener <note>Sravaka</note>. Likewise, the diligence, mindfulness, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and wisdom-vision of liberation belonging to the level of a Buddha are not present in the Listeners. Therefore, by not attaining those seven phenomena like aspiration and so forth, they are "lost" in the sense of being deficient.

The Buddhas are never without the attainment of these distinguished qualities. Since they have understood all phenomena, they do not have even the slightest loss. In this way, the Buddhas' aspiration to act for the benefit of sentient beings arises uninterruptedly at all times. Their aspiration toward phenomena like great love and great compassion, teaching the Dharma, maturing sentient beings, and—having perfectly adopted the Bodhicitta <note>mind of awakening</note>—their aspiration to never interrupt the lineage of the Three Jewels, arises uninterruptedly. The Tathagata

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
does not enter <note>referring to a state of mental non-engagement or distraction</note>. This is the fifth of the eighteen unmixed qualities <note>original: "ma 'dres pa'i chos"; these are qualities unique to a Buddha</note>.

Regarding the statement "there is no equanimity that is not based on discernment" <note>original: "so sor ma brtags pa'i btang sྙoms"</note>, it means that just as <term>Arhats</term> <gloss>worthy ones who have attained liberation for themselves</gloss> might neglect the welfare of sentient beings without careful discernment, a <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus-Gone One; a Buddha</gloss> does not act in such a way. A Buddha remains indifferent only after discerning whether the time is right or wrong, whether a being is fortunate or unfortunate, and whether it is meaningful or meaningless to act. He never acts otherwise. This is the sixth quality.

There is no decline in aspiration. There is no decline in diligence. There is no decline in mindfulness. There is no decline in meditative concentration. There is no decline in wisdom. There is no decline in total liberation. There is no decline in the wisdom-vision of total liberation. 

Regarding these points, due to the influence of their limited spheres of activity, <term>Arhats</term> do not naturally develop an aspiration for the level of a Buddha or for the natural activities of a Buddha. Instead, they possess aspirations only for the deeds of a <term>Shravaka</term> <gloss>Hearer; a disciple on a path toward personal liberation</gloss>. Similarly, the diligence, mindfulness, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and wisdom-vision of liberation belonging to the level of a Buddha are absent in Hearers. Therefore, they are said to have a "decline" in these seven qualities, such as aspiration, because they have failed to attain them.

Buddhas, however, never fail to possess these distinguished qualities. Because they have fully realized all phenomena, they do not experience even the slightest decline. Thus, the aspiration of Buddhas to work for the benefit of sentient beings arises continuously at all times. Their aspiration for qualities such as great love and great compassion, for teaching the Dharma, for maturing sentient beings, and for maintaining the continuity of the <term>Three Jewels</term> <gloss>the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha</gloss> after having committed to the <term>Bodhicitta</term> <gloss>the mind of enlightenment</gloss>, arises without interruption. Likewise, the <term>Tathagata</term> possesses diligence—

<summary>This page explains the unique qualities of a Buddha, specifically focusing on how their equanimity and aspirations differ from those of Arhats and Hearers. It emphasizes the Buddha's continuous and undiminishing commitment to the welfare of all beings through the eighteen unmixed qualities.</summary>
<keywords>Buddha qualities, Arhat, Shravaka, aspiration, diligence, equanimity, eighteen unmixed qualities, Bodhicitta, Three Jewels</keywords>

A.text:
"Because of not perceiving mindfulness" means suchness is not the sphere of the consciousness that practices mindfulness. "Because of not perceiving calling" means it is not the sphere of names; for names are "callings." "Because of not perceiving enthusiasm for phenomena" means all phenomena are unmoving. "Because of not perceiving the dense" means the conceptualization of density has been reversed.

"Because of not perceiving accomplishment" refers to the arrangement of formations, which is called "accomplishment"; it is not perceived because it does not exist. "Because of the absence of afflictions" means being free from the afflictions of the afflictions and the afflictions of conceptualization. "Because of not perceiving the result" means not perceiving the form of a result within resultant phenomena.

"Because of not perceiving the aggregates" <term>skandhas</term> means the absence of the aggregates of afflictions, karma, and maturation. "Because of not perceiving aging" means the absence of aging characterized by the change of what remains. "Because of not perceiving conduct" means not perceiving the conduct of coming and going. "Because of not perceiving sin" means the absence of harm. "Because of not perceiving 'I'" means the absence of the "I" that is the nature of views and the nature of pride.

"That by which conventions are attached, that by which things are expressed, and that by which things are shown" refers to the dharma of the speaker. "That by which one conceptualizes and that by which one sees" refers to the dharma of the listener. Regarding "that by which conventions are attached": this is expressed through the sixteen conventions, such as the power of what is seen, heard, distinguished, and known by the noble ones and the non-noble ones, and the power of what is not seen, not heard, not distinguished, and not known.

B.text:
Because mindfulness is not perceived <note>original: "dran pa mi dmigs pa"</note>, it means that suchness <term>tathatā</term> <gloss>the true nature of reality</gloss> is not an object of the knowledge that performs mindfulness. Because calling out <note>original: "bod pa," referring to naming or addressing</note> is not perceived, it is not an object of names. A name is a calling out. Because enthusiasm for phenomena is not perceived, it means all phenomena are without movement or agitation.

Because thickness <note>original: "stug po," often referring to the density of material or conceptual obscuration</note> is not perceived, it means the conceptualization of thickness has been reversed. Because accomplishment <note>original: "rnam par bsgrub pa"</note> is not perceived, it refers to the arrangement of conditioned factors <term>saṃskāra</term> <gloss>formative forces or mental constructions</gloss> as accomplishment; since that arrangement is absent, it is not perceived.

Because there is no affliction <term>kleśa</term> <gloss>disturbing emotions or mental poisons</gloss>, it means one is free from the affliction of the afflictions themselves and from the affliction of conceptualization. Because the result is not perceived, it means the aspect of a result is not perceived within the phenomena that constitute the result. Because the aggregates <term>skandha</term> <gloss>the five heaps of physical and mental components</gloss> are not perceived, it means the aggregates of afflictions, karma, and ripening results are absent.

Because aging is not perceived, it means there is no aging characterized by the change of a state into something else. Because conduct is not perceived, it means the conduct of coming and going is not perceived. Because sin <note>original: "sdig pa"</note> is not perceived, it means there is no harmfulness. Because the "I-grasping" <term>ahaṃkāra</term> <gloss>the ego-sense or self-identification</gloss> is not perceived, it means there is no "I-grasping" consisting of the nature of views or the nature of pride.

That which establishes conventions, that which expresses, and that which teaches: these are the phenomena of the speaker. That which conceptualizes and that which sees: these are the phenomena of the listener. Regarding the phrase "that which establishes conventions," this refers to what is seen, heard, distinguished, and cognized by the noble ones and those who are not noble ones. This is expressed through the power of the sixteen conventions, which include what is seen and not seen, heard and not heard, distinguished and not distinguished, and cognized and not cognized.

<summary>This page provides a philosophical commentary on the non-perception of various concepts such as mindfulness, naming, results, and aging within the framework of emptiness. It also distinguishes between the roles of the speaker and listener in establishing linguistic conventions.</summary>
<keywords>emptiness, non-perception, aggregates, mindfulness, conventions, speech, listening, ego-grasping, suchness</keywords>

A.text:
Then, the Blessed One, being greatly pleased by the very cycles spoken by the Elder, taught in the previously explained sequence that phenomena such as the perfections, which have become the nature of maturation, are included in the <term>dharmakaya</term> and are the Great Vehicle itself. After showing the Great Vehicle in that way through the six perfections and so forth, the Elder then spoke five phrases: "it will emerge having surpassed the world of gods, humans, and <term>asuras</term>," "that vehicle is equal to space," "Blessed One, for example, space provides opportunity for countless, limitless, and immeasurable sentient beings," "coming or going is not perceived," and "the prior limit or the later limit is not perceived."

The Blessed One then mentioned those phrases individually, saying: "Subhuti, as for what you said: 'that vehicle will emerge having surpassed the world of gods, humans, and <term>asuras</term>'..." and so forth, and explained them extensively. "Subhuti, if the desire realm were suchness, and were unerring..." and so forth. What is being shown? If all phenomena such as the desire realm were not imagined and were not unreal, but were the essence of the thoroughly established reality, then this Great Vehicle would not emerge from them and would not abandon them. But since all these phenomena are imagined and unreal, for that reason, this Great Vehicle abandons them; this is what is shown. "Subhuti, if the desire realm were suchness, and were unerring, and were not otherwise..."

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>explained. Then, following the series of statements spoken by the Elder <note>referring to Subhuti</note>, the Blessed One expressed his great delight. Through the sequence previously explained, he showed that the qualities such as the <term>paramitas</term> <gloss>perfections</gloss> possess the nature of full maturation. He demonstrated that these are contained within the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss> and constitute the <term>mahayana</term> <gloss>great vehicle</gloss> itself.

Having thus shown the Great Vehicle by means of the six perfections and so forth, the Elder then addressed the Blessed One with five specific statements: that this vehicle emerges having surpassed the world of gods, humans, and <term>asuras</term> <gloss>demigods</gloss>; that this vehicle is equal to space; that just as space provides room for immeasurable, infinite, and limitless sentient beings; that neither coming nor going is perceived; and that neither a prior limit nor a posterior limit is perceived. 

The Blessed One then took up each of these statements individually, starting with: Subhuti, as for what you said, that this vehicle will emerge having surpassed the world of gods, humans, and demigods; and he explained them extensively. 

If one asks how the teaching is presented in the passage beginning with: Subhuti, if the desire realm were suchness, unerring and so forth: if all phenomena such as the desire realm were not conceptually constructed and unreal, but were instead the truly established nature of reality itself, then this Great Vehicle would not emerge from them and would not abandon them. However, since all these phenomena are conceptually constructed and unreal, it is taught that this Great Vehicle completely abandons them. 

Subhuti, if the desire realm were suchness, unerring and not otherwise <unclear>...</unclear>

<summary>This page explains the nature of the Great Vehicle as being equal to space and transcending the world. It argues that the Mahayana emerges by abandoning the desire realm and other phenomena because they are conceptually constructed rather than being inherently real suchness.</summary>
<keywords>Mahayana, Paramitas, Dharmakaya, Subhuti, Suchness, Conceptually Constructed, Desire Realm, Space</keywords>

A.text:
Since that itself is <term>kun brtags pa</term> <gloss>the imagined nature</gloss>, it does not exist. If emptiness does not exist, the meaning of the phrase "form would exist within it" is expressed as "it would transform into form."

After showing that the qualities such as the <term>paramita</term> <gloss>perfection</gloss> of generosity are not perceived within the equality of the three times <note>past, present, and future</note>, one might ask: what is intended by the statement, "If even equality itself is not perceived in equality?" On the level of the ultimate <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss>, all phenomena such as the perfections become the nature of full maturation. They follow the essence of emptiness. Therefore, in that state, even what is called the equality of the three times does not exist. Nor do the perfections of generosity and the rest, which belong to the three times, exist there. Consequently, the text asks: "How could the perfections of generosity of the past, future, and present be perceived within equality?" The same logic should be applied to all other factors.

The categories of analysis should be understood as follows:
*   The category of analyzing the equality of the three times.
*   The category of analyzing all phenomena through the gate of duality.
*   The category of analyzing the three times regarding the phenomena of the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss>.
*   The category of analyzing the phenomena of the five aggregates belonging to the three times within emptiness.
*   The category of analyzing the six perfections within the equality of the three times.
*   The category of analyzing emptiness within those perfections.
*   The category of analyzing everything from the <term>smrtyupasthana</term> <gloss>four applications of mindfulness</gloss> up to the final unmixed qualities.
*   The category of analyzing the <term>prthagjana</term> <gloss>ordinary beings</gloss>.
*   The categories of analyzing the <term>Sravakas</term> <gloss>Hearers</gloss>, <term>Pratyekabuddhas</term> <gloss>Solitary Realizers</gloss>, <term>Bodhisattvas</term>, and <term>Tathagatas</term> <gloss>Buddhas</gloss>.

Therefore, the phrase "This is called the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, the great beings" uses a definitive term to show that because it is the vehicle of great beings, it is called the Great Vehicle.

The Blessed One addressed the Elder Subhuti: "This is the wisdom..."

<summary>This page discusses the non-duality of the three times and the perfections within the state of emptiness. It explains the etymology of the Great Vehicle as being the path specifically for great beings who realize the equality of all phenomena.</summary>
<keywords>Great Vehicle, emptiness, three times, perfections, equality, Bodhisattva, Subhuti, aggregates</keywords>

B.text:
Since that itself is <term>imputational</term> <gloss>conceptual construction</gloss>, it does not exist. The meaning of the phrase "form exists within emptiness" refers to the transformation within form. After teaching that phenomena such as the <term>paramita</term> <gloss>perfection</gloss> of generosity are not observed within the equality of the three times, one might ask: what is the intention behind saying "if equality itself is not observed within equality"? On the ultimate stage of the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss>, all phenomena such as the perfections become the nature of complete maturation. They follow the essence of emptiness itself. Therefore, within that state, there is no such thing as the "equality of the three times," nor are there perfections like generosity that belong to the three times. For this reason, it is said: "How could one observe the perfection of generosity of the past, future, or present within equality?" The same should be applied to all things.

The systematic sequences <note>the repetitive structures or "wheels" of the argument</note> should be understood as:
* The sequence of examining the equality of the three times.
* The sequence of examining all phenomena through the gate of duality.
* The sequence of examining the phenomena of the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss> in the three times.
* The sequence of examining the phenomena of the five aggregates belonging to the three times within emptiness.
* The sequence of examining the six perfections within the equality of the three times.
* The sequence of examining emptiness within those perfections.
* The sequence of examining everything from the <term>applications of mindfulness</term> <gloss>smrtyupasthana</gloss> up to the ultimate <term>unmixed qualities</term> <gloss>avenika-dharma</gloss> within those.
* The sequence of examining <term>ordinary beings</term> <gloss>prthagjana</gloss>.
* The sequences of examining <term>Hearers</term> <gloss>Sravakas</gloss>, <term>Solitary Realizers</term> <gloss>Pratyekabuddhas</gloss>, <term>Bodhisattvas</term>, and <term>Tathagatas</term> <gloss>Buddhas</gloss>.

Therefore, the statement "this is called the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva Mahasattvas" is an explanation using a definitive term: it is called the Great Vehicle because it is the vehicle of the Great Beings. Then, the Elder Subhuti addressed the Blessed One, saying "This <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss>..."

<summary>This page discusses the non-conceptual nature of the Great Vehicle, explaining how phenomena and the three times are not found within the state of ultimate equality and emptiness. It lists the systematic sequences of Buddhist categories used to analyze reality and defines the Mahayana as the vehicle of great beings.</summary>
<keywords>Emptiness, Three Times, Equality, Mahayana, Perfections, Skandhas, Subhuti, Prajnaparamita</keywords>

A.text:
Since form and the other aggregates are like an illusion, they are by nature without substance. Because they are not produced, they lack the characteristic of being manifest <term>abhisamaya</term> <gloss>actualization or clear realization</gloss>. Following that, in order to show that there is no lack of the characteristic of manifestation, the text says: "That which is manifest is not form," and so forth. The meaning is that the characteristic of non-manifestation is the perfected characteristic <term>pariniṣpanna</term> <gloss>the nature of reality as it is</gloss>, but it is not the imagined form <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>the mentally constructed nature</gloss> and so forth.

Thus, having shown that the imagined bodhisattva does not exist and is therefore not a fit object for instruction, the text now addresses the bodhisattva from the perspective of ultimate reality. It asks: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva who practices for the sake of enlightenment cannot be found apart from non-manifestation, should I then provide instruction and guidance in the Perfection of Wisdom, where non-manifestation is itself manifestation?" The meaning is that because the ultimate bodhisattva is the essence of the sphere of phenomena <term>dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>the absolute field or reality-constituent</gloss>, they possess the characteristic of non-manifestation. Furthermore, because that state transcends all conceptual elaborations, it is not a fit object for instruction or guidance.

Having thus shown the ultimate bodhisattva, the text says: "If, when this is taught, the bodhisattva mahasattva does not become discouraged, one should know that this bodhisattva mahasattva is practicing the Perfection of Wisdom." This explains the ultimate practice. 

From this point onward, among the twenty-nine points previously discussed, we shall now present the twelve categorical phrases beginning with: "Subhuti, you teach the Great Vehicle in accordance with the Perfection of Wisdom." After presenting them, they shall be explained. 

The Venerable Shariputra said: "Since sentient beings do not exist, a bodhisattva is [not found] previously..."

<summary>This page discusses the ontological status of the bodhisattva and the aggregates, explaining that because they are like illusions and lack inherent production, they cannot be conceptually instructed. It clarifies the distinction between imagined constructs and the perfected nature of reality within the context of the Perfection of Wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>bodhisattva, perfection of wisdom, abhisamaya, pariniṣpanna, parikalpita, dharmadhātu, emptiness, non-manifestation</keywords>

B.text:
Form, and other such phenomena, are like illusions; therefore, they possess a nature of non-existence. Because they are unproduced, they lack the characteristic of actualization <note>original: མངོན་པར་འགྲུབ་པ་, literally "manifest establishment" or "actualization"</note>. Following that, in order to demonstrate that there is no characteristic lacking actualization, the text says: "That which is actualized is not form," and so forth. This implies that the characteristic of non-actualization refers to the <term>pariniṣpanna</term> <gloss>thoroughly established nature</gloss>, and not to phenomena such as form as they are conceptualized in the <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>imaginary nature</gloss>.

After demonstrating that the imaginary <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>hero of awakening</gloss> does not exist and is therefore not a fit object for instruction, the text now addresses the <term>bodhisattva</term> from the perspective of the ultimate reality of things. It asks: "Blessed One, if a <term>bodhisattva</term> who practices for the sake of awakening cannot be found apart from non-actualization, then should instruction and guidance be given regarding the Perfection of Wisdom, where non-actualization is itself actualized?"

The meaning is that the ultimate <term>bodhisattva</term> is the essence of the <term>dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss>. As such, the <term>bodhisattva</term> has the characteristic of non-actualization. Furthermore, because this reality transcends all conceptual elaborations <note>original: སྤྲོས་པ་, refers to the mental tendency to construct or complicate reality</note>, it is not a fit object for verbal instruction and guidance.

Having thus explained the ultimate <term>bodhisattva</term>, the text states: "If, when this is explained, the <term>bodhisattva mahāsattva</term> <gloss>great hero of awakening</gloss> does not become discouraged, then that <term>bodhisattva mahāsattva</term> should be known to be practicing the Perfection of Wisdom." This demonstrates the ultimate mode of practice.

From this point onward, among the twenty-nine topics previously discussed, I shall now present the twelve sets of definitive words starting from the passage: "Subhūti, you teach the Great Vehicle in accordance with the Perfection of Wisdom." It demonstrates that although the ultimate truth is only one and is non-dual, it is taught by dividing it into many aspects—such as the form of reality, the feeling of reality, the perception of reality, the mental formations of reality, and the consciousness of reality—using various terms for that single, non-dual ultimate truth.

Third: "Whatever constitutes the diminishing of form is not form itself."

Venerable Sariputra asked: "What is called 'the perfection of wisdom' is that which has gone far." This means that the wisdom which has gone beyond all phenomena is called "perfection of wisdom" because it has become distant from all those phenomena. "Venerable Saradvatiputra <note>another name for Sariputra</note>, form is empty of form." This means that conceptually constructed form does not exist as a formal entity. 
"That which is the emptiness of form is not form and is unproduced." This means that the emptiness which is the nature of the form of reality is neither the essence of form nor the essence of production. 
"Venerable Saradvatiputra, in that way, that which is the unproducedness of form is not form." This means that conceptually constructed form is unproduced and is not the essence of production. Thus, it is established that the unproduced is not form.

Following that is the occasion for the third cycle of reasoning: "Venerable Subhuti, why do you say 'that which is the depletion of form is not form'?" and so forth.
"Whatever is form and whatever is depletion, both are neither joined nor disjoined." This means that, according to the previously explained method, both form and depletion are conceptually constructed; therefore, both are without inherent characteristics.

"Venerable Sharadvatiputra, form is empty of intrinsic nature" <note>original: "rang bzhin gyis stong pa"</note> refers to the form of the nature of phenomena <note>the ultimate nature of form</note>. Therefore, he said: "It does not abide internally, it does not abide externally, and it is not perceived as being in neither." If it were to abide in something, it would have to abide internally, externally, or in something other than both. However, it does not exist in any of those three in the ultimate sense; therefore, it is non-abiding. 

Having shown that, he precisely expanded upon the characteristics of abiding and non-abiding to show the method for practicing the path to enlightenment, saying: "There is the worldly, and there is the transcendent," and so forth. "Not wavering, not rising, and not passing beyond the world" means [not passing beyond] the mentally constructed. There are three types based on the power of the lesser, middling, and great patience. The rest of the meaning is clear.

Regarding the seven phrases such as "those by which the world comes to be" and so forth, in some contexts the word "world" <note>term: loka</note> refers to the five aggregates. In some, it refers to the world of sentient beings. In some, it refers to the vessel world <note>the physical environment</note>. In some, it refers to the world of ordinary beings. In some, it refers to cyclic existence <note>term: samsara</note>. In some, it refers to mentally constructed phenomena. In some, it refers to the five objects of desire. 

"Those by which the world comes to be" refers to the world of the aggregates. "Those which establish the world" refers to the vessel world. "Those which are equal to the world" refers to being equal to mentally constructed phenomena. "Those by which one gives for the sake of the world" refers to giving the five objects of desire for the sake of the world.

Having shown that everything from <note>the first stages of the path</note> up to the state of an omniscient buddha is without birth, the text concludes: Venerable <term>Sharadvatiputra</term> <gloss>Sariputra</gloss>, in this enumeration, what is expressed is without birth. The eloquence is without birth, and the phenomena are without birth. Those phenomena which serve as the basis for eloquence are also without birth.

Venerable <term>Sharadvatiputra</term>, the statement that form is empty by its very nature refers to the form of the <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>intrinsic nature of reality</gloss>. Therefore, it does not abide within, it does not abide without, and it is not observed as something existing apart from both. If it were to abide somewhere, it would have to abide within, without, or in some third place other than those two. However, in the ultimate sense, it does not exist in any of those three. Therefore, it is non-abiding.

Having shown this, the text extensively expands on the definition of abiding and non-abiding to teach the method for practicing the path to enlightenment. This includes the distinction between what is worldly and what is transcendent. The phrase "not moving, not rising above, and not passing beyond the world" means that these are beyond what is mentally constructed. There are three types based on the levels of small, medium, and great patience. The meaning of the remaining parts is clear.

Regarding the seven phrases beginning with "those by which it becomes a world," the term "world" is applied in several ways. In some contexts, it refers to the five <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss>. In others, it refers to the world of sentient beings, the container world <note>the physical universe</note>, the world of ordinary beings, <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss>, mentally constructed phenomena, or the five objects of sensory desire. "Those by which it becomes a world" refers to the world of the aggregates. "Those which establish the world" refers to the container world. "Those which are equal to the world" refers to being equal to mentally constructed phenomena. "Those through which gifts are given for the sake of the world" refers to the five objects of sensory desire given for the sake of the world.

Regarding that, in the initial stage, "instruction" is the turning away from what is improper by saying "do not do these things." "Teaching" is the engagement by saying "do these things."

<meta>continues from previous page</meta> and since there is not the slightest attachment to the notion that this is the truth as a self-entity of truth, and because one does not perceive any engagement with the objects of the white or black sides <note>referring to virtuous and non-virtuous actions or phenomena</note>, there is neither grasping nor rejecting. At that time, because one abides in the essence of <term>Sarvajna</term> <gloss>all-knowingness or omniscience</gloss>, it is said that one attains omniscience. It is also said that one attains nothing at all.

### The Great Wonder of Wisdom

When it is said, "Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom is a great wonder," it refers to the fact that because all phenomena do not exist, they do not arise, they do not cease, they are not composed, they are not observed, and they do not perish. Therefore, in that state, they are described by terms such as "non-arising" and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "The Perfection of Wisdom brings about the attainment of all phenomena; the Perfection of Wisdom does not bring about the attainment of all phenomena," if one were to have such a perception, it is said that this is because of conceptualizing both existence and non-existence.

The phrase "one will not have conviction in form" means that one has reached conviction and internal understanding that form has the characteristic of non-existence. The same should be applied to the other <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss> as well.

### Conviction Through Non-Observation

Subhuti, because one does not observe form, one will have conviction in the Perfection of Wisdom. This means that by understanding all phenomena, such as form, to be non-existent by their very nature, one gains conviction in the Perfection of Wisdom and will manifest it directly.

When it says, "It does not make form large and it does not make form small," it means that it does not make the form of the <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>intrinsic nature</gloss>, which is thoroughly established, large; nor does it make the <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>imagined or imputed</gloss> form small. This should be applied to all things in the same way.

Blessed One, a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> <gloss>Great Hero of Awakening</gloss> who has such a perception regarding the Perfection of Wisdom...

<summary>This page discusses the non-conceptual nature of the Perfection of Wisdom, explaining that true omniscience involves neither grasping nor rejecting phenomena. It clarifies that understanding the non-existence of form and other aggregates leads to direct realization of ultimate reality.</summary>
<keywords>omniscience, Perfection of Wisdom, non-arising, form, aggregates, Subhuti, intrinsic nature, non-existence</keywords>

"Whatever is the purity of the feeling caused by the contact of the mind, that is the purity of omniscience. Thus, the purity of the Perfection of Wisdom, the purity of the feeling caused by the contact of the mind, and the purity of omniscience are non-dual," and so on. 

Then, taking the purity of the Perfection of Concentration up to the phenomena ending in feeling, and the purity of omniscience, their non-duality is shown. Similarly, the purity of all the Perfections, the purity of all the Sunyatas <gloss>emptinesses</gloss>, the purity of phenomena up to feeling, and the purity of omniscience are shown to be non-dual. 

Likewise, all phenomena from the "applications of mindfulness" <note>original: "smṛtyupasthāna"</note> up to omniscience, and phenomena from form up to the six groups of feelings, and the purity of omniscience—these should be applied and explained as being one. 

Then, the sequence of the purity of the conditioned <note>original: "saṃskṛta"</note> and the unconditioned <note>original: "asaṃskṛta"</note> is shown, and the sequence of the purity of the three times.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Whatever is the complete purity of <note>purity implies the essential nature or emptiness of a phenomenon</note> is the complete purity of form. Whatever is the complete purity of form is the complete purity of omniscience itself. In this way, the complete purity of the perfection of wisdom, the complete purity of form, and the complete purity of omniscience itself are non-dual. They cannot be divided into two; they are not separate; they are not distinct.

This same logic should be applied to feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the perfection of wisdom. Whatever is the complete purity of the feelings conditioned by mental contact <note>the sixth sense consciousness and its interaction with mental objects</note>, that is the complete purity of omniscience itself. In this way, the complete purity of the perfection of wisdom, the complete purity of feelings conditioned by mental contact, and the complete purity of omniscience itself are non-dual. This should be applied to all such categories.

Furthermore, the complete purity of the perfection of meditative concentration <note>term: Dhyana-paramita</note>, the complete purity of all phenomena starting from the aggregates <note>term: Skandhas</note> up to the end of feelings, and the complete purity of omniscience itself are shown to be non-dual.

Similarly, the complete purity of all perfections <note>term: Paramitas</note> and all aspects of emptiness <note>term: Shunyata</note>, the complete purity of all phenomena up to the end of feelings, and the complete purity of omniscience itself are shown to be non-dual.

Likewise, it should be explained in a unified way that the phenomena ranging from the applications of mindfulness <note>term: Smrityupasthana</note> up to omniscience itself, and the phenomena ranging from form to the six collections of feelings, and the complete purity of omniscience itself, are all one. Because knowledge is unattached and unimpeded in all things, the knowledge of a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment-being</gloss> is everywhere free from attachment and free from obstruction. Therefore, it is called the Perfection of Perfect Discriminations.

Because it completely transcends all the qualities of <term>Shravakas</term> <gloss>Hearers</gloss> and <term>Pratyekabuddhas</term> <gloss>Solitary Realizers</gloss>, and because this Perfection of Wisdom does not exist in the Hearers and so forth, it is counted as the Unmixed <note>unique or unshared</note> Qualities of a Buddha.

This is the Perfection of the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus-Gone One</gloss>. Because everything spoken by all the Buddhas is the state of the Thus-Gone One itself, it is called "Tathagata" by etymology, meaning "one who speaks in that very way" <note>original: "de bzhin du gsung ba"</note>. The Perfection of Wisdom that perceives everything spoken by the Buddha in that very same way is called the Perfection of the Tathagata.

This is the Perfection of the Self-Arisen, because it exercises mastery over all phenomena. In this way, all phenomena come under its power. Therefore, because it overwhelms all phenomena by itself, it is called the Perfection of the Self-Arisen.

The words of praise by <term>Shakra</term> <gloss>Lord of the Gods</gloss>, the words of the Elder Shariputra, and the words of rejoicing by the Blessed One are easy to understand as they appear in the <term>Sutra</term> <gloss>scriptural discourse</gloss>.

When practicing the Perfection of Wisdom, not abiding in form is what is called "exerting oneself in form." This means that the knowledge of the <term>Bodhisattva</term>, which is the knowledge of the aspects of the path, does not abide in any phenomenon at all. Therefore, that very state of non-abiding is called "exerting oneself."

Furthermore, Kaushika <note>an epithet for Shakra</note>, a Bodhisattva does not exert himself in form in such a way...

Subhuti, when it is said that "the Perfection of Wisdom lacks eloquence," it is because it is non-conceptual. When it is said to be "inconceivable," it is because it has completely transcended the domain of logic. When it is said to be "without birth and without cessation," it is #because of its perfect establishment in an unchanging state. When it is said to be "without affliction and without purification," it is because it is pure by its very nature.

When it is said to be # "without agitation," it is because it is always in meditative equipoise. When it is said to be "inexpressible," it is because it is known through individual self-cognition. When it is said to be "unspeakable," it is because it has completely transcended sound. When it is said to be "utterly inexpressible," it is because it has completely #transcended conceptual thought and analytical examination. When it is said to be "non-perceptible," it is because it is free from all perceptions of substantial entities.

When it is said that "perceiving this profound Perfection of Wisdom as a non-entity is also the work of Mara <note>original: "Mara-karma", referring to demonic interference or obstacles on the path</note>," it refers to the fault of failing to show respect for the explanation of the #Perfection of Wisdom through the perception of non-existence. When it is said that "this Perfection of Wisdom is without letters," it is because it is inexpressible and cannot be #heard. The remaining works of Mara are easy to understand through their respective signs.

Subhuti, by stating that "this Perfection of Wisdom generates the ten powers of a Tathagata <gloss>One Gone Thus, an epithet for a Buddha</gloss>," and so forth, it is shown that #because it generates the qualities of a Buddha, it generates the ultimate #Tathagata. The phrase #"Teacher of the World" is explained as being a teacher of the world in eleven ways: being a teacher of the world of the aggregates <note>original: "skandhas"</note>, and the non-perception of the examined nature of all phenomena...

That criticism should be applied in the same way. It is like the analogy of following the tracks of an ox <note>This refers to a seeker trying to find the source through secondary signs</note>, or a carpenter who wishes to build the **Palace of Victory** <note>original: "Vaijayanta," the celestial palace of Indra</note> by searching for the mandala of the sun and moon's celestial mansions, and saying, "The Palace of Victory is exactly this large."

Subhuti, the statement that "the Perfection of Wisdom has no inspired eloquence" is because it is non-conceptual. The statement that "it is inconceivable" is because it completely transcends the domain of logic <note>original: "tarka"</note>. The statement that "it is without birth and without cessation" is because it is established as the unchanging, perfected nature <term>parinispanna</term> <gloss>the thoroughly established nature of reality</gloss>.

The statement that "it is without affliction and without purification" is because it is pure by nature. The statement that "it is without agitation" is because it is always in a state of meditative equipoise. It is "ineffable" because it is known by personal self-awareness <term>svasamvedana</term>. It is "unspeakable" because it completely transcends sound. It is "utterly inexpressible" because it completely transcends conceptual thought and analytical examination. It is "unobservable" because it is free from all observations of entities as things.

The statement "if one perceives this profound Perfection of Wisdom as a non-entity, that too is the work of Mara <gloss>the Tempter or personification of obstacles</gloss>" refers to the fault of failing to show respect when the Perfection of Wisdom is explained, due to an obsession with the notion of nothingness. The statement "this Perfection of Wisdom is without letters" is because it cannot be spoken or heard. The remaining works of Mara are easy to understand through their respective signs.

Subhuti, when it is said that "this Perfection of Wisdom generates the ten powers of a Tathagata <gloss>One Thus Gone; a Buddha</gloss>," and so forth, it demonstrates that the ultimate Tathagata is generated because the qualities of a Buddha are generated.

Regarding the term **Teacher of the World**, it is explained that the world is shown in eleven ways: showing the world of the aggregates <term>skandha</term> <gloss>the five components of individual existence</gloss>, and the lack of observing a self-nature in any phenomena <unclear>...</unclear>

intentions; having no doubt about one's own stage; giving up even one's life for the sake of upholding the Dharma; and not letting the Dharma one has upheld be wasted. In that regard, the statement "whatever that suchness is, there is no doubt that it is neither one nor both" shows the single nature of the Tathāgatas by the power of the suchness of all persons. This means that whatever is the essence or the essence of both is not the essence of suchness. "All phenomena are without aspect, without sign, and without mark" is because there are no aspects within suchness.

The statement beginning "Blessed One, if all phenomena are without aspect..." demonstrates this: if there are no aspects and no signs, how can the aspects and signs of non-retrogression be explained? "Subhūti, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva turns back from form..." and so forth shows that the very knowledge of being without aspects is the sign. It is called "turning back from the aspects of form and the signs of form." "Knowing the knowable" means knowing the objects of knowledge. "Seeing the visible" means seeing the view.

"Not considering oneself purified by wonders or auspiciousness" means that the auspiciousness of wonders and miracles is merely created by thought. This refers to rituals like bathing, fasting, remaining in isolation, entering initiations, and the rituals of the extremists and sacrifices. All the signs of non-retrogression are easy to understand. Although one becomes non-retrogressive merely by attaining the first stage, the second type of turning back which occurs on the eighth stage was also shown. Regarding "turning back and not turning back," one is "turned back" by turning back from the stages of Listeners and Solitary Buddhas. One is "non-retrogressive" by not turning back from the stage of a Buddha.

B.text:
Entering into the intention, having no doubt regarding one’s own <term>bhūmi</term> <gloss>spiritual level or stage</gloss>, sacrificing even one’s life for the sake of completely upholding the <term>Dharma</term> <gloss>Buddha’s teachings</gloss>, and doing so so that the grasped teachings do not go to waste. Regarding this, the phrase there is no doubt that <term>tathatā</term> <gloss>suchness or reality as it is</gloss> is neither one nor both shows that because of the suchness of all individuals, the <term>Tathāgata</term> <gloss>the Thus-Gone One; the Buddha</gloss> is shown to be singular. The meaning is that whatever is the essence, or the essence of both, is not the essence of suchness.

All phenomena are without aspects, without signs, and without characteristics because suchness has no aspects. Regarding the phrase O Blessed One, if all phenomena lack aspects <note>original: "bhagavan yadi sarvadharmā nirākārāḥ"</note> and so forth, it demonstrates the following: if there are no aspects and no signs, how can the aspects and signs of <term>avaivartika</term> <gloss>the state of non-retrogression or never falling back</gloss> be explained? This is the meaning of the question.

The phrase O Subhūti, a <term>bodhisattva mahāsattva</term> <gloss>great heroic being striving for enlightenment</gloss> who turns back from form <note>original: "rūpād vinivartate"</note> and so forth shows that the very knowledge of the absence of aspects is the sign. This is called turning back from the aspects of form and the signs of form. To know what is to be known means to know the object of knowledge. To see what is to be viewed means to see the view.

The phrase does not regard purity through wonders and auspicious signs refers to the auspiciousness of wonders and miracles created merely by thought. This includes rituals such as bathing, fasting, spiritual engagements, the practices of <term>tīrthika</term> <gloss>non-Buddhist extremists</gloss>, and sacrificial offerings.

All the signs of non-retrogression are easy to understand through conventional terms. Although one becomes non-retrogressive simply by attaining the first <term>bhūmi</term> <gloss>spiritual stage</gloss>, a second type of non-retrogression pertaining to the eighth stage is also taught. Regarding the terms retrogression and non-retrogression: one is retrogressive because of turning back from the levels of the <term>śrāvaka</term> <gloss>pious hearer</gloss> and <term>pratyekabuddha</term> <gloss>solitary realizer</gloss>. One is non-retrogressive because of not turning back from the level of a Buddha.

<summary>This page explains the signs of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva, emphasizing that true reality or suchness lacks formal aspects and that spiritual progress involves turning away from mundane rituals and lower spiritual paths.</summary>
<keywords>non-retrogression, suchness, tathatā, bhūmi, signs, Subhūti, Bodhisattva, emptiness of aspects</keywords>

A.text: is the **seventy-fifth**. "By the Blessed One, it was said thus" is the **seventy-sixth**. Blessed One, "if a beginner person is to seek for the emptiness of essence, how should they be instructed and advised?" is the **seventy-seventh**. All these inquiries should be understood as being for the benefit of the non-returning Bodhisattvas present in that circle, and for the benefit of future generations. **Twenty-third volume** <note>term: bam po</note>. Regarding that, Subhūti, "form is profound" means that here, the suchness of form is expressed by the word "form." Therefore, when it was asked, "how is it profound?", [it means] "Subhūti, form is profound just as the suchness of form is [profound]." This shows it to be only suchness. The meaning is that form is called profound by the same manner in which suchness is profound. When it was asked, "Blessed One, what is the suchness of form?", what was intended? Suchness is without any characteristics. It neither has the characteristics of form and so on, nor is it dependent upon form and so on. Thus, the question was: "How can the suchness of form or the suchness of feeling be expressed by the words 'form' and so on?" "Subhūti, in that suchness of form, there is no form; yet apart from form, there is no suchness." This means that after abandoning the imagined <note>term: parikalpita</note>, the thoroughly established suchness <note>term: pariniṣpanna</note> that exists apart from the imagined is free from all characteristics, and it is improper to express it with terms like "form." For the sake of indicating the state of that suchness which ordinary foolish beings cannot distinguish from the imagined "form" and so on, it is designated through the convention of terms like "form."

This phrase refers to the seventy-fifth chapter. The phrase, "The Blessed One spoke thus," refers to the seventy-sixth chapter. The phrase, "Blessed One, if a beginner <note>literally: a person of the first action</note> seeks to fully investigate emptiness by its very essence, how should they be instructed and taught?" refers to the seventy-seventh chapter.

It should be understood that all these questions were asked for the benefit of the non-returning <term>bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>those awakened beings who will not fall back into cyclic existence</gloss> sitting in that assembly, and for the sake of helping future generations.

### Fascicle Twenty-Three

Regarding the statement, "Subhuti, form is profound":
In this context, the <term>tathata</term> <gloss>suchness or true nature</gloss> of form is expressed using the word "form." Therefore, when asked how it is profound, the answer is given: "Subhuti, just as the suchness of form is, so form is profound." This shows that it is indeed suchness itself. The meaning is that form is profound through the same manner in which suchness is profound.

When the question was asked, "Blessed One, what is the suchness of form like?", what was the underlying intent? Suchness is without any characteristics. It is neither the characteristic of things like form, nor is it dependent on form and so on. The question asks how one can use words like form to say "the suchness of form" or "the suchness of feeling."

The reply, "Subhuti, in that suchness of form, form does not exist, nor is there suchness apart from form; such is the suchness of form," means that the <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>imagined or constructed nature</gloss> has been abandoned. That <term>parinispanna</term> <gloss>perfected nature</gloss> of suchness, which exists apart from the imagined, is free from all characteristics. It is improper to express it using terms like "form." For ordinary childish beings, that defiled suchness, which cannot be said to be the same as or different from the imagined "form" and so on, is metaphorically designated by terms such as "form" in order to point toward its state.

<summary>This page concludes the seventy-seventh chapter and begins fascicle twenty-three with a commentary on the profundity of form and its relationship to suchness. It explains that while the ultimate nature of reality is beyond verbal description, terms like form are used metaphorically to guide practitioners toward understanding.</summary>

<keywords>Tengyur, Subhuti, suchness, tathata, emptiness, form, bodhisattva, perfected nature, imagined nature</keywords>

<meta>This page contains commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom sutras, specifically focusing on the nature of non-attachment and the realization of phenomena as they are.</meta>

The phrase "that Bodhisattva will decline from the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss>" refers to the fault of perceiving signs <note>original: mshan mar dmigs pa; refers to the cognitive error of grasping at marks or characteristics of objects</note>, which results in attachment.

The phrase "not grasping any phenomena" refers to that very same lack of attachment toward the Perfection of Wisdom. This is "not grasping." The wisdom of a Bodhisattva does not attach to anything and does not grasp at anything at all.

Regarding the phrase "in this way, the Perfection of Wisdom is not separated from the Perfection of Wisdom," the meaning is that the Perfection of Wisdom is, at all times, never separated from the essential nature of the Perfection of Wisdom itself.

Since all phenomena, likewise, are never separated from their suchness <note>original: ji lta bu; refers to the ultimate nature or "thusness" of things</note>, one might ask: "Then how is the Perfection of Wisdom to be fully accomplished?" This is an inquiry: "If all phenomena are never separated from their essential nature, then how can they be taken up through the roots of virtue and so forth?"

The text explains through phrases such as "there is no persistent attachment to form; there is no persistent attachment thinking 'this is form' or 'that is form'." This demonstrates the following: Phenomena do not establish other phenomena, because there is no persistent attachment to any phenomena.

By not perceiving things incorrectly <note>literally: "not seeing correctly" in the sense of not seeing falsely constructed images</note>, one realizes the reality of phenomena according to the character of how they truly abide. This realization itself is what is called "full accomplishment," and it is not otherwise. This is what is being shown. This should also be understood through the examples of the <term>Chakravartin</term> <gloss>Universal Monarch</gloss> and the charioteer.

Then there is the inquiry: "Blessed One, if the Perfection of Wisdom does not produce any phenomena and does not cease any phenomena..." and so forth. This asks: "If the wisdom of a Bodhisattva does not produce any phenomena and does not even cease dark <note>non-virtuous</note> phenomena, then what is the purpose of the six perfections? How are the six perfections to be brought to completion?"

<term>Subhuti</term> <gloss>One of the Buddha's main disciples, known for his insight into emptiness</gloss>, it is in the state of <term>Sarvajñata</term> <gloss>All-Knowledge or Omniscience</gloss>...

<summary>This page explains that the Perfection of Wisdom consists of non-attachment and the refusal to grasp at the characteristics of phenomena. It addresses the paradox of how to practice the path if all things are already inseparable from their ultimate nature.</summary>
<keywords>Prajnaparamita, non-attachment, suchness, roots of virtue, Subhuti, six perfections, emptiness</keywords>

B.text:
That which is called "the <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment being</gloss> will fall away from the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss>" refers to the attachment caused by the fault of perceiving signs <note>referring to the error of viewing phenomena as having inherent, concrete characteristics</note>. 

That which is called "not grasping all phenomena" means that very lack of attachment to the Perfection of Wisdom is itself "not grasping." The wisdom of a Bodhisattva is not attached to anything at all, nor does it grasp anything. 

In this way, that which is called "the Perfection of Wisdom is not separated from the Perfection of Wisdom" means that the Perfection of Wisdom is, at all times, not separated from the essential nature of the Perfection of Wisdom. This is the intended meaning. 

If all phenomena are never separated from their respective essential natures in such a manner, then the question "How should the Perfection of Wisdom be accomplished?" asks: if all phenomena are never separated from their essential nature, then how can they be apprehended through the roots of virtue and so forth? 

The phrase "there is no clinging to form; one does not cling by thinking 'this is form, this is form'" and so on, demonstrates the following: phenomena do not accomplish phenomena, because there is no clinging to any phenomena. 

By not seeing things as real entities, one realizes the reality of phenomena just as they are, in accordance with their abiding nature. This realization itself is called "accomplishment," and it is not accomplished in any other way. This is what is being shown. 

This should also be understood through the examples of the <term>Chakravartin</term> <gloss>Universal Monarch</gloss> and the chariot driver. 

"O Blessed One, if the Perfection of Wisdom does not produce any phenomenon and does not cease any phenomenon," and so forth, asks the following: if the wisdom of a Bodhisattva does not produce any phenomenon at all, and does not even cease "black phenomena" <note>unwholesome or negative states of being</note>, then what is the purpose of the six perfections? How are the six perfections to be brought to completion? 

Subhuti, regarding the state of omniscience...

<summary>This page discusses the non-attachment and non-grasping central to the Perfection of Wisdom, explaining that realization consists of seeing phenomena as they are without clinging to their signs. It addresses the paradoxical nature of spiritual accomplishment where no phenomena are produced or destroyed.</summary>
<keywords>Perfection of Wisdom, Prajnaparamita, Bodhisattva, non-attachment, emptiness, essential nature, Subhuti, six perfections, omniscience</keywords>
