When it was asked, "Is the abandoning of afflictions without having attained omniscience not an unconditioned act?" it was said because it is of the nature of cessation. Since cessation is merely abandonment, movements of body and speech still occur. By saying "These do not harm ordinary childish beings," it is like looking in a mirror or jumping while walking, or like Pilindavatsa using the words of a low-caste woman; these do not harm ordinary childish beings or noble ones in any way.

The Blessed One then replied to the conceptualization "Does one abide by staying on the path or by staying on what is not the path?" and so forth, stating that because the path is of the nature of a non-entity, it is improper to speak of "abiding."

When it was asked, "O Blessed One, if the path is a non-entity and nirvana is also a non-entity, then why is it said 'this is a Stream-enterer' or 'this is a Once-returner'?" and so forth, the underlying thought is: "If the noble persons and the Buddha are described by the power of the path, or by the attainment of nirvana, then if both are non-existent, how are noble persons established?" The Blessed One replied, "Subhuti, all of them are distinguished by the unconditioned." This means that although the path and nirvana do not exist <note>as entities</note>, they are distinguished by suchness, which is the nature of the absence of the conditioned.

When it was asked, "O Blessed One, does the unconditioned distinguish by saying 'this is a Stream-enterer'?" and so forth, the thought was: "If they are distinguished by the unconditioned, does the unconditioned itself distinguish or produce those persons?" The answer was: "Subhuti, the unconditioned does not distinguish, however..."

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
"Is it unconditioned?" <note>original: "’dus ma bgyis"</note> This was asked because the nature of cessation is exactly that. Since cessation is merely the exhaustion of abandonment, changes in body and speech do indeed occur. "These do not cause harm to childish ordinary beings" <note>original: "byis pa so so'i skye bo"</note> refers to actions like looking in a mirror or #jumping and moving about#. It is like when the monk <term>Pilindavatsa</term> spoke to a low-caste woman using harsh words; such actions do not cause harm to either childish ordinary beings or to noble beings.

"Does one abide in the path or abide in what is not the path?" and so forth. Regarding such conceptualizations, the Blessed One replied: because the path is of the nature of non-entity <note>original: "dngos po med pa'i ngo bo nyid"</note>, it is not suitable as a place to abide. 

"Blessed One, if the path is a non-entity and <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>extinction of suffering</gloss> is also a non-entity, then for what purpose is it said: 'This is a Stream-Enterer' or 'This is a Once-Returner'?" and so forth. By this, the speaker asks about the noble individuals and the Buddha. If they are described by virtue of the path or described by the attainment of <term>Nirvana</term>, yet if both path and <term>Nirvana</term> are non-existent, how can the noble individuals be established?

"Subhuti, all of them are distinguished by the unconditioned," the Buddha replied. This means that although the path and <term>Nirvana</term> do not exist as entities, they are distinguished by <term>Tathata</term> <gloss>Suchness</gloss>, which is the nature of the absence of the conditioned.

"Blessed One, does that which is unconditioned distinguish and say, 'This is a Stream-Enterer'?" By asking this, Subhuti is thinking that if they are distinguished by the unconditioned, does the unconditioned itself categorize or produce those individuals? 

"Subhuti, while the unconditioned does not categorize," the Buddha replied, meaning that while the unconditioned does not produce anything, nevertheless...

<summary>The text discusses the ontological status of the path and Nirvana as non-entities and explains how noble individuals are categorized through the unconditioned nature of reality.</summary>
<keywords>unconditioned, Nirvana, path, noble individuals, Subhuti, Pilindavatsa, Suchness, non-entity</keywords>

A.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>

"Is not able" refers to being without skillful means due to the power of perception, as will be explained immediately below.

Regarding the question, "How does one embrace the <term>Paramita</term> <gloss>Perfection</gloss> of Generosity?" it was asked with the thought that if one gives a gift while perceiving enlightenment as an object, it would then be called the Perfection of Generosity.

The statement "does not practice the Perfection of Generosity by way of duality" means that one does not practice by conceptually discriminating between two entities: the object to be perceived, thinking "this must be done for the sake of enlightenment," and the one who perceives.

"Blessed Lord, if one does not practice the Perfection of Generosity by way of duality," refers to the question: "If one does not dedicate and act for the sake of enlightenment by way of duality, how will the roots of virtue increase?"

"Subhuti, those who practice within the two <note>referring to the two truths or the dualistic mode</note> will cause virtuous qualities to increase" is a teaching showing that practicing non-dually is itself the cause for the increase of the roots of virtue, whereas practicing in duality is not. This is called the Perfection of Wisdom that practices without duality.

Furthermore, practicing the six perfections with <term>upaya</term> <gloss>skillful means</gloss>, practicing the factors of enlightenment, practicing the qualities of a Buddha, and the Bodhisattvas remaining immovable from the nature of praise, are all easily understood from the main text itself.

Regarding the four conceptualizations, such as "is it possible to manifest perfect enlightenment through non-entities by means of non-entities?" there is no means of knowing this because it is not appropriate to exert oneself through such conceptualizations regarding perfect enlightenment.

Just as something is neither an entity nor a non-entity, seeing that equality is called "clear realization." This is like an illusion: the imagined nature is not the form of an entity, yet it is not like a rabbit's horn <note>a classic metaphor for something that is utterly non-existent</note>, which is completely non-existent.

<summary>This page explains that true practice of the Perfections must be non-dual and free from the conceptual trap of distinguishing between the practitioner and the goal of enlightenment. It clarifies that while the imagined nature of things is not a solid entity, it also differs from total non-existence, comparing it instead to an illusion.</summary>
<keywords>non-duality, Paramita, Generosity, skillful means, upaya, Subhuti, roots of virtue, conceptualization, illusion, rabbit's horn</keywords>

B.text:
The phrase "incapable" is explained immediately below as being due to the power of objective perception <note>referring to the cognitive tendency to grasp at objects as having inherent existence</note> and therefore lacking in skillful means. The question "How can the Perfection of Generosity be fully embraced?" was asked with the thought that if one gives a gift while focusing on enlightenment, it becomes designated as the "Perfection of Generosity." The statement "one does not practice the Perfection of Generosity through the mode of duality" means that one does not practice by conceptually imagining the duality of the thing to be aimed for—thinking "this is for the sake of enlightenment"—and the person who is aiming.

The question, "Blessed One, if one does not practice the Perfection of Generosity through the mode of duality," asks how roots of virtue can increase if one does not dedicate them for the sake of enlightenment through that dualistic mode. 

The reply, "Subhūti, those who practice within duality <note>The text here clarifies the Buddha's intent</note> cause their virtuous qualities to increase," demonstrates that practicing non-dually is itself the cause for the increase of roots of virtue, whereas practicing with duality is not. This is what is called the "Perfection of Wisdom that practices without duality." 

Furthermore, the practice of the six perfections through skillful means, the practice of the factors of enlightenment, the practice of the qualities of a Buddha, and the remaining unshakable from the essential nature of a Bodhisattva's praise, are easily understood from the main text itself.

Regarding the four conceptualizations, beginning with "Is one able to realize perfectly complete enlightenment through the non-existence of entities?", there is no teacher for this because such conceptualizations are not suitable to be applied to perfectly complete enlightenment. To see equality in such a way that it is neither an entity nor a non-entity is called "clear realization." This is like an illusion; that which is conceptually constructed <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>the imagined nature</gloss> is not the form of an actual entity, yet it is not absolutely non-existent like a rabbit's horns <unclear>one line of text regarding the nature of existence and non-existence</unclear>

<summary>This page explains that true Perfection of Generosity must be practiced without dualistic grasping between the practitioner and the goal. It clarifies that non-dual realization is the actual source of increasing virtuous merit and defines clear realization as seeing beyond the duality of existence and non-existence.</summary>

<keywords>Perfection of Generosity, non-duality, skillful means, roots of virtue, clear realization, parikalpita, Subhūti, Perfection of Wisdom</keywords>

A.text:
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom from the previous section, specifically addressing the discipline of the noble ones and the nature of conceptual fabrication.</meta>

Through such methods as training and the completion of training, it is shown as the defining characteristic of abiding in discipline. This discipline of the noble ones <note>original: "aryadharma-vinaya"</note> is what is called the Perfection of Wisdom <note>original: "prajnaparamita"</note>. 

The phrase "this is the complete destruction of the cultivation of all phenomena" means that it renders the cultivation of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, non-existent. The statement "one does not cultivate the idea that form is a substantial entity" means one does not cultivate the thought that form possesses the nature of a substantial entity.

Regarding the phrase "clinging to the two extremes by thinking of a substantial entity 'this is I,'" it refers to one who possesses the perception of substantiality. It means thinking either "this is the self and it exists separately," or "the self is form," "the self is feeling," and so on. This expresses the meaning of clinging to the two extremes of nihilism and eternalism.

The statement "Subhuti, the perception of form is duality" means that wherever the perception of "form" exists, the conceptualizations of existence and non-existence, or substantiality and non-substantiality, will inevitably arise. Alternatively, it is called "duality" because it turns into the substantial relationship of the perceived object and the perceiving subject.

The phrase "as long as there is a substantial entity, there is volitional action" <note>original: "samskara"</note> means that through the conceptualization of substantiality, volitional actions such as merit and non-merit are produced. 

"One completely discards substantial entities" refers to not discarding the maturation of results <note>original: "vipaka"</note>. "Mastery over all phenomena" refers to perfect and complete enlightenment <note>original: "samyaksambodhi"</note>. "Having attained mastery over the object" refers to the higher knowledges <note>original: "abhijna"</note> and the ten powers <note>original: "dashavashita"</note>.

Then the Blessed One addressed Subhuti, saying, "In the past, when I was practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva in the six perfections," and so forth, showing that when I was practicing the perfections and entering into meditative equipoise upon the higher knowledges and so forth, there was no attachment to the taste of signs <note>original: "nimitta"</note>.

<summary>This text explains the relationship between the Perfection of Wisdom and the cessation of conceptual duality. It defines the discipline of the noble ones as the removal of substantialist views and the avoidance of the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism.</summary>
<keywords>Perfection of Wisdom, Subhuti, duality, substantiality, two extremes, volitional action, mastery, higher knowledges</keywords>

<meta>This page provides a philosophical commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom, likely from a sub-commentary in the Tengyur. It focuses on the transcendence of duality and the conceptualization of phenomena like form.</meta>

Through such means, one is disciplined, and by attaining <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>accomplishment</gloss>, the characteristics of abiding in discipline are shown. This discipline of the noble Dharma is known as the Perfection of Wisdom <note>original: "Prajnaparamita"</note>. Regarding the phrase "this is the destruction of the meditation on all phenomena," the meaning is that it eliminates the meditation on all phenomena such as form and the like.

The statement "one does not meditate that form is an existing entity" means one does not meditate with the thought that form possesses an essential nature of being an existing thing. As for the phrase "clinging to the two extremes by thinking: this is the self regarding the entity," it refers to those who possess the perception of entities. This means thinking "this is the self, existing separately," or "the self is form," or "the self is feeling," and so forth. The meaning is that one clings to the two extremes of nihilism and eternalism.

Subhuti, the statement "perceiving form is duality" means that for whoever has the perception of "form," conceptualizations of existence and non-existence, or entity and non-entity, will inevitably arise. Alternatively, it is called "duality" because it results in the duality of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject. 

The phrase "as long as there is an entity, to that extent there is formative action" <note>original: "samskara"</note> means that through the conceptualization of entities, formative actions such as merit and non-merit are produced. Regarding "one thoroughly relinquishes entities," this means not relinquishing the results of maturation <note>original: "vipaka"</note>.

"The mastery over all phenomena" refers to perfect and complete enlightenment <note>original: "samyaksambodhi"</note>. "Achieving mastery over the objects" refers to the higher knowledges <note>original: "abhijna"</note> and the ten powers. Then the Blessed One addressed Subhuti: "In the past, when I practiced the conduct of a Bodhisattva in these six perfections," and so forth, showing that while practicing the perfections and entering into meditative absorption on the higher knowledges and so on, there was no savoring of signs <note>conceptual marks or characteristics</note>.

<summary>This text explains how the Perfection of Wisdom transcends the duality of subject and object and the extremes of eternalism and nihilism. It defines mastery over phenomena as the attainment of full enlightenment and the higher knowledges.</summary>
<keywords>Perfection of Wisdom, Subhuti, duality, form, self, nihilism, eternalism, formative action, enlightenment, higher knowledges</keywords>

A.text:
By eliminating the perception that takes objects as real and by generating and practicing the perception that is naturally and completely pure, one attains complete and perfect awakening through the mental engagement with space itself. Subsequently, through the primordial wisdom attained after meditation, one achieves complete and perfect awakening regarding the four noble truths. Having directly realized the qualities of a Buddha and by engaging the mind with relative truth <term>samvrti</term> <gloss>conventional or worldly reality</gloss>, one provides the prophecy for sentient beings within the three categories <note>referring to the three vehicles or types of practitioners: listeners, solitary realizers, and bodhisattvas</note>. Therefore, because the practice is conducted through non-apprehension <note>not grasping at things as having inherent existence</note> and awakening is achieved through non-apprehension, there is no fault.

Regarding the phrase, "Blessed One, how can the Tathagata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One..." and so forth, the Elder <note>Subhuti</note> asks: "If meditative concentrations, clairvoyant powers, and sentient beings are all of the nature of non-entities <note>lacking inherent substance</note>, how are they generated? And how are those sentient beings prophesied?"

To this, the Blessed One replied with, "Subhuti, if desires and sinful, non-virtuous phenomena..." and so forth, demonstrating that because everything is of the nature of a non-entity, all things are established; otherwise, they would not be. In this way, because desires and sinful, non-virtuous phenomena are of the nature of non-entities, they can be prophesied and meditative concentrations can be generated.

When speaking of "entity," "non-entity," "self-entity," or "other-entity," it is shown that these do not exist through the nature of a conceptually imputed entity. However, they also do not exist as absolute non-entities like the horns of a rabbit <note>a classic Buddhist metaphor for something that is completely non-existent and impossible</note>. They do not exist as any kind of self-inherent entity, nor do they exist as any kind of entity dependent on another. This is how it is taught. 

Regarding the question, "How can there be gradual practice, gradual training, and gradual application?" <unclear>it is explained as follows</unclear>

<summary>This page discusses the paradox of how spiritual progress and Buddha-qualities are possible within the framework of emptiness. It explains that because things lack inherent substance, they are fluid and capable of transformation and prophecy.</summary>
<keywords>non-apprehension, non-entity, four noble truths, Subhuti, gradual practice, emptiness, meditative concentration</keywords>

B.text:
By eliminating the perception of objects and cultivating a perception that is naturally and completely pure, one attains perfect awakening through the contemplation of space itself. Furthermore, through the subsequent primordial wisdom <term>jnana</term> <gloss>highest cognitive faculty</gloss> attained after that awakening, one perfectly realizes the four noble truths. Having manifested the qualities of a Buddha, one then uses conventional contemplation <note>relative or mundane mental engagement</note> to provide prophecies regarding the three categories <note>or "lineages"</note> of sentient beings. Therefore, because one practices and awakens precisely through non-apprehension <note>the state of not grasping at inherent existence</note>, there is no fault or error. This is the essential meaning.

When the text asks: How does the Blessed One, the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus Gone One</gloss>, the Arhat, the perfectly completed Buddha, and so forth, develop meditations and clairvoyance if sentient beings possess the nature of non-existence? And how are these beings then given prophecies? This was the question asked by the Elder <note>referring to Subhuti</note>. 

In response, the Blessed One said: Subhuti, if desires and sinful, unwholesome states, and so forth, exist as they do, it is because everything is established through the nature of non-existence, and not otherwise. Thus, because desires and unwholesome states have the nature of non-existence, prophecies can be given. Meditations can be generated. 

Regarding the terms "existence," "non-existence," "self-existence," or "other-existence": these do not refer to the nature of objects as they are mentally constructed. Nor do they refer to a state of absolute non-existence like the horns of a rabbit. They do not exist in any sense of an inherent self-nature, nor do they exist as some "other" nature. This is what is being taught.

<summary>This page explains how spiritual attainment and the guidance of beings are possible only because all phenomena lack inherent existence. It clarifies that emptiness is not total nothingness but the very basis that allows for meditation and awakening.</summary>
<keywords>non-apprehension, four noble truths, emptiness, non-existence, gradual practice, Subhuti, Buddha nature</keywords>

A.text:
<meta>continues from previous page: this discussion details the ten masteries or powers of a bodhisattva</meta>

Transforming things exactly as one wishes: this is the mastery over karma <note>the power to influence the results of actions and intentionality</note>. Being reborn in any place of birth, however and wherever one desires: this is the mastery over birth. Whichever objects one resolves upon being accomplished exactly as intended: this is the mastery over resolve <note>the power of firm conviction or interest</note>.

The accomplishment of all one's prayers exactly as desired: this is the mastery over aspiration <note>prayers or vows made for the benefit of beings</note>. The accomplishment of all necessary miracles exactly as desired: this is the mastery over miracles <note>supernormal powers or psychic displays</note>. Quickly understanding whatever profoundly deep objects of knowledge one wishes to know: this is the mastery over primordial wisdom <note>the direct, non-conceptual realization of reality</note>. Obtaining collections of names, collections of phrases, and collections of syllables exactly as desired, and skill in perfectly arranging all phenomena: this is the mastery over the Doctrine <note>mastery over the Dharma and its expression through language</note>.

Regarding the question: what are the three ways in which a <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus-Gone One; a Buddha</gloss> is without need for protection? These three are easily understood from the main text itself <note>referring to the Buddha's purity of body, speech, and mind which requires no concealment</note>. The three applications of mindfulness—being without attachment or aversion—are also easily understood.

The quality of having no forgetfulness refers to whenever and however the <term>Tathagata</term> acts for the benefit of sentient beings; at that time, his accomplishing it in that very way is the quality of having no forgetfulness.

The thirty-two marks of a Great Being <note>original: "mahapurusha-lakshana"</note> are displayed in order to inspire faith in those individuals who take physical form as their standard. Because of the greatness of their lineage, intentions, resolve, aspirations, application of diligence, engagement, perfect accomplishment, wisdom, and skillful means, the Great Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas are called "Great Beings." Because they are Great Beings, these physical signs express and clarify them; therefore, they are called the marks of a Great Being. Now, regarding those...

<summary>This page defines the masteries of a Bodhisattva including control over rebirth, aspirations, and wisdom. It also explains the significance of the Buddha's lack of concealment and the purpose of the thirty-two physical marks of a Great Being.</summary>
<keywords>ten masteries, Bodhisattva, Tathagata, mindfulness, thirty-two marks, Great Being, karma, rebirth, Buddha-nature</keywords>

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Transforming things just as one wishes is the mastery of action <note>original: "las la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "karmavashitā"</note>. Taking birth in any place of birth, wherever one wishes and exactly as one desires, is the mastery of birth <note>original: "skye ba la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "janmavashitā"</note>. When whatever things one resolves upon are accomplished exactly as intended, this is the mastery of resolve <note>original: "mos pa la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "adhimuktivashitā"</note>. 

When all of one's prayers are fulfilled exactly as desired, this is the mastery of prayer <note>original: "smon lam la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "pranidhānavashitā"</note>. When all necessary miraculous feats are accomplished exactly as one wishes, this is the mastery of miracles <note>original: "rdzu 'phrul la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "riddhivashitā"</note>. Regarding any profound object of knowledge, the ability to understand it instantly whenever one wishes to know it is the mastery of primordial wisdom <note>original: "ye shes la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "jñānavashitā"</note>. Attaining collections of names, collections of phrases, and collections of syllables just as one wishes, and being skilled in correctly arranging all phenomena, is the mastery of dharma <note>original: "chos la dbang ba," Sanskrit: "dharmavashitā"</note>.

Regarding the question, "What are the three ways in which a Thus-Gone One <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>an epithet of the Buddha</gloss> is beyond the need for protection?", these three are easily understood from the main text itself. The three applications of mindfulness, characterized by the absence of attachment and the absence of aversion, are also easily understood. 

The quality of having no forgetfulness <note>original: "bsnyel ba mi mngat ba'i chos nyid"</note> means that whenever and however he acts for the benefit of sentient beings, the Thus-Gone One accomplishes it precisely in that way; this is the quality of never forgetting. 

As for the thirty-two marks of a great man <note>original: "skyes bu chen po'i mtshan," Sanskrit: "mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa"</note>, these are displayed in order to inspire faith in those individuals who take physical form as their standard of measurement. Because of the greatness of their lineage, intention, resolve, prayer, exertion, engagement, perfect accomplishment, wisdom, skillful means, and so forth, the great Bodhisattvas and Buddhas are called "Great Beings." Since they are Great Beings, these marks which express and distinguish them are the marks of a Great Being. Now, through these...

<summary>This page explains the various masteries of a Bodhisattva, such as the masteries of action, birth, and wisdom. It also discusses the Buddha's lack of forgetfulness and the purpose of the thirty-two marks of a Great Being.</summary>
<keywords>ten masteries, vashitā, Tathagata, mindfulness, thirty-two marks, Great Being, mahapurusha</keywords>

A.text: If one asks: Since the major limbs and minor appendages do not differ at all in their manifestation of a Great Being, and since it is inappropriate to say "it is exactly this many," does the number thirty-two not become meaningless? While that is true, nevertheless, based on what has been heard and remembered, the following definite number was taught in accordance with that meaning, and here also it is taught by this very number. These marks are presented in four ways: the brief summary, the detailed explanation, the causes, and the results. First is the brief summary. After that, the commentary on those marks is the detailed explanation. Mentioning the past actions <note>original: "karma"</note> is the cause. Mentioning the signs is the result. Regarding the phrase "having the marks of a wheel on the palms and soles," there are two types of wheels in the world: a wheel used as a weapon and a wheel used for movement, such as the wheel of a chariot. These appear on both the hands and the feet. The past actions for this are also of two types. One is included in the Perfection of Ethics <note>original: "shila-paramita"</note>, involving the practice of seeing off and welcoming Gurus; as a result of this, the wheel for movement appears on the soles of the feet. The other is included in the Perfection of Generosity <note>original: "dana-paramita"</note>, involving listening to the Dharma, stringing garlands, going to temples and stupas, and providing service; as a result of this, they appear on both palms. Regarding the phrase "having a wheel with a thousand spokes, a rim, and a hub," if these three features are not complete, one becomes a Universal Monarch <note>original: "chakravartin"</note> and then renounces the world. At that time, one does not attain perfect Buddhahood; an example is the king named Shanka and others. When all of these are complete in every aspect, one attains perfect Buddhahood.

B.text:
<meta>The text discusses the thirty-two major marks of a Great Being, specifically focusing on the Thousand-Spoked Wheel mark found on the palms and soles.</meta>

Regarding the limbs and appendages that manifest on a Great Being: if there were no distinction among them at all, it would be inappropriate to say there are exactly this many, and the number thirty-two would become meaningless. While that is true, based on what has been heard and remembered, the fixed number is taught accordingly, and here as well, it is presented by this very number. 

These marks are presented through four aspects: the brief summary, the explanation, the cause, and the result. 
First is the brief summary. 
Following that, the commentary on those marks is the explanation. 
The mention of past actions <term>karma</term> <gloss>intentional actions from previous lives</gloss> is the cause. 
The mention of the signs is the result.

Regarding the statement "having the mark of a wheel on the palms and soles," there are two types of wheels in the world: the wheel as a weapon, and the wheel that facilitates movement, such as the wheel of a chariot. These appear on both the hands and the feet. 

The past actions <note>original: "sngon gyi las"</note> that cause this are also of two types:
One type is included within the <term>Paramita</term> <gloss>Perfection</gloss> of Ethics, involving the practice of escorting and welcoming one's teachers <term>Guru</term> <gloss>spiritual preceptors</gloss>. As a result of this, the wheel that facilitates movement appears on the soles of the feet. 

The other type is included within the Perfection of Generosity, involving listening to the Dharma, stringing garlands, visiting temples and <term>stupa</term> <gloss>relic monuments</gloss>, and providing attendants. As a result of this, the marks appear on the two palms of the hands. 

Regarding the description "a wheel with a thousand spokes, a rim, and a hub": at the time when these three components are not fully complete, one becomes a Universal Monarch <term>Chakravartin</term> <gloss>wheel-turning king</gloss> through those marks and then enters the religious life. At that time, one does not attain complete awakening. This is exemplified by figures such as King Shankha. However, when all these components are fully complete in every aspect, one attains complete and perfect Buddhahood.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic and karmic origins of the Buddha's thirty-two major marks, specifically the wheel marks on the hands and feet. It distinguishes between the physical marks of a Universal Monarch and those of a fully awakened Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>Thirty-two marks, Great Being, Karma, Paramita, Chakravartin, Thousand-spoked wheel, King Shankha, Buddhahood</keywords>

A.text: They do not mean "excessively long" or "excessively broad." Regarding the explanation of past actions, "by liberating those to be killed, providing food and drink, performing service for life, and practicing the abandonment of taking life": by liberating those who were to be killed from a short life, they remain in an ordinary lifespan, but it does not mean they suddenly become long-lived. Similarly, by giving the necessities of life, one prevents a short life, but does not suddenly make it long. Likewise, here also, the "long" fingers and heels simply mean they are not short; it does not mean they are excessively long. "Towering seven cubits high" means being taller than the body of an ordinary person; it refers to the measure of the ordinary body. Because the crown of his head <note>original: "ushnisha"</note> cannot be seen, the exact measure of the Blessed One's form body <note>original: "rupakaya"</note> cannot be determined. Abandoning the taking of life corresponds to a straight body because there is no crookedness in the actions of the body. "Feet without protruding joints" refers to the bones of the knee joints and ankle joints; if they are prominent, they are called "bumpy." When they are not like that but are very clear yet well-set and recessed, it is called "feet without protruding joints." In others, because those two bones are large, the feet and calves are unattractive. Because they are not supple, walking is uncomfortable and the gait becomes unattractive. Because the Blessed One's joints are not protruding, his calves are beautiful. Because they are supple, his gait is attractive. Others say that in ordinary people, the ankle bones appear on the back of the foot; therefore, their feet are like they have been pierced with nails, and because they are not supple, they cannot be moved freely, and the soles do not appear when walking. In Great Beings, the ankle bones appear in the upper part of the foot's arch. Only their lower bodies move; the upper bodies

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
The term refers to words that are appropriate, and does not denote a sound that is excessively long or excessively broad. Regarding the explanation of previous karma, it states that by liberating those destined for execution, by performing life-sustaining rites through giving food and drink, and by consistently practicing the abandonment of taking life, people who were meant to be killed are saved from a short life. In this way, they remain at their natural lifespan, but it does not mean their life is suddenly made unnaturally long. Similarly, by providing the necessities of life, one removes the conditions for a short life, but does not suddenly create an elongated life. Likewise, in this context, the fact that the heels and fingers are not short is what is meant by "long," rather than them being excessively long.

Regarding the phrase "rising seven cubits in height," this means rising higher than the body of an ordinary person, referring to the proportions of the ordinary physical form. Because the crown of the head cannot be seen <note>referring to the *ushnisha* or cranial protuberance which is invisible to ordinary beings</note>, the exact dimensions of the Blessed One’s <term>rupakaya</term> <gloss>form body</gloss> cannot be determined. Because he abandoned the taking of life, there is no crookedness in his physical actions, and thus his body is perfectly straight.

The phrase "feet without protrusions" <note>referring to the ankles and joints</note> means that the bones of the knee joints and the ankle joints, which are normally prominent, are called "protrusions" when they stick out. When these are not visible but are well-fleshed and fully recessed, it is called having "feet without protrusions." In others, these two bones are large, making the feet and calves unattractive. Because they are not supple, walking is uncomfortable and the gait becomes ungraceful. Because the Blessed One's joints are not prominent, his calves are beautiful. Because he is supple, his gait is graceful. Others say that in ordinary people, the ankle bone protrudes toward the back of the foot; therefore, their feet are as if pierced by nails, and because they lack suppleness, they cannot move comfortably, and the soles of their feet are not visible when they walk. In Great Beings, the ankle bone emerges toward the upper part of the top of the foot. Their bodies move only from the lower torso, while the upper torso...

<summary>This page explains the physical marks of a Buddha, specifically focusing on the karmic causes for a long lifespan and the aesthetic qualities of his limbs and joints. It clarifies that these marks represent a perfection of natural proportions rather than supernatural distortions.</summary>
<keywords>Buddha's physical marks, karma, lifespan, rupakaya, anatomy of a Great Being, gait</keywords>

A.text: "Color like gold" indicates that the body is firm, smooth, and its color is very bright. "Thin skin" indicates that the body is not stained by external or internal dust, dirt, and so forth. The washing of the hands and feet and the taking of baths are performed for the sake of conventional usage, to allow attendants to gain merit and to provide comfort at the proper times. "Each hair growing individually and curling to the right" means that only a single hair grows from each pore. "Curling in a circle" means curling to the right, like a coiled bracelet or a coiled snake; both curl to the right. "Having the mark of the <term>urnā</term> <gloss>treasure hair</gloss> on the face" refers to the spot between the eyebrows where there is a hair that is supple, soft, white in color, and glossy. If pulled, it extends for one, two, or three cubits; if released, it curls to the right with the tip pointing upward. It is like a silver egg the size of an <term>amyurura</term> <gloss>myrobalan</gloss> fruit, sitting beautifully on the face. Regarding the past actions for these two marks: by avoiding busy social distractions, the hairs became individual. By placing parents and others in their proper positions, performing service, giving gifts, and not causing displeasure, the hair became right-curling, long, and well-shaped. "Upper body like a lion" is so called because his upper body is like that of a lion; the chest is broad and large, and because the flesh is full, it is vast and perfect.

B.text:
This page discusses the specific physical characteristics of a Buddha, known as the minor marks and major signs of a great being.

The sign called the "hidden organ retracted into a sheath" refers to how the private area is concealed within a sheath, similar to the golden essence of a lotus retracted into its bud. This physical trait is the result of past karmic actions, such as reconciling friends and relatives and preventing their separation. Because the Buddha kept such matters private and harmonious, his own anatomy became similarly unified and concealed.

The description "color like gold" indicates that the Buddha’s body is firm, smooth, and possesses an exceptionally clear and radiant complexion. The description "thin skin" indicates that no dust or impurities from the outside or inside can adhere to his body. Regarding actions like washing the hands and feet or bathing, these are performed as a matter of conventional social custom <note>original: "samvriti-vyavahara"</note> to allow attendants to accumulate merit and to ensure comfort according to the seasons.

The description "each hair grows individually and curls to the right" means that only a single hair grows from each pore. "Curling in a circle" means they spiral toward the right side, resembling the way a serpent coils or the circular shape of a coiled snake; both are coiled to the right.

The sign "possessing a hair-treasure <term>urna</term> <gloss>a circle of hair between the eyebrows</gloss> on the face" refers to a spot between the eyebrows where a single hair grows. It is soft, smooth, white in color, and oily. If stretched, it can reach a length of one cubit, two cubits, or even three cubits. When released, it curls back to the right with its tip pointing upward. It sits beautifully on the face like a silver egg about the size of an emblic myrobalan fruit <note>the amla fruit</note>.

The past karma for these two marks is as follows: by avoiding busy distractions and noise, the hairs grew individually. By placing parents and others in their proper positions, serving them, giving gifts, and not causing them displeasure, the hairs became long, well-shaped, and curled to the right.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic and karmic origins of the Buddha's physical marks, including his golden skin, the urna hair between his brows, and his unique hair growth patterns.</summary>
<keywords>Buddha's marks, karma, urna, physical perfection, golden skin, Derge Tengyur</keywords>

A.text:
means "exclusively." Worldly beings do not know things exclusively as they truly are. Because they do not know, they become obsessed with them and accumulate <term>karma</term>, grasping and taking up the results of form and so forth. Through the cause of taking up, they become part of existence; the meaning is that they are not liberated from suffering.

"The emptiness of nature does not disturb form by thinking 'it is empty' or 'it is not empty'" means that through the perception of duality, one does not disturb the emptiness of form; this is because they are non-dual. "There is no such nature that disturbs them by thinking 'this is form' and 'this is emptiness'" means the absence of the essence of a thing's self-nature.

"A Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not practice on enlightenment and form by dividing them into two" means he does not practice on form by making a duality of enlightenment. "A Bodhisattva practices on enlightenment" means that by making a duality of the Bodhisattva and enlightenment, he does not practice on form. "Subhuti, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not think 'I am practicing on enlightenment and form'" means he does not practice on form by creating a duality while thinking "I am practicing on enlightenment."

"Practicing on grasping" means practicing on signs. "Abiding in the nature of form" means abiding in the emptiness of form. "Taking up what is designated in worldly convention" shows that even unexcelled perfect enlightenment does not exist in the ultimate sense. "Practicing in those very phenomena" means that although the gift, the giver, and so forth are not perceived, he still practices in those very things like giving; this is the meaning.

B.text:
The action is truly singular, which means that worldly beings do not understand reality exactly as it is. Because they lack this understanding, they develop a strong attachment to things and accumulate karma, thereby grasping at and clinging to the karmic maturation of form <term>rupa</term> and the other aggregates.

Due to the cause of clinging, they continue to exist within the cycle of becoming <term>bhava</term>. This is the meaning of the statement that they will not be liberated from suffering. The nature of emptiness does not cause form to be disturbed by thinking of it as either empty or not empty. This means that form is not disturbed by the perception of duality because emptiness and form are non-dual. Among these things, there is no such nature that creates a disturbance by thinking, "This is form" and "This is emptiness." This refers to the absence of an inherent essence or self-nature in any thing or entity.

The statement that a <term>bodhisattva mahasattva</term> <gloss>great heroic being of awakening</gloss> does not practice by making a dual distinction between awakening <term>bodhi</term> and form means that they do not treat awakening as a dualistic concept while practicing with regard to form. The phrase means that when it is said a bodhisattva practices toward awakening, they do not treat the bodhisattva and the awakening as two separate things while practicing with regard to form.

Subhuti, the statement that a bodhisattva mahasattva does not think "I am practicing toward awakening and form" means they do not practice with regard to form by creating a duality through the thought "I am practicing toward awakening." The phrase "practicing with grasping" means practicing with signs <term>nimitta</term> <gloss>mental constructs or conceptual characteristics</gloss>.

The phrase "abiding in the nature of form" means abiding in the emptiness of form. Furthermore, the statement "by relying on the designations of worldly conventions" demonstrates that even unexcelled, perfect awakening does not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth <term>paramartha</term>. The phrase "practices those very phenomena" means that although the act of giving <term>dana</term> and the giver and so forth are not observed as having independent existence, the bodhisattva still practices those very acts of giving and so on.

Worldly Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahasattva practice the perfection of wisdom <term>prajnaparamita</term>? <note>The text breaks here mid-question.</note>

<summary>This page explains the non-duality of form and emptiness, emphasizing that bodhisattvas avoid conceptual grasping and dualistic distinctions during their practice. It clarifies that while phenomena like awakening and giving are designated conventionally, they lack inherent existence in ultimate truth.</summary>
<keywords>non-duality, emptiness, bodhisattva, form, grasping, conventional truth, ultimate truth, Subhuti, perfection of wisdom</keywords>

A.text:
"Subhuti, realization does not occur through duality, nor does realization occur through non-duality." This means: if one were to see some conditioned or unconditioned entity, realization would occur through duality. If it were something utterly non-existent like a rabbit's horn, then realization would occur through non-duality <note>mere negation</note>. Therefore, the reversal of those two modes is the realization of equality, which is true realization. 

"Ineffable" refers to that which is not an object of expression or detailed description. To this, he says, "Subhuti, it should be treated as a conventional worldly designation." 

Regarding "The Tathagata has perfectly awakened to the Dharma," this refers to the ultimate transformation of the basis. Because he abides in equality, having abandoned all conceptualization and proliferation <note>original: <term>prapanca</term></note>, there is not even any "thing to be known." Since he does not see any object to be known, he shows: "what is there to be perfectly awakened to?" 

The question "Blessed One, what is this called 'equality' among phenomena whose essence is non-existence?" was asked with the thought that if phenomena exist, then "equality" must also exist. 

"Subhuti, in this case, that itself is equality" means that the equality of phenomena whose essence is non-existence is itself the essence of non-existence. This is because conceptualization of them as "entities" has been abandoned. 

"Subhuti, the equality of phenomena is not even the sphere of a Tathagata" means that the equality of phenomena is not the object/sphere of anyone; even the Tathagata does not see the equality of phenomena as an essence <note>objectively</note>. 

The passage "In the equality of phenomena, ordinary childish people..." and so forth shows that the equality of phenomena is the same for ordinary childish people, all noble ones, and the Tathagata. 

"He does not move from the equality of phenomena, yet he also performs the arrangement of phenomena" means he does not move from the ultimate truth, yet he performs the arrangement in the conventional sense.

B.text:
One does not attain realization through duality. Nor does one attain realization through non-duality. This means that if one were to perceive any entity, whether <term>conditioned</term> <gloss>products of causes and conditions</gloss> or <term>unconditioned</term> <gloss>phenomena like space or nirvana that do not arise from causes</gloss>, then realization would occur through duality. If things were utterly non-existent, like the horns of a rabbit, then realization would occur through non-duality. Therefore, reversing those two modes is the thorough realization of <term>equanimity</term> <gloss>the essential sameness of all things</gloss>; this is what is shown to be realization.

The phrase "inexpressible" refers to that which is neither an object of verbal expression nor a subject of thorough description, yet Subhuti, it is spoken of in the terms of worldly convention. The statement "The Tathagata <gloss>One Gone Thus; the Buddha</gloss> has perfectly awakened to the Dharma" refers to the ultimate transformation of the basis. Because one dwells in equanimity, having abandoned all conceptual construction and <term>proliferated thought</term> <gloss>the tendency of the mind to elaborate on perceptions</gloss>, there is nothing even to be known. Since no object to be known is seen, what is there to be perfectly awakened to? This is what is being shown.

The question "Blessed One, what is this called 'equanimity' regarding phenomena that are non-existent by nature?" reflects the thought that if phenomena existed, then equanimity would also exist. The reply, "Subhuti, herein that itself is equanimity," means that the equanimity of phenomena that are non-existent by nature is itself their non-existent nature. This is because even the conceptualization of them as entities has been abandoned.

The phrase "Subhuti, the equanimity of phenomena is not even the sphere of the Tathagata" means that the equanimity of phenomena does not become the sphere of anyone at all. Even the Tathagata does not perceive the essence of the equanimity of phenomena as an object. Regarding the phrase "In the equanimity of phenomena, ordinary childish beings..." and so on, the equanimity of the Dharma is the same for ordinary childish beings, for all noble ones, and for the Tathagata. It does not waver from the equanimity of phenomena, yet the arrangement of phenomena <unclear>one line of text not transcribed</unclear>

<summary>This page explains the nature of realization and equanimity in the context of the Perfection of Wisdom. It clarifies that true realization transcends the duality of existence and non-existence, and that the ultimate nature of reality is beyond the reach of conceptual thought or even the Buddha's objective perception.</summary>
<keywords>realization, duality, equanimity, non-existence, Tathagata, Subhuti, conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena, conceptual construction</keywords>

A.text:
At the time of non-conceptualization, because there is no <note>distorted</note> other-dependency, it is non-erroneous; the meaning is that one observes the ultimate itself. When asked this, the Noble Maitreya accepted it, saying, "Blessed One, it is so." 

Then the Blessed One said: "Maitreya, if that is the case, is it not merely conceptualization?" Having established it as mere conceptualization, in order to then negate the existence of an entity, he said: "When he thus dwells in the non-conceptual sphere and becomes free from conceptualizations, what existence is there for him?" Here, "he" refers to the Bodhisattva. "Thus" means "if it does not exist in the ultimate sense." "Dwell in the non-conceptual sphere" means dwelling in the ultimate sphere. "What existence is there for him" refers to what existence is there for that entity of the marks of conditioned factors; the meaning is that it simply does not exist. "Whatever exists would be observed" means that if it were to exist, it would be observed. 

Thus, having correctly shown that the entity of conditioned factors does not exist, and further, in order to show the Noble Maitreya the classifications of all phenomena such as form through the influence of the conventional and the ultimate, it was then asked: "Blessed One, how many types of imagined classifications of form should a Bodhisattva, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom and has entered into the skill of classifying phenomena, understand?" 

Then the Blessed One showed the classifications by saying: "Maitreya, they should be understood in three ways," and so forth. He showed that all mundane and supramundane

B.text:
When there is no conceptualization, because it is no longer dependent on others <note>referring to the lack of dependency on external conditions or deluded causal chains</note>, it is unerring. This is a definition for observing the ultimate truth itself. When this was asked, the Noble Maitreya agreed, saying, Blessed One, it is so.

Then the Blessed One said: Maitreya, if that is the case, is it not merely conceptualization? By establishing it as mere conceptualization, and subsequently in order to eliminate the existence of entities <note>the belief in the inherent existence of things</note>, he dwells in that way in the non-conceptual sphere. When one becomes free from conceptualizations, what is it that exists for them? In this context, "them" refers to the Bodhisattva. "In that way" means when things do not exist in an ultimate sense. "In the non-conceptual sphere" means dwelling in the ultimate sphere. "What is it that exists for them?" means what entity of conditioned phenomena <term>samskara</term> <gloss>mental formations or conditioned factors</gloss> exists for them? The meaning is that nothing exists at all.

"Whatever exists would be observed" means that if something were to exist, it would be perceived. In this way, the non-existence of conditioned entities was perfectly demonstrated. Furthermore, in order for Noble Maitreya to show the classification of all phenomena such as form, through the power of the conventional <term>samvrti</term> <gloss>relative or superficial truth</gloss> and the ultimate <term>paramartha</term> <gloss>absolute truth</gloss>, he asked the following: Blessed One, since a Bodhisattva practicing the Perfection of Wisdom <term>Prajnaparamita</term> has engaged in the skill of classifying phenomena, how many kinds of conceptualizations of the classification of form should be understood? 

Then the Blessed One taught the classification by saying: Maitreya, they are to be understood in three ways. These range from the imagined form, the conceptualized form, and the form of the nature of phenomena <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>the intrinsic nature of reality</gloss>, up to the imagined qualities of a Buddha, the conceptualized qualities of a Buddha, and the qualities of a Buddha as the nature of phenomena. Through these, the worldly and the transcendent <note>the text continues to describe the categories of existence from mundane forms to the attributes of enlightenment</note>

<summary>This page explains the transition from conceptual thought to the non-conceptual ultimate sphere, where conditioned entities are shown to lack inherent existence. It introduces a threefold classification system applied to all phenomena, from basic form to the qualities of a Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>Maitreya, non-conceptualization, ultimate truth, conditioned phenomena, three natures, Buddha qualities, Perfection of Wisdom</keywords>

A.text:
at that time, that manner which dwells in its own inexpressible, non-conceptual nature is called "<term>dharmata</term> form." It is called "essenceless" because it lacks the imagined essence. It is called "selflessness of phenomena" because it lacks the manner of a phenomenal self. "Suchness" <term>tathata</term> refers to the non-erroneous manner. "Ultimate reality" <term>bhutakoti</term> refers to the finality of such a manner. The same should be applied to feeling and so forth. 

"Maitreya, whatever is imagined form should be viewed as non-substantial" means it is completely non-existent. "Whatever is conceptualized form should be viewed as substantial, because conceptualization is substantial" means it exists because it exists conventionally. It is a substance in the sense that it perishes in the manner of conditioned things and exists as form; therefore, the meaning is that it is explained as existing conceptualization and being a substance. "It does not function independently" was said because it is the other-dependent essence. "Whatever is <term>dharmata</term> form is neither non-substantial nor substantial." "<term>Dharmata</term> form" is that which is distinguished by the ultimate. Because it exists in an inexpressible nature, it is not suitable to say it does not exist; therefore, it is not non-substantial. Because it does not exist in the manner of a conceptualized entity, it is not suitable to say it exists; therefore, it is not substantial. Thus, having abandoned the two extremes, the Middle Way is shown. "Distinguished by the ultimate" means the essence of the ultimate. The word "distinguished" <note>original: rab tu phye ba</note> means the sense of the "essence." The same should be applied up to the limit of the qualities of a Buddha. 

Thus, having mentioned the three characteristics by way of the three essences, and in order to open the occasion for showing the characteristic of non-duality, the Noble Maitreya said: "Previously, in the context of the summary of the Perfection of Wisdom, twenty-eight questions were shown, such as:

B.text:
At that time, the state of remaining in the essence of the <term>unutterable</term> <gloss>indescribable by words</gloss> and the <term>non-conceptual</term> <gloss>free from discursive thought</gloss> is called the form of the nature of phenomena <note>original: "chos nyid kyi gzug" / dharmatā-rūpa</note>. Regarding the phrase lack of nature <note>original: "ngo bo nyid med pa" / niḥsvabhāvatā</note>, this refers to the lack of nature of the <term>imagined</term> <gloss>the mentally constructed or conceptualized nature</gloss>. The selflessness of phenomena means the absence of an inherent essence within phenomena.

<term>Suchness</term> <gloss>tathatā</gloss> refers to the aspect that is unerring and non-distorted. The <term>ultimate reality</term> <gloss>bhūtakoṭi</gloss> refers to reaching the limit of that very aspect. The same logic should be applied to feelings and the other aggregates <note>the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness</note>.

Maitreya, the statement that imagined form should be viewed as non-substantial is because it is utterly non-existent. Regarding the statement that the <term>dependent form</term> <gloss>paratantra-rūpa</gloss> should be viewed as existing substantially because conceptualization exists substantially, this means it exists in a relative or conventional sense. It is considered a substance because it undergoes destruction in the manner of conditioned things and possesses the qualities of form. Therefore, it is explained as having a conceptual existence and being a substance.

The statement that it does not function independently is said because its nature is dependent on other factors. That which is the form of the nature of phenomena is neither substantially non-existent nor substantially existent. The phrase distinguished by the ultimate refers to the form of the nature of phenomena. Because it exists as an unutterable essence, it is incorrect to say it does not exist; therefore, it is not substantially non-existent. However, because it does not exist in the manner of a conceptually constructed thing, it is incorrect to say it exists; therefore, it is not substantially existent. Thus, by abandoning the two extremes <note>the extremes of eternalism/existence and nihilism/non-existence</note>, the Middle Way is shown.

The phrase distinguished by the ultimate is a synonym for the ultimate nature. The word distinguished conveys the meaning of essence. This same application should be made up to the final qualities of a Buddha.

After mentioning the three characteristics according to the three natures in this way, the Noble Maitreya spoke to introduce the section on the characteristic of non-duality. In this context of establishing the summary of the Perfection of Wisdom, twenty-eight questions were presented as follows:

<keywords>Three Natures, Middle Way, emptiness, suchness, Maitreya, non-duality, ultimate reality, dependent nature, imagined nature</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: Quickly the accumulations are fully</meta> perfected, and one attains the meditative absorption that manifests omniscience. One then appears to act for the benefit of as many worlds and sentient beings as exist; this too is the accomplishment. The Explanation of the Noble Dharani of the Six Gates, composed by the Master Vasubandhu, is complete.

# The Explanation of the Noble Four Dharmas
I bow down to Manjushri, the youthful.

Why was this discourse <note>the Four Dharmas Sutra</note> composed, which states: "A <term>bodhisattva mahasattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment being, great being</gloss> should not abandon these four dharmas <note>qualities or principles</note> as long as they live, even for the sake of their own life"?

It was taught to correctly guide those who are confused about the methods for obtaining unsurpassed enlightenment after having correctly entered the Great Vehicle <note>Mahayana</note>, to cause those who are heedless to correctly take it up, to correctly encourage those who are discouraged, and to cause those who have correctly entered to be truly joyful.

The reason the number "four" is mentioned is to prevent those who do not wish to listen from being discouraged by the fear of vast complexity. By mentioning a specific number, it is easily remembered. Furthermore, as will be seen below, the qualities of patience and gentleness are treated as inseparable since they have a single purpose.

Although there are many terms for those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle, two names <note>Bodhisattva and Mahasattva</note> are mentioned for three reasons: through aspiration, through application, and through understanding.

Regarding aspiration: they are called a <term>bodhisattva</term> because they aspire toward the profound objects of knowledge; they are called a <term>mahasattva</term> because they aspire toward great power.

Regarding application: it is because they strive for the sake of their own unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and for the sake of completely protecting all sentient beings from suffering.

Regarding understanding: it is because they realize enlightenment through two powers. Which two? The power of intelligence and the power of diligence. One cannot realize enlightenment through ignorance or through little diligence. As for the phrase "as long as one lives"

B.text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>completing and attaining the meditative concentration <term>samadhi</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> that accomplishes omniscience. One also manifests the accomplishment of acting for the benefit of all sentient beings, as far as the world extends.

The Commentary on the Noble Dhāranī of the Six Gates <note>original: "Arya-ṣaṇmukhi-dhāraṇī-vyākhyāna"</note>, composed by the Master Vasubandhu <note>a prominent 4th-century Indian Buddhist scholar and philosopher</note>, is complete.

# The Commentary on the Noble Four Dharmas
<note>original: "Arya-caturdharma-vyākhyāna"</note>

Homage to Mañjuśrī in youthful form.

Why was this sūtra composed, which states: "A Bodhisattva, a great being, should not give up these four dharmas <gloss>qualities or principles</gloss> even for the sake of his life, for as long as he lives"?

It was composed to correctly teach those who are confused about the methods for attaining unexcelled enlightenment after having correctly entered the Great Vehicle <term>Mahāyāna</term>. It is also to cause the heedless to correctly hold these principles, to correctly encourage those who are discouraged, and to correctly delight those who have entered the path.

The number four is mentioned to avoid the concern that the teachings are too extensive, which might cause some to be unwilling to listen. By stating the number, they can be easily remembered. Furthermore, because patience and gentleness, which appear below, have the same purpose, they are not differentiated.

Although there are many categories for those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle, two names <note>Bodhisattva and Mahāsattva</note> are mentioned for three reasons: through aspiration, through application, and through realization.

How is it through aspiration? One is called a Bodhisattva because of aspiration toward profound objects of knowledge. One is called a Great Being <term>Mahāsattva</term> because of aspiration toward great power.

How is it through application? Because of striving for the sake of one's own unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and for the sake of completely protecting all sentient beings from suffering.

How is it through realization? Because enlightenment is realized through two strengths. What are these two? The strength of intelligence and the strength of diligence. One cannot realize enlightenment through ignorance or through minor diligence. For as long as one lives...

<summary>This page concludes Vasubandhu's commentary on the Six Gates and begins his commentary on the Four Dharmas Sūtra. It explains the purpose of the text and provides etymological reasons for the titles Bodhisattva and Mahāsattva.</summary>
<keywords>Vasubandhu, Four Dharmas, Bodhisattva, Mahāsattva, Mahayana, diligence, enlightenment</keywords>

A.text:
"should not abandon," this shows that these dharmas must be practiced continuously. By saying "even for the sake of one's life," it shows they must be practiced with great respect.

Why is it said there are "four" dharmas? Is it because they are neither too few nor too many? There are four dharmas that create obstacles to the accumulations of enlightenment, and these four serve as their remedies.

What are the four obstructing dharmas? They are: lack of interest, ignorance of the methods, lack of concern for sentient beings, and being oriented toward worldly objects. Again, there are four: not undertaking the work, undertaking it wrongly, abandoning the work, and being distracted from the work.

Furthermore, there are four dharmas that are conducive to the accumulations of enlightenment; these four are for the sake of providing a foundation for them. What are the four dharmas conducive to the accumulations of enlightenment? They are: the desire for instructions and teachings, the attainment of them, being a fit vessel for them, and their accomplishment.

Again, there are four: interest, knowledge of the methods, and accomplishment. Accomplishment here is of two kinds: bringing sentient beings to maturity and bringing the qualities of a Buddha to maturity.

Again, there are four: not abandoning the cycle of existence, being free from afflictions while within it, gathering sentient beings, and having purified diligence.

Furthermore, by four causes, one crosses over the path that is difficult to travel: the desire to go, knowledge of the path, not being bothered by weariness, and being heedful. In that way, one crosses over the path of the cycle of existence; these four are for the sake of providing the foundation for that.

Why are those who strive for the enlightenment of the <term>shravaka</term> <gloss>hearer</gloss> and <term>pratyekabuddha</term> <gloss>solitary realizer</gloss> not called bodhisattvas? It is because the name is established for that which has nothing higher, just like the sun <note>which is the preeminent source of light</note>.

In brief, the Blessed One has fully shown in this sutra the actions that are consistent for those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle, and how their results will not be in vain.

The Explanation of the Noble Four Dharmas, composed by the Master Vasubandhu, is complete.

B.text:
The phrase "never to give them up in the meantime" indicates that one should engage in these practices continuously. The phrase "even at the cost of one's life" indicates that they should be performed with great devotion.

One might ask: why are there four qualities? Why are they neither fewer nor more? 

There are four qualities that create obstacles to the accumulations of <term>bodhi</term> <gloss>enlightenment</gloss>. Thus, there are four qualities as their remedies. 

What are the four qualities that create obstacles? They are: 
1. Lacking the aspiration for the goal.
2. Not knowing the methods.
3. Not being oriented toward sentient beings.
4. Being oriented toward worldly objects.

Alternatively, there are another four:
1. Not undertaking the work.
2. Undertaking the work incorrectly.
3. Abandoning the work once started.
4. Being distracted while working.

Furthermore, there are four qualities that are conducive to the accumulations of enlightenment. There are four because they serve as the basis for those accumulations. What are the four qualities conducive to the accumulations of enlightenment? They are:
1. Desiring instruction and advice.
2. Obtaining those instructions.
3. Being a fit vessel for them.
4. Accomplishing them.

Again, there are four:
1. Having the aspiration for the goal.
2. Knowing the methods.
3. Practice <note>The text explains that practice is twofold: ripening sentient beings and ripening the qualities of a Buddha</note>.

There are yet another four:
1. Not abandoning <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss>.
2. Remaining untainted by afflictions while within it.
3. Gathering sentient beings.
4. Purifying one's diligence.

Furthermore, through four causes one crosses the path that is difficult to travel. These are:
1. The desire to go.
2. Knowing the path.
3. Not being discouraged by hardships.
4. Acting with conscientiousness.

In this way, one crosses the path of cyclic existence. There are four because they serve as the basis for that crossing.

Why is someone who strives for the enlightenment of a <term>shravaka</term> <gloss>pious hearer</gloss> or a <term>pratyekabuddha</term> <gloss>solitary realizer</gloss> not called a <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment being</gloss>? Because the name is established for that which has nothing superior to it, just as with the sun <note>original: "snang byed", the bringer of light</note>.

To summarize the meaning: in this <term>sutra</term> <gloss>scripture</gloss>, the Blessed One has fully shown the appropriate actions for those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle <note>Mahayana</note>, and how their results will not be lost.

The Explanation of the Noble Four Qualities composed by the Master Vasubandhu is complete.

<summary>This page concludes Vasubandhu’s commentary on the Four Qualities Sutra by categorizing the spiritual obstacles and remedies into groups of four. It emphasizes the unique status of the Bodhisattva path compared to other Buddhist paths and confirms that correct practice leads to certain results.</summary>
<keywords>Vasubandhu, Four Qualities, Bodhisattva, Samsara, Accumulations of Enlightenment, Mahayana, Buddhist Philosophy</keywords>

{D4377} In the language of India: <term>Arya Bhadra Charya Pranidhana Raja</term>. In the language of Tibet: <term>Phakpa Zangpo Chöpe Mönlam gyi Gyalpo</term> <gloss>The Sovereign Prayer of Exceptionally Good Conduct</gloss>.

I bow down to the youthful and noble Manjushri <note>the Bodhisattva of Wisdom</note>.

To all the Lions among Men <note>an epithet for the Buddhas</note> who have appeared in the three times <note>past, present, and future</note> within the worlds of the ten directions, I offer prostrations to every single one without exception, with a pure mind of body, speech, and soul.

By the power of this prayer for exceptionally good conduct, I manifest all the Victorious Ones <note>Buddhas</note> directly within my mind. With bodies as numerous as the atoms of the world, I bow deeply and offer prostrations to all the Victorious Ones.

Upon a single atom sit Buddhas as numerous as all atoms, each residing in the midst of the Sons of the Buddha <note>Bodhisattvas</note>. In this way, I am convinced that the entire expanse of reality <note>Dharmadhatu</note> is completely filled with the Victorious Ones.

With an ocean of inexhaustible praise, and through the sounds of an ocean of melodic branches, I describe the excellent qualities of all the Victorious Ones and sing the praises of all those who have gone to bliss <note>Sugatas</note>.

I offer to these Victorious Ones the finest flowers and the finest garlands, music, scented ointments, magnificent parasols, superior lamps, and the most excellent incense.

I offer to these Victorious Ones the finest garments and superior fragrances, and powdered perfumes piled as high as Mount Meru <note>the sacred mountain at the center of the universe</note>, all arranged in the most sublime and extraordinary displays.

Whatever offerings are unsurpassed and vast, I dedicate those with conviction to all the Victorious Ones. Through the power of my faith in exceptionally good conduct, I prostrate and offer to all the Victorious Ones.

Whatever sinful acts I have committed through the power of desire, hatred, and ignorance, whether by body, speech, or likewise by the mind, I now confess each and every one of them individually.

I rejoice in the merit of all the Victorious Ones of the ten directions, the Buddha’s Sons, the Solitary Realizers <note>Pratyekabuddhas</note>, those still training and those beyond training, and indeed all living beings.

To those who are the Lamps of the Worlds in the ten directions...

B.text:
{D4377}
In the language of India: <term>Arya Bhadracarya Pranidhana Raja</term> <gloss>The Noble King of Prayers for Excellent Conduct</gloss>
In the language of Tibet: <term>Phags pa bzang po spyod pa'i smon lam gyi rgyal po</term>

I pay homage to the youthful and noble Manjushri <note>the bodhisattva of wisdom</note>.

To all the lions among men <note>an epithet for Buddhas</note>, those who have gone before in the three times <note>past, present, and future</note> throughout the worlds of the ten directions, I pay homage to every one of them without exception, with body, speech, and a devoted mind.

By the power of this prayer for excellent conduct, I manifest all the Victorious Ones <note>Buddhas</note> clearly in my mind. With bodies as numerous as the atoms of the world, I bow deeply and pay homage to all the Victorious Ones.

Upon every single atom are Buddhas as numerous as all atoms, each sitting in the midst of the sons of Buddhas <note>bodhisattvas</note>. In this way, I am convinced that the entire sphere of phenomena <note>the <term>dharmadhatu</term></note> is entirely filled with Victorious Ones.

With an ocean of inexhaustible praise, through the sounds of an ocean of melodic parts, I express the qualities of all the Victorious Ones and praise all those who have gone to bliss <note>the <term>Sugatas</term></note>.

With the finest flowers and the finest garlands, with music, scented ointments, and supreme parasols, with the best lamps and the finest incense, I make offerings to those Victorious Ones.

With the finest garments and supreme fragrances, with powdered incense piled high as Mount Meru <note>the central mountain of Buddhist cosmology</note>, and with all kinds of supreme and extraordinary arrays, I make offerings to those Victorious Ones.

Whatever offerings are unsurpassed and vast, I have faith in them for all the Victorious Ones. Through the power of my faith in excellent conduct, I pay homage and make offerings to all the Victorious Ones.

Whatever negative actions I have committed through the influence of attachment, hatred, and ignorance, whether by body, speech, or likewise by mind, I individually confess every one of them.

In the merit of all the Victorious Ones of the ten directions, the sons of Buddhas, the solitary realizers <note><term>Pratyekabuddhas</term></note>, those in training, those beyond training <note><term>Arhats</term></note>, and all wandering beings, I rejoice.

To those who are the lights of the worlds in the ten directions <unclear>...</unclear>
